The Supreme Pontiff, however, personally reviewed this latest *schema* with the help of certain experts and in consultation with the pro-president of the Pontifical Commission for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law. After mature consideration the Supreme Pontiff decreed that the new Code was to be promulgated on January 25, 1983, i.e., the anniversary of the first announcement by Pope John XXIII of the undertaking of the Code's revision.

Since after nearly twenty years the pontifical commission established for this purpose has felicitously completed the difficult task entrusted to it, there is now available to pastors and other members of the Christian faithful the most recent law of the Church, which is characterised by simplicity, precision, elegance and true legal science. Furthermore, since it is fully pervaded by charity, equity, humanity and a true Christian spirit, it attempts to correspond to the divinely given external and internal characteristics of the Church. It also seeks to take cognisance of the conditions and needs of the contemporary world. But if on account of the excessively swift changes in contemporary human society certain elements of the new law become less perfect and require a new review, the Church is endowed with such a wealth of resources that, not unlike prior centuries, it will be able to undertake the task of renewing the laws of its life.

Now, however, the law can no longer be unknown. Pastors have at their disposal secure norms by which they may correctly direct the exercise of the sacred ministry. To each person is given a source of knowing his or her own proper rights and duties. Arbitrariness in acting can be precluded. Abuses which perhaps have crept into ecclesiastical discipline because of a lack of legislation can be more easily rooted out and prevented. Finally, all the works, institutes and initiatives of the apostolate may progress expeditiously and may be promoted since a healthy juridical organisation is quite necessary for the ecclesiastical community to live, grow and flourish. May our most gracious God grant this through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Mother of the Church, her spouse St. Joseph, Patron of the Church, and Saints Peter and Paul.

**\**
**CHAPTER III:\
PHYSICAL AND JURIDICAL PERSONS IN CANON LAW\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book I, canons 96-123; Book II, canons 204-206; Book III, canon 751; Book V, canon 1303; Book VI, canons 1331-1336.

**1. Notion of person in canon law**

For the purposes of determining who can hold rights and duties in the Church, the Code of Canon Law (canons 96-123) -- in common with secular legal systems -- recognises the existence of two kinds of "person": **the physical (human) person**, and **the juridical person**.

As will be seen below, by "juridical person" is meant a corporate body (such as an association, a foundation, a parish, a diocese, a seminary, etc.) which, without being a natural person, is nevertheless the holder of rights and duties. The juridical life of this body is independent of the human persons who happen to belong to it or who may represent it at any particular time.

> A thirteenth-century canon lawyer, Sinibaldo Fieschi (later to become Pope Innocent IV), was the first to understand that this type of body could be treated by the law in a similar way to a physical person: *fingatur una persona*: "let it be deemed a person".

In relation to rights and duties a distinction is to be drawn between **juridical capacity** -- the capacity to *hold* rights and duties -- and the **capacity to act** -- the capacity to *exercise* rights and duties: that is, to carry out acts that have juridical relevance. **Only the human person, capable of understanding and loving, can have capacity to act**, although not every person is capable of performing any juridical act.

> The fact that a child or someone with, for example, mental difficulties may not be capable of carrying out juridically binding acts does not prevent them from having rights based on their fundamental dignity as human beings.

Canon law establishes, for the performance of specific acts, a number of personal conditions that need to be fulfilled (see below).

Juridical persons, while having juridical capacity, do not act by themselves but through their representatives, who are human persons (acting not in their own name but in that of the body they represent, which is the true title-holder of rights and obligations).

**2. Physical persons**

**a) Rights and duties in the Church**

The Church, like every human society, recognises every individual as being capable of holding rights and duties (as having juridical capacity, as explained above). However, only those who are incorporated into the Church by means of baptism are members of the **faithful**, and have the rights and duties proper to Christians.

Canon 96[^5] states that one becomes a "person" in the Church by baptism, with the rights and duties proper to Christians. Canon 204 §1[^6] refers to "Christ's faithful" as those who are "incorporated into Christ through baptism". Both these canons refer to the same reality, namely that "persons in the Church" are those who are baptised: Christ's faithful.

Nevertheless, it is apparent from other parts of the Code that those who are not baptised (in particular, catechumens) can also be "persons in the Church", with limited rights and duties.

> In a sense a non-baptised person in relation to the Church is like a foreigner in relation to a State legal order: lacking the rights and duties of a citizen, but still recognised as a person.
>
> Those who are not baptised have rights and duties in the Church to the degree in which they enter into relationship with her. Examples include the rights and duties of catechumens (canons 206[^7], 788[^8], 1170[^9], 1183 §1[^10]); a non-baptised person married to a Catholic (canon 1135[^11]); those who acquire ecclesiastical property (canon 1255[^12]); the right of every person to be evangelised and therefore to be baptised (canons 748[^13], 851[^14]); and procedural rights (canon 1476[^15]).
>
> The unborn also have rights that are recognised and protected: see canons 864[^16], 871[^17], and 1397 §2[^18].

**b) Factors affecting a physical person's capacity to exercise rights and duties**

A physical person's capacity to *exercise* his or her rights and duties (capacity to act) may be affected by the following factors:

**(i) Ecclesiastical communion**

Canon 205[^19] sets out the fundamental requirements for full communion, namely, unity with the Church through the bonds of profession of faith, the sacraments and ecclesiastical governance. **Apostates** (completely lacking in communion), **heretics** (lacking communion in faith) and **schismatics** (lacking communion in governance: see canon 751[^20] for the definitions), are not "faithful" in a full sense (even though they remain "faithful" in the sense of having been baptised). Consequently their rights within the Church are suspended until they return to full communion.

**(ii) Lawfully imposed sanctions**

There may be other situations -- specifically, offences committed by members of the faithful -- which lead to the imposition of penalties restricting the exercise of their rights. In this connection the canons on excommunication (canon 1331), interdict (canon 1332), suspension (canons 1333-1334), and prohibitions and deprivations (canon 1336) are of particular relevance. These penalties involve the suspension of certain rights. The most serious of them, excommunication, excludes the faithful from ecclesiastical communion.

> For fuller details refer to chapter XXX on Canonical Offences and Punishments, where the text of these canons is provided in the footnotes.

**(iii) Personal circumstances**

There are a number of personal situations which affect whether or not rights can be exercised. These include:

- **Age** (cf. canons 97[^21] and 98[^22]): for example. a person must be 21 to make a perpetual religious profession (canon 658 1º [^23]); a priest must be 25 (canon 1031 §1[^24]); a bishop must be 35 (canon 378 §1, 3º [^25]);

- **Use of reason** (cf. canon 99[^26]): use of reason is a prerequisite, for example, for making one's first Communion (canon 914[^27]), for marrying validly (canon 1095 1º [^28]), or for being held fully or partially responsible for an offence (canons 1323 6º [^29] and 1324 §1, 1º-2º [^30]);

- **Territory** (cf. canons 100-102[^31]): the concepts of "domicile" and "quasi-domicile" determine where a person is considered to be "based" juridically, and consequently who his or her proper parish priest and bishop are (see canon 107 §1[^32]), unless these are determined by rite (canon 372 §2[^33]) or language (canon 518[^34]). Domicile and quasi-domicile are also relevant for determining the competent tribunal for a marriage nullity case (cf. the new canon 1672[^35], as established by the 2015 *motu proprio* [*Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20150815_mitis-iudex-dominus-iesus.html)), and in relation to the faculty to hear confessions (canons 967 §2[^36] and 971[^37])

- **Relationship** (cf. canons 108[^38]-109[^39]): certain kinds of relationships arising through blood (consanguinity: e.g. uncles, aunts, first cousins) or marriage (affinity: e.g. in-laws, step-children) constitute an impediment to marriage (canons 1091[^40] and 1092[^41]: see chapter XXVII on the Sacrament of Marriage), or may exempt from the duty to testify (canon 1548 §2, 2º [^42]); they may also be a reason for raising an objection against a particular judge (canons 1448[^43] and 1449 §1[^44]);

- **Rite** (cf. canons 111[^45]-112[^46], as amended by the *motu proprio* [*De Concordia inter Codices*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/la/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20160531_de-concordia-inter-codices.html), 31 May 2016): this determines whether a Catholic belongs to the Latin Church or to one of the Eastern Catholic Churches (this is especially important for the celebration of the sacrament of marriage). Normally the faithful belong to the rite in which they have received baptism.

> In canon 111 §§1-2 various scenarios involving the baptism of children are envisaged: a) if both parents are Latin-rite Catholics, the child baptised belongs to the Latin rite; b) if one parent is Latin-rite and the other belongs to another Catholic Church *sui iuris*, the parents can agree to the child belonging to the Latin Church; but if they cannot mutually agree, the child belongs to the Church *sui iuris* to which the father belongs; c) if one parent is Catholic and the other is not, the child belongs to the Church *sui iuris* of the Catholic parent.
>
> A person over the age of fourteen who wishes to be baptised can freely choose to be baptised in the Latin Church or in another Church *sui iuris*, and belongs to the rite he or she has chosen (canon 111 §3).
>
> After baptism one can change rite by permission of the Holy See; by reason of marrying a person of another rite; or in certain cases by choice (cf. canon 112).
>
> The importance of rite can be seen, for example, in relation to the constitution of particular Churches (canon 372 §2[^47]) and personal parishes (canon 518[^48]); and it forms the basis of the obligation of the minister to celebrate the sacraments in accordance with his own rite (canon 846 §2[^49]) (see also canons 29-38 of the [*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf));

- **Sex**: for example, only a male may be ordained (canon 1024[^50]; cf. John Paul II's Letter [*Ordinatio sacerdotalis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_letters/1994/documents/hf_jp-ii_apl_19940522_ordinatio-sacerdotalis.html), 22 May 1994); there are different minimum ages for men and women for marriage (canon 1083 §1[^51]); the matrimonial impediment of abduction applies only when it is the woman who has been abducted (canon 1089[^52]).

- **Status or condition in the Church**: some faithful acquire the clerical condition, giving rise to specific rights and duties as clerics; some consecrate themselves to God through the evangelical counsels, thereby acquiring new rights and obligations; etc.

**3. Juridical persons**

**a) Corporations and foundations**

As previously seen, it is not only the physical person that is capable of holding rights and duties: there are also entities -- corporate bodies -- which, without being natural persons, have juridical capacity and are known as **juridical persons**.

Juridical persons in the Church are divided into **corporations** (*universitates personarum*, where the underlying basis is a community or aggregate of persons) and **foundations** (*universitates rerum*, where the basis is an aggregate of goods -- a patrimony): see canon 115[^53].

> The 1917 Code distinguished between physical and moral persons. This terminology is not retained in the 1983 Code, expect in relation to the Church and the Apostolic See: cf. canon 113 §1[^54].

For a **corporation** at least three physical persons are required. It is called **collegial** when its members take part in its most important decisions; otherwise it is **non-collegial**. Examples of collegial juridical persons are the cathedral chapter, an association of the faithful, or an episcopal conference. Canon 119[^55] deals with collegial acts in relation to elections and other matters. Examples of non-collegial juridical persons are the diocese and the parish.

**Foundations** may arise, for example, as a result of a stable endowment for the purposes of worship, charity, etc. A canonical foundation with juridical personality is called an **autonomous foundation**, and acts through its own organs of governance (one or more physical persons, or a college). If it does not have personality of its own, but belongs or is linked to a corporation, it is a **non-autonomous foundation** (cf. canon 1303 §1[^56]).

**b) Establishment and purposes of juridical persons**

Juridical persons in the Church need to have purposes befitting the mission and life of the Church (cf. canon 114[^57], which refers to works of piety, the apostolate and charity, whether spiritual or temporal).

The Catholic Church and the Apostolic See have juridical personality "by divine disposition" (canon 113 §1[^58]), by which is meant that their origin is independent of any human law or authority.

Other ecclesiastical entities acquire juridical personality by law or by decree of the competent authority:

- those that automatically acquire juridical personality by law include dioceses, parishes, seminaries, etc.;

- those that acquire juridical personality by decree might include, for example, a group of persons who wish to form an association and who ask the diocesan bishop for the relevant decree.

Juridical persons are in principle perpetual, but can be extinguished by the relevant authority, or by inactivity for a hundred years, or in other ways determined in the statutes (cf. canons 120[^59], 123[^60]). Juridical persons can also be merged or divided: cf. canons 121[^61], 122[^62].

**c) Public and private juridical persons**

One of the novelties of the 1983 Code is that juridical persons can be either **public** or **private.**

**Public juridical persons** (canon 116 §1[^63]) are established by the competent ecclesiastical authority and act in the name of the Church (e.g. a diocese or a seminary).

**Private juridical persons** (i.e. those which are not public: canon 116 §1) arise out of the private initiative of the faithful, who run them under their own responsibility, without officially committing the Church and the hierarchy.

All juridical persons act through their representatives: the diocesan bishop, for example, represents the diocese (canon 393[^64]); the parish priest represents the parish (canon 532[^65]). In the case of private juridical persons, the representatives are determined by the statutes (canon 118[^66]).

**d) Entities without personality**

Juridical personality is an instrument which the law uses to enable entities distinct from physical persons to act at law as a single subject.

There can, however, be entities distinct from individual persons which have not yet acquired juridical personality, but which nevertheless have a certain relevance within the canonical order.

An example is to be found in canon 310[^67], which speaks of a private association which has not been constituted as a juridical person, in which "the faithful who are joined together in it can jointly contract obligations. As joint owners and joint possessors they can acquire and possess rights and goods. They can exercise these rights and obligations through a delegate or proxy."

See also canon 433 §2[^68], which implies that an ecclesiastical region (a grouping of ecclesiastical provinces) may or may not have juridical personality.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the advantages in canon law of being able to treat certain groups of people or things as though they constituted a single corporate body?

2\. What is the difference between a corporation and a foundation?

**\**
**CHAPTER IV:\
LAWS, CUSTOMS, AND ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book I, canons 7-95, 124-144; Book II, canons 331, 336-367, 381, 391.
>
> St Thomas Aquinas, [*Summa Theologiae*, I-II, q.95 a.2](https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2095.htm)*.*
>
> Benedict XVI's [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2012/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20120121_rota-romana.html), 21 January 2012.

**1. Separation of powers in canon law**

Although in civil society the legislative, executive (or administrative) and judicial powers of government are to a greater or lesser extent independent of one another, in the Church these powers are, by the Will of Christ, concentrated in the holders of supreme power: the Pope and the College of Bishops for the universal Church, and the bishop for the particular Church.

However, in accordance with the seventh of the Guiding Principles for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law[^69] (see the Appendix to chapter II), in practice the administrative and judicial functions are generally delegated to different bodies, so that at the level of the *exercise* of each of the powers, the principle of separation is observed in the Church to the extent possible.

The judicial function will be studied at a later stage. In this chapter, after a reference to what is meant by a "juridical act", attention will be paid primarily to the provisions of the 1983 Code that deal with acts of legislative and executive (administrative) power.

**2. Juridical acts and private autonomy**

**a) Juridical acts**

A juridical act is any declaration of will or knowledge which has juridical relevance (e.g. a will, a contract, a singular decree, a judicial sentence: cf. canons 124-128[^70]).

An act of this nature may emanate from the **ecclesiastical authority**, or it may be an act of **private autonomy** (such as a contract or will, or the setting up of an association, or incorporation into the clerical state or consecrated life).

**b) Private autonomy: the sphere of liberty and normative power**

"Private autonomy" refers to the juridical power which the person has to regulate freely the juridical relationships that correspond to his or her sphere of personal freedom and initiative: see for example canons 211[^71] (freedom in making known the message of salvation), 215[^72] (freedom of association), 219[^73] (freedom to choose a state in life), and 227[^74] (freedom in secular affairs).

A typical instance of private autonomy is a contract, which acquires legal force as between the parties, provided it conforms to certain requirements established by the legal order.

> Note that canon law does not "grant" spheres of autonomy but rather "recognises" them, although it needs to determine which acts are proper to the private sphere and which are not.

The public authority also needs to set limits or boundaries to freedom, within the limits set out by divine law or the prudent judgement of the authority, for example by prohibiting activities considered unsuitable in certain cases or for certain individuals (cf. canons 278 §3[^75], 285 §3[^76], 286[^77]), or determining the substantial content of the matter agreed between the parties (e.g. marriage: cf. canons 1055-1056[^78]), or requiring the intervention of the hierarchy to give effect to certain acts of private autonomy (for example, approval of the statutes of a private association as a requirement for the granting of juridical personality: cf. canon 322[^79]).

**c) Acts of autonomy** **relating to the establishment of private juridical persons**

Of particular importance in canon law are the acts of autonomy whereby private juridical persons, such as associations of the faithful, are established, as also are the acts of joining or being incorporated into such juridical persons.

The establishment, governance and operation of private juridical persons are governed by their statutes (cf. canon 94[^80]).

**d) Other examples of private autonomy**

Among the many examples of acts of private autonomy are the following:

- canon 1057[^81] (marriage contracts);

- canon 1290[^82] (patrimonial contracts, in which the Church accepts into canon law the corresponding civil laws);

- canon 296[^83] (joining a personal prelature);

- canon 1026[^84] (being ordained);

- canon 656[^85] (entering into consecrated life).

**3. Singular administrative acts**

**a) Concept of the singular administrative act**

In State law, the concept of the singular administrative act was introduced after the French Revolution to refer to unilateral executory decisions issued by the administrative authority ("executory" meaning that the decision is effective without the need for any action on the part of the person affected).

In canon law, although administrative acts have always existed, the concept was not very clearly worked out until recent times, as there was no real distinction between the different powers (legislative, judicial and executive), nor any system of recourse different from judicial recourse.

The 1917 Code prohibited judicial recourse against administrative acts of the bishop, and any recourse in such cases had to be made to the relevant dicastery of the Roman Curia as an administrative matter. In 1967 the possibility of a contentious-administrative recourse (that is, a judicial resolution of a dispute arising out of an administrative act) was introduced.

The Apostolic Constitution *Regimini Ecclesiae Universae* \[REU\], no. 106 authorised a judicial recourse to the Apostolic Signatura in order to resolve conflicts arising out of "acts of the ecclesiastical administrative power" (once the matter had been unsuccessfully referred to the relevant dicastery of the Roman Curia).

The 1983 Code uses terminology similar to that of REU in canons 1400 §2[^86] and 1445 §2[^87]. More importantly, Title IV of Book I (canon 35-93) is headed "Singular Administrative Acts", and for the first time regulates such acts. In addition, Section I, Part V of Book VII (canons 1732-1739 -- these canons will be looked at in chapter XXXI on The Protection of Rights in the Church) establishes the "hierarchical recourse procedure" against administrative acts.

> The 1988 Apostolic Constitution *Pastor Bonus* superseded REU and dealt with judicial recourses against administrative acts in art. 123. *Pastor Bonus* has in its turn been superseded by the Apostolic Letter [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html) of 19 March 2022, which deals with the matter in its no. 197 §2.

**b) Characteristics of the singular administrative act**

The singular administrative act is:

- a **juridical act**: a declaration of the will aimed at producing juridical effects;

- **unilateral**: a declaration of the will of the authority alone (therefore excluding contracts, etc.); cf. canons 35[^88], 48[^89], 59[^90];

- "**singular**": i.e. for a concrete situation or person, not a norm of a general nature for an indeterminate number of cases or persons;

- **extrajudicial**: it is not part of a judicial process;

- **issued by the** **executive (administrative) authority**: cf. canons 35, 48, 59, 76[^91].

As will be seen below, the 1983 Code reserves the granting of certain administrative acts to the legislator: see canon 90[^92]; also canons 35, 76.

**c) Types of administrative act**

**(i) Singular decree and singular precept**

The **singular decree** is the principal type of administrative act. By it "a decision is given or a provision made for a particular case; of its nature this decision does not presuppose that a petition has been made by anyone" (canon 48).

The **singular precept** is referred to in canon 49[^93]. It can sometimes take the form of a **penal precept** (canons 1314[^94], 1319[^95]) by which the authority attaches a penalty for non-fulfilment of the precept.

**(ii) Rescript**

The rescript is dealt with in canon 59 §1[^96]:

- it involves a **response to a request** (cf. canons 60[^97], 61[^98]);

- it is given **in writing** (canon 59 §2[^99]);

- it contains **the granting of a privilege, dispensation or other favour**;

- it sets out the **reasons** **for granting what is requested** (cf. canon 63 §2[^100] on "obreption");

- it has the immediate purpose of **conferring a benefit on one or several specific persons**.

**(iii) Privilege**

A privilege (canon 76[^101]) goes against or beyond the general law, and is defined as "a favour given by a special act for the benefit of certain persons, physical or juridical".

It can be perpetual (which is normally the case) or temporary; personal (attaching to a person) or real (attaching to a thing or place: canon 78[^102]).

Although it is an administrative act, the one granting it also needs legislative power (canon 76 §1).

Canon 59 §1[^103] refers to the rescript as being the appropriate administrative act for granting a privilege.

In canon law there are many "favourable" laws: some confer advantages on certain kinds of person directly; other such laws do so indirectly, in that they bestow power on the ecclesiastical authority to confer advantages in concrete cases. In such cases the conferral would constitute an administrative act, and what is conferred is a privilege or a dispensation (see, for example, canons 858 §2[^104], 905 §2[^105], 930 §1[^106], 936[^107]).

**(iv) Dispensation**

A dispensation is the relaxation of a merely ecclesiastical law in a particular case (canon 85[^108]). It is a type of privilege granted by one who has executive power, in the form of a rescript (canon 59).

Faculties which the bishop has for dispensing are specified in canons 14[^109], 87[^110], 88[^111], 1047 §4[^112], 1078-1080[^113], 1127 §2[^114], 1196[^115], and 1203[^116].

Other clerics have certain faculties for dispensing: cf. canons 89[^117], 1079[^118], 1196[^119], 1245[^120], etc. (powers given by the law); and canon 131[^121] (powers given by delegation).

A just and reasonable cause is required (canon 90[^122]).

Canon 86[^123] specifies which laws do not allow dispensation. Some laws are not dispensable by certain authorities (e.g. the bishop cannot dispense from procedural laws or other laws whose dispensation is reserved to the Apostolic See: canon 87[^124]).

**(v) Administrative silence**

Canon 57[^125] states that if a reply to a request has not been received within three months (or other specified period: cf. canon 1735[^126]) a negative reply is presumed.

**4. Canonical norms and laws**

**a) Canonical norms**

The term "norm" here is used as distinct from a juridical "act".

A norm in general is an **objective rule of law (written or unwritten)** which is not exhausted in a single application (as would happen in the case of an act such as a decision of the bishop, a sentence given by the judge, or a contract between two parties).

**b) Characteristics of canonical norms**

A norm is an **ordinance of reason promulgated by the authority for the common good** (cf. St Thomas Aquinas, [ST I-II, q.95, a.2](https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2095.htm)):

- its principal feature is therefore **rationality;**

- it must be made by the **competent authority;**

- it must serve the **common good;**

- and it must be **promulgated** (cf. canons 7-8: see below).

**c) Canonical laws**

A **law** is a **general written norm**, promulgated by one who has legislative power. Laws are the most important canonical norms, and generally prevail over all other norms.

The 1983 Code deals with the requirements and characteristics of canonical laws in canons 7-22.

**d) Legislative power**

Legislators, or the "active subjects of canon laws", can be **universal** or **particular**.

**(i) Universal legislators** are:

- the **Roman Pontiff** when he passes a law for the whole Church (cf. canon 331[^127]);

- the **College of Bishops** (normally acting through an ecumenical council: cf. canons 336[^128], 337[^129]).

> The most solemn laws issued by the Pope are generally in the form of an Apostolic Constitution. The Pope may also issue laws by means of an Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* (literally, "on his own impulse"). Other papal documents such as Encyclicals and Apostolic Exhortations tend to be of a more doctrinal nature.
>
> An example of an Apostolic Constitution is [*Anglicanorum Coetibus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apc_20091104_anglicanorum-coetibus.html), 4 November 2009, providing for the possibility of Personal Ordinariates for Anglicans wishing to join the Catholic Church. An Apostolic Constitution is the normal means by which the Pope erects a new diocese or particular Church. Recent examples include [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html), 19 March 2022, on the reform of the Roman Curia (to be dealt with in chapter XI) and [*Pascite gregem Dei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/papa-francesco_costituzione-ap_20210523_pascite-gregem-dei.html), 23 May 2021 (to be dealt with in chapter XXX).
>
> The *motu proprio* is Pope Francis's favoured way of introducing legislative changes. Since the start of his pontificate he has issued over 50 such documents: some of the more significant ones are [*Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20150815_mitis-iudex-dominus-iesus.html) of 15 August 2015, reforming the marriage nullity process; [*As a Loving Mother*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20160604_come-una-madre-amorevole.html) of 4 June 2016 on the bishop's duty of vigilance in protecting children and vulnerable adults; [*Maiorem hac dilectionem*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20170711_maiorem-hac-dilectionem.html) of 11 July 2017 on the heroic offering of life as a cause for the beatification and canonisation procedure; [*Spiritus Domini*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio-20210110_spiritus-domini.html) of 10 January 2021 regarding access of women to the ministries of lector and acolyte; [*Traditionis custodes*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20210716-motu-proprio-traditionis-custodes.html) of 16 July 2021 on the use of the Roman liturgy prior to the reform of 1970; [*Ad charisma tuendum*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20220714-motu-proprio-ad-charisma-tuendum.html) of 14 July 2022 concerning the charism of Opus Dei; and *[Vos estis lux mundi](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20230325-motu-proprio-vos-estis-lux-mundi-aggiornato.html)* (updated version) of 25 March 2023 on reporting and investigating crimes of sexual abuse. In addition he issued a number of Apostolic Letters *motu proprio* effecting changes to the Roman Curia, which were to culminate in the Apostolic Constitution [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html) of 19 March 2022, mentioned above.

**(ii) Particular legislators** are:

- the **Roman Pontiff** and the **College of Bishops** when they pass a law for a particular territory or group of faithful;

- the **diocesan bishop** (cf. canon 391 §2[^130]);

- the **heads of other hierarchical structures equivalent to dioceses** (cf. canon 381 §2[^131]);

- **particular councils**, which can be **plenary** (canon 439 §1[^132]: involving all the particular Churches in the same Episcopal Conference), or **provincial** (canon 440 §1[^133]: involving particular Churches belonging to the same ecclesiastical province); cf. canon 445[^134], which refers specifically to the particular Council's legislative power;

- **episcopal conferences**, within certain limits, and for specified matters: cf. canon 455 §1[^135]. Examples are to be found in canons 284[^136], 522[^137], 844[^138], 1031 §3[^139], 1251[^140] and elsewhere.

**e) Legislative decrees and statutes established or promulgated by virtue of legislative power**

Canon 29[^141] states that **a general decree** issued by a competent legislator is **a** **true law**, and is governed by the canons on laws.

**Statutes** -- which are **norms for juridical persons** -- if established and promulgated by virtue of legislative power **are also** **governed by the canons on laws** (cf. canon 94 §3[^142]).

**f) Delegated legislative power**

Although the legislator normally legislates directly, there are instances in which he delegates the power of legislating to another (cf. canon 135 §2[^143]). In such cases one who has executive authority may issue a law (a general decree), provided the requirements of canon 30[^144] are met, namely:

- the power applies to particular cases;

- the legislator has given express authorisation;

- the conditions prescribed in the act of authorisation are observed.

**g) The "canonical order"**

Canon law, or the "canonical order", is a wider notion than that of "the Code of Canon Law". There are many norms which fall outside the Code of Canon Law; and in any event care should be taken to avoid adopting a merely positivist outlook that would attribute value to laws purely on the basis of the human power issuing them.

The canonical order is the fruit of the systematic study of the various aspects of canon law (law of the person, patrimonial law, sacramental law, penal law, etc.) which are brought together to form a unified and interconnected corpus.

**5. Efficacy of canon laws**

**a) Promulgation and "vacatio legis"**

If it is to be obeyed, the law needs to be accurately known. **Promulgation** is the way in which a law is officially made known to those for whom it is intended: cf. canon 7[^145].

Canon 8[^146] makes a distinction between universal and particular laws (see below). The term *vacatio legis* is used to refer to the time between the official publication of the law and its coming into force. In principle, unless the legislator indicates otherwise, this period is three months for universal laws and one month for particular laws.

**b) Passive subjects of canon laws**

By "passive subject" of the law is meant a person for whom the law is intended.

Canon 11[^147] states that to be a passive subject of a merely ecclesiastical law one must be baptised or received in the Catholic Church, have sufficient use of reason, and unless the law expressly states otherwise have completed seven years of age.

**c) Binding force of canon laws**

Canon laws, like every just law, of course oblige in conscience. From a juridical point of view canon laws may command, prohibit, permit, penalise or invalidate (or incapacitate).

In relation to invalidating and incapacitating laws canon 10 establishes: "Only those laws are to be considered invalidating or incapacitating which expressly prescribe that an act is null or that a person is incapable."

Some examples from among the many invalidating laws in the Code:

- canon 125 §1: "An act is invalid if performed as a result of force imposed from outside on a person who was quite unable to resist it";

- canon 135 §2: "A lower legislator cannot validly make a law which is contrary to that of a higher legislator";

- canon 149 §3: "The provision of an office made as a result of simony, is invalid by virtue of the law itself";

- canon 1003: "Every priest, but only a priest, can validly administer the anointing of the sick".

Some examples of incapacitating laws:

- canon 97 §2: "A minor who has not completed the seventh year of age is called an infant and is considered incapable of personal responsibility";

- canon 171 §1: "The following are legally incapable of casting a vote: 1° one incapable of a human act; 2° one lacking active voice; 3° one who is excommunicated, whether by judgement of a court or by a decree whereby this penalty is imposed or declared; 4° one who notoriously defected from communion with the Church";

- canon 1073: "A diriment impediment renders a person incapable of validly contracting a marriage";

- canon 1095: "The following are incapable of contracting marriage: 1° those who lack sufficient use of reason; 2° those who suffer from a grave lack of discretionary judgement concerning the essential matrimonial rights and obligations to be mutually given and accepted; 3° those who, because of causes of a psychological nature, are unable to assume the essential obligations of marriage".

**d) Non-retroactivity of the law**

The principle of non-retroactivity of the law means that "laws concern matters of the future, not those of the past, unless provision is made in them for the latter by name" (canon 9).

Retroactivity may apply in respect of some offences, where this proves more favourable to an offender (cf. canon 1313[^148]).

**e) Universal and particular laws**

Universal laws are for the whole Church, and are issued by those who have power for this kind of law, namely the Roman Pontiff and the College of Bishops.

Particular laws are those which apply only within a specified territory or to certain individuals.

**f) Personal and territorial laws**

A law can be issued in respect of those who live in a certain place (territorial) or those who have some personal characteristic (personal); the latter would include, for example, members of the Armed Forces, emigrants, or those who belong to a particular rite: cf. canons 12-13[^149]; 100[^150].

**g) Doubt, ignorance and error about the law**

According to canon 14[^151], laws do not oblige when there is a **doubt of law** (e.g. where it is not clear whether a law has been abrogated by a contrary custom, or whether it applies to this or that concrete situation). Traditionally it is considered that the doubt should be positive -- i.e. supported by reasons -- objective and probable.

If there is a **doubt of fact** (e.g. as to whether a person is baptised, or has jurisdiction) the Ordinary can dispense (if it is a dispensable ecclesiastical law), provided, if it involves a reserved dispensation, it is one that would normally be granted (cf. canon 87 §2[^152]).

Doubt tends to nullify the force of a law; but in some cases the public good demands that this should not be so: cf. canon 1060[^153] on the *favor iuris* in respect of marriage; canon 1084 §2[^154] on the right to contract marriage where there is a doubtful impediment of impotence).

Canon law is also quite sensitive (unlike civil legal systems) to **ignorance** and **error**: this is because if affects not only external conduct but also the realm of the conscience.

**Ignorance is not presumed** (canon 15 §2[^155]); but if there really is ignorance, and it is not culpable, then it impedes the efficacy of the law, except in the case of incapacitating and invalidating laws, when ignorance does not prevent the effect of those laws.

However, in some instances of **common error** (error into which anyone could fall, without malice or fault, because it is based on a public fact having the appearance of truth) the Church "supplies" for the invalidity of the act (cf. canons 144[^156], 883[^157], 966[^158], 1111 §1[^159]).

In relation to **penal laws** error and ignorance have a significant influence (cf. canons 1323-1325, to be studied in chapter XXX on Canonical Offences and Punishments).

**h) Interpretation and "lacunae legis"**

Interpretation of the law is an intellectual operation which attempts to discover its genuine meaning. This operation is needed when it is necessary to discover the true sense and scope of the legal text, for its correct application.

The principles on doubt, ignorance and error in canons 14[^160] and 15[^161] need to be taken into account.

The principal types of interpretation are:

- **authentic interpretation**, which is made by the legislator himself or the one whom the legislator has given power to interpret authentically (cf. canon 16 §1[^162]) and which has the force of the law itself. [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html) (cf. art. 175-178) gives this power, for universal laws, to the Dicastery for Legislative Texts; at the request of interested parties, it can also determine whether laws or general decrees issued by legislators below the level of the Roman Pontiff are in conformity with the Church's universal law (art. 181).

- an authentic interpretation can be **declaratory** (declaring the clear meaning of the law), **explanatory** (explaining a doubtful law), **restrictive** (limiting the scope of the law) or **extensive** (broadening its scope). In the last three cases authentic interpretation does not have retroactive effect (cf. canon 16 §2[^163]);

- **interpretation by judicial sentence or administrative act**, which does not have the force of law but refers only to a specific case and is a response to a doubt or conflict which has arisen over a doubtful or contested fact. It binds only those persons and affects those matters for which it was given (cf. canon 16 §3[^164]);

- **other criteria** for interpretation appear in canon 17: "Ecclesiastical laws are to be understood according to the proper meaning of the words considered in their text and context. If the meaning remains doubtful or obscure, there must be recourse to parallel places, if there be any, to the purpose and circumstances of the law, and to the mind of the legislator"

  - "parallel places": means other texts dealing with the same (not "similar") matter;

  - "circumstances of the law": occasion, time, place, etc.;

  - for some laws there are also specific criteria for interpretation: e.g. penal laws and laws which restrict the free exercise of rights or contain an exception to the law: these are to be interpreted strictly (cf. canon 18[^165]); these criteria are a practical application of the principle *favorabilia amplianda, odiosa restringenda* -- benefits are to be expanded, burdens to be restricted;

- canon 19[^166] gives criteria to be considered when there is no express provision of law on a specific matter.

> On the authentic interpretation of laws, see Pope Benedict XVI's [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2012/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20120121_rota-romana.html) of 21 January 2012.

**i) Revocation of the law**

The law can be revoked by the legislator himself.

Canon 20[^167] deals with the ways in which a later law may revoke an earlier one:

The later law may **expressly revoke** the earlier one (e.g. canon 6 §1[^168]); it may **directly contradict** the earlier one (in such cases canon 21[^169] should be taken into account); or it may **integrally reorder** the whole subject matter of the earlier law (examples of where this has *not* happened are canons 335[^170], 346 §1[^171], 360[^172], which refer to special laws that are remained in force when the 1983 Code of Canon Law was promulgated).

Sometimes there is doubt as to whether a matter has been integrally reordered or not.

**6. Customs**

**a) Nature and function of custom in canon law**

Customs and usages are part of the life of people and communities; they establish models of conduct commonly accepted as just, and which are therefore to be respected.

**Canonical custom** refers to a general norm (such as a law) introduced through community use, whose juridical efficacy is confirmed by the legislator.

It involves a **material element** -- the community usage -- and a **formal element** -- the conditions by which that conduct can truly be considered a juridical norm.

**b) Types of custom**

Customs can be

- *secundum legem* (according to the law), confirming what the law disposes. If there are several ways of fulfilling the law, custom can "consecrate" one of them: in this sense it is said to be the best interpreter of the law (cf. canon 27[^173]);

- *contra legem* (against the law), putting a contrary usage in place of the law. For this to be valid it must be observed for 30 complete and continuous years. If it is against a law which forbids contrary customs this period becomes 100 years (cf. canon 26[^174]);

- *praeter legem* (apart from the law), in respect of matters not regulated by the law. The time required is also 30 years (cf. canon 26).

**c) Requirements for customs**

Canon 23[^175] says that a custom has the force of law only if it is approved by the legislator, in accordance with the canons that follow.

Canon 24[^176] requires **reasonableness**: a custom, like a law, should be an *ordinatio rationis* -- thus its basis as a norm is not its repeated use but its truth and rationality, i.e. its justice. Thus it must respect above all divine law (cf. canon 24 §1).

> Customs expressly reprobated by the law are not reasonable (cf. canon 24 §2; see e.g. canons 423 §1[^177]; 526 §2[^178]; 1076[^179]); nor are those that are indecent, lead to sin, affect aspects of the Church's life which even though disciplinary pertain to the mystery of the Church (e.g. customs against priestly celibacy), harm the constitutional and organisational structure of the Church, or impede the exercise of power.

There must also be the intention on the part of the community of being bound -- the *animus iuris inducendi*, the intention to introduce the custom.

> The *animus* of the community thus means the intention to introduce "law", a norm (cf. canon 25[^180]). If the conduct is the fruit of some other intention -- apathy, indifference, etc. -- it is not a custom in the juridical sense.

It is the bishop's duty to be on guard against the introduction of abuses (cf. canon 392 §2[^181]).

> Cf. also the Instruction *[Redemptionis Sacramentum](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccdds/documents/rc_con_ccdds_doc_20040423_redemptionis-sacramentum_en.html)* issued by the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments on 25 March 2004, dealing with "certain matters to be observed or to be avoided regarding the Most Holy Eucharist".

**7. Normative activity of the ecclesiastical Administration**

**a) Legislative activity and executive or administrative activity in the Church**

A fundamental principle of the Church's constitution is the unity of power in the Roman Pontiff and the diocesan Bishops. The power of government is one.

As mentioned earlier, a distinction is drawn between the legislative, executive (administrative) and judicial functions: cf. canons 135 §1[^182], 391 §1[^183]. This does not imply any partition of power, contrary to divine law, but a delineation within the Church's organisation of the different functions of government.

In broad terms, legislative power consists in the possibility of issuing general norms; executive (or administrative) power in that of satisfying specific and practical needs; and judicial power in resolving conflicts impartially and independently. Nevertheless, it is possible for the executive authority to issue general norms, subject to certain precise conditions.

A key principle in administrative activity is subordination to the law, meaning that acts of executive power are accessory and inferior to the law. Thus they cannot change or contradict the law; if they do, they are invalid.

Administrative authorities and organisms include those who exercise executive power and who jointly or individually receive the name of "Public Ecclesiastical Administration".

**b) Normative power of the ecclesiastical Administration**

> **Legislative decrees**: in accordance with canon 30[^184], an executive authority can issue general decrees having the force of law (cf. canon 29[^185]) when it has received appropriate delegation (cf. canon 135 §2[^186]).
>
> **Executory norms**: these are aimed at developing, completing or implementing a law. They can be:

- **general executory decrees**: in accordance with canon 31[^187], these can be issued by executive authorities within the limits of their competence, in order to "define more precisely the manner of applying a law, or ... urge the observance of laws": cf. canons 32-33[^188];

- **instructions**: according to canon 34[^189], these can be issued by the competent executive authority and are aimed at those whose job it is to ensure the fulfilment of laws. They have a double objective: to clarify the content of laws and to develop the manner in which the laws are to be put into effect.

? QUESTIONS

1\. Why is it more accurate to speak of a "distinction of powers" in the Church, rather than a strict "separation of powers"?

2\. What is meant by the terms "singular administrative act", "singular decree", "singular precept", "rescript", "privilege", and "dispensation"?

3\. Who may issue universal and particular laws in the Church?

4\. What are the conditions for the introduction of a canonical custom?

**\**
**CHAPTER V:\
RIGHTS AND DUTIES OF THE FAITHFUL\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 204-223.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 31.

**1. Notion of "faithful"**

Through baptism a person is incorporated in the Church and acquires the condition of "faithful" (*Christifidelis*): see canon 204 §1[^190].

Canon 208 states that "there is a genuine equality of dignity and action among all of Christ's faithful. Because of this equality they all contribute, each according to his or her own condition and office, to the building up of the Body of Christ".

> This fundamental equality of all the faithful applies at the **personal level** (all are children of God), the **social level** (all have the same faith, sacraments and governance) and the **juridical level** (all have the same fundamental rights and duties).

**2. The faithful's participation in the Church's mission**

Canon 204 §1 goes on to say that the faithful "participate in their own way in the priestly, prophetic and kingly office of Christ. They are called, each according to his or her particular condition, to exercise the mission which God entrusted to the Church to fulfil in the world".

This needs to be read in the light of canon 207 §§1-2[^191], in which it is stated that in the Church there are sacred ministers (clerics) and lay people; and, drawn from both groups, consecrated persons. Thus while all are called to share in the Church's mission, the contribution of each group varies according to their condition:

- **clerics** are involved primarily with continuing the ministry of the Apostles;

- the principal role of **consecrated persons** is to give "eschatological" witness: to be "a splendid sign in the Church, as they foretell the heavenly glory" (canon 573 §1[^192]);

- the mission of the **laity** is to "seek the kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and by ordering them according to the plan of God" (*Lumen Gentium*, no. 31).

**3. The fundamental rights and duties of the faithful**

In the course of the revision of the Code of Canon Law, it was envisaged that there would also be a separate constitutional law known as the "Fundamental Law of the Church" (*Lex Ecclesiae Fundamentalis*) which would set out the basic rights and obligations of the faithful. Because of the theological and practical problems which this entailed, the project was ultimately abandoned, and the relevant canons were incorporated into both the Code of Canon Law and the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches.

> The rights and duties are listed in canons 208-223 of the 1983 Code. Since these were originally framed to form part of a "constitutional" document, they are worded in broad and general terms, and refer to:

- the "equality of dignity and action among all of Christ's faithful" (canon 208[^193]);

- the duty of ecclesial communion (canon 209[^194]);

- the universal call to holiness and apostolate (canon 210[^195]);

- the right to do apostolate (canon 211[^196]);

- the duty of obedience to the sacred Pastors (canon 212 §1[^197]);

- the right to make one's needs and wishes known (canon 212 §2[^198]);

- freedom of opinion and expression (canon 212 §3[^199]);

- the right to the means of sanctification (canon 213[^200]);

- the right to one's own rite and spirituality (canon 214[^201]);

- the right of association and meeting (canon 215[^202]);

- the right of initiative (canon 216[^203]);

- the right to Catholic formation (canon 217[^204]);

- scientific (academic) freedom (canon 218[^205]);

- freedom in choosing one's state in life (canon 219[^206]);

- the right to one's good name and privacy (canon 220[^207]);

- the right to judicial protection (canon 221 §1[^208]) and a fair hearing (§2[^209]);

- the right not to be punished except in accordance with the law (canon 221 §3[^210]);

- the duty to support the Church financially (canon 222[^211]).

> The Eastern Code also establishes the right and duty to preserve one's own rite in every place ([*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf), canons 38-41, 403 §1).

The following chapters will look specifically at the rights and duties of sacred ministers or clerics, and the rights and duties of the laity, before studying the right of association (cf. canon 215) which is enjoyed by all the faithful, whether clerical or lay.

? QUESTION

Describe how the rights and duties which pertain to all the faithful are to be exercised in different ways, according to each individual's status in the Church.

**\**
**CHAPTER VI:\
SACRED MINISTERS OR CLERICS\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 232-264, 273-289; Book IV, canons 1008-1009.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 10, 31.
>
> Vatican II, Decree on Priestly Training [*Optatam Totius*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_optatam-totius_en.html), 28 October 1965*.*
>
> Vatican II, Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), 7 December 1965, no. 16
>
> John Paul II, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Pastores Dabo Vobis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031992_pastores-dabo-vobis.html), 25 March 1992.
>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P4X.HTM), nos. 1579-1580.
>
> Benedict XVI, Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* [*Omnium in Mentem*,](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_letters/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apl_20091026_codex-iuris-canonici.html) 26 October 2009.
>
> Benedict XVI, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Verbum Domini*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_ben-xvi_exh_20100930_verbum-domini.html), 30 September 2010, nos. 47, 80, 82.
>
> Congregation for the Clergy, *[The Gift of the Priestly Vocation](https://www.clerus.va/content/dam/clerus/documenti/ratio-2026/Ratio-EN-2017-01-03.pdf)* \[*Ratio Fundamentalis Institutionis Sacerdotalis*\], 8 December 2016.

**1. Juridical consequences of the sacrament of order**

"By divine institution, some among Christ's faithful are, through the sacrament of order, marked with an indelible character and are thus constituted sacred ministers". Through this sacrament they are called to "serve the People of God by a new and specific title" (canon 1008[^212]).

The sacrament of order brings about the **hierarchical distinction** in the Church: the **ministerial priesthood**, which differs from the **common priesthood of all the baptised** "in essence and not only in degree" ([*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 10), although the two are nevertheless interrelated.

The sacrament of order gives the ordained person the capacity to act *in nomine et in Persona Christi Capitis --* in the name and in the Person of Christ.

> The Apostolic Letter *motu proprio [Omnium in Mentem](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_letters/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apl_20091026_codex-iuris-canonici.html)*, 26 October 2009, introducing amendments to canons 1008 and 1009[^213] of the 1983 Code, clarifies that it is the bishop and the priest, and not the deacon, who receive the mission and capacity to act in the person of Christ the Head. The deacon is empowered "to serve the People of God in the ministries of the liturgy, the word and charity".

The sacrament of order confers *sacra potestas* -- the sacred power to carry out ministerial acts. It also confers the "capacity" to assume certain ecclesiastical functions involving the *power of governance*. This capacity is actuated when the ordained person receives a stable "ecclesiastical office" (see canon 145[^214]).

Non-ordained persons, without holding power of governance, may "cooperate" in the exercise of power in certain situations.

> Canons 1421 §2[^215] and 1673 §3[^216], for example, allow for the possibility of lay judges forming part of a college of judges.

**2. Rights and duties of clerics**

Canons 273-289[^217] set out the obligations and rights of clerics. These include, among others, the right of association of clerics "for the achievement of purposes befitting the clerical state" (canon 278 §1; see the general right of association of all the faithful in canon 215[^218]).

One of the chief obligations is that of **celibacy** (canon 277), which is at the same time to be "embraced and esteemed as a gift": see the Vatican II Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 16. Although not of the essence of the priesthood, celibacy is nevertheless to be seen as the fruit of the action of the Holy Spirit.

> [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 16, explains the fittingness of celibacy for priests, and calls not only on priests but on all the faithful to "receive this precious gift of priestly celibacy in their hearts and ask of God that he will always bestow this gift upon his Church". See also the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P4X.HTM), nos. 1579-1580, explaining that this charism is required for receiving ordination, and also referring to the discipline of the Eastern Churches, in which bishops are required to be celibate, but married men may be ordained as deacons and priests.

**3. Formation of clergy**

> Key documents on this topic are the Vatican II Decree on Priestly Training [*Optatam Totius*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_optatam-totius_en.html), 28 October 1965, and Pope John Paul II's post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Pastores Dabo Vobis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031992_pastores-dabo-vobis.html), 25 March 1992, dealing with the formation of priests in the circumstances of the present day.

Canons 232-264 make clear that the training given to candidates for the priesthood aims not simply at imparting intellectual knowledge, but at providing an integral formation. Primary responsibility lies with the bishop (see [*Pastores Dabo Vobis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031992_pastores-dabo-vobis.html), no. 65)

> The normal period of seminary training is seven years (see canon 250[^219] and the Congregation for the Clergy, *[The Gift of the Priestly Vocation](https://www.clerus.va/content/dam/clerus/documenti/ratio-2026/Ratio-EN-2017-01-03.pdf)* \[*Ratio Fundamentalis Institutionis Sacerdotalis*\], 8 December 2016, which establishes the need for a propaedeutic year prior to the commencement of studies of philosophy and theology). This training should cover human formation (canon 244[^220]; *Pastores Dabo Vobis*, nos. 43-44); spiritual formation (canons 245-247[^221]; *Pastores Dabo Vobis*, nos. 45-50); doctrinal formation (canons 248-252[^222]; *Pastores Dabo Vobis*, nos. 51-56); and pastoral formation (canons 255-258[^223]; *Pastores Dabo Vobis*, nos. 57-59). See also Pope Benedict XVI's post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Verbum Domini*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_ben-xvi_exh_20100930_verbum-domini.html) (30 September 2010), no. 82, on the role which the Word of God must play in the spiritual life of candidates for the priesthood; see also nos. 47 and 80 of the same document.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the chief juridical consequences of receiving the sacrament of order?

2\. What are the principal rights and duties of clerics as set out in the Code of Canon Law?

**\**
**CHAPTER VII:\
THE LAITY\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 207, 224-231.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 31.
>
> Vatican II, Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), 7 December 1965, no. 36.
>
> John Paul II, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Christifideles Laici*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_30121988_christifideles-laici.html), 30 December 1988, nos. 9, 15, 17.
>
> Holy See, [*Instruction on Certain Questions Regarding the Collaboration of the Non-Ordained Faithful in the Sacred Ministry of the Priest*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cclergy/documents/rc_con_interdic_doc_15081997_en.html), 15 August 1997.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Address to the participants in the 56th National Study Congress organised by the Union of Italian Catholic Jurists*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/december/documents/hf_ben_xvi_spe_20061209_giuristi-cattolici.html), 9 December 2006.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Address at the inauguration of the Ecclesial Convention of the Diocese of Rome*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2009/may/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20090526_convegno-diocesi-rm.html), 26 May 2009.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Homily at Bellahouston Park, Glasgow*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/homilies/2010/documents/hf_ben-xvi_hom_20100916_glasgow.html), 16 September 2010.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Message on the occasion of the Sixth Ordinary Assembly of the International Forum of Catholic Action*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/messages/pont-messages/2012/documents/hf_ben-xvi_mes_20120810_fiac.html), 10 August 2012.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Exhortation [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html#_ftnref176), 24 November 2013, no. 102.

**1. The necessary distinction between the notions of "faithful" and "laity"**

While all those who are baptised are "faithful", [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 31, states: "The term laity is here understood to mean all the faithful except those in holy orders and those in the state of religious life specially approved by the Church".

> It should be noted that there are various meanings of "laity" in the 1983 Code. According to canon 207 §1[^224], laity are those who are not clerics. Canon 207 §2[^225], reflecting [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 31, refers to the laity as those who are not clerics and not religious. Canon 711[^226] mentions laity who are consecrated as members of a secular institute. Canon 731 §1[^227] introduces another possibility, membership of a society of apostolic life.
>
> In the following considerations the term "laity" will be taken primarily to refer to those of the faithful who are not ordained, not religious, and not members of a secular institute or of a society of apostolic life. To put it in positive terms, it refers to those Christians whose vocation it is to remain immersed in the realities of the world, and whose calling it is to seek holiness and carry out apostolate precisely as "ordinary lay faithful".

**2. Secularity as the proper characteristic of the laity**

The [*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf) is much more precise than the 1983 Code in describing the mission of the laity. In its canon 399 it states: "In this Code, the name of lay persons is applied to the Christian faithful whose proper and special state is secular and who, living in the world, participate in the mission of the Church, and are not in holy orders nor enrolled in the religious state."

> This reference to "secularity" had already been clearly stated by the Second Vatican Council in the second paragraph of [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 31. For a detailed exposition of the positive and secular nature of the vocation of the laity, and the secular world as the place in which they receive their call from God, see the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Christifideles Laici*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_30121988_christifideles-laici.html), nos. 9, 15 and 17.
>
> See also Pope Benedict XVI's [*Address to the participants in the 56th National Study Congress organised by the Union of Italian Catholic Jurists*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/december/documents/hf_ben_xvi_spe_20061209_giuristi-cattolici.html), 9 December 2006, in which the Pope explains the various meanings of the word "secularity". In modern times an ideological understanding has come to be attributed to the term which is the opposite of its original meaning. It is therefore the task of Christians "to help formulate a concept of secularity which, on the one hand, acknowledges the place that is due to God and his moral law, to Christ and to his Church in human life, both individual and social; and on the other, affirms and respects the 'rightful autonomy of the earthly affairs', if by this phrase, as the Second Vatican Council affirms, is meant man's 'gradual rediscovery, exploitation and ordering of the laws and values of matter and society' ([*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 36)".
>
> More recently Benedict XVI stated: "Co-responsibility demands a change of mindset especially concerning the role of lay people in the Church. They should not be regarded as 'collaborators' of the clergy, but as people who are really 'co-responsible" for the Church's being and acting" ([*Message on the occasion of the Sixth Ordinary Assembly of the International Forum of Catholic Action*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/messages/pont-messages/2012/documents/hf_ben-xvi_mes_20120810_fiac.html), 10 August 2012).
>
> And in the words of Pope Francis: "There has been a growing awareness of the identity and mission of the laity in the Church ... \[but\] a clear awareness of this responsibility of the laity, grounded in their baptism and confirmation, does not appear in the same way in all places. ... Even if many are now involved in the lay ministries, this involvement is not reflected in a greater penetration of Christian values in the social, political and economic sectors. It often remains tied to tasks within the Church, without a real commitment to applying the Gospel to the transformation of society. The formation of the laity and the evangelisation of professional and intellectual life represent a significant pastoral challenge" (Apostolic Exhortation [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html#_ftnref176), no. 102).

**3. Rights and duties of the laity**

> The rights and duties of the laity are set out in canons 224-231.

In addition to the rights and duties applicable to all the faithful, the Code of Canon Law specifies that the laity are bound by the obligation and have the right to spread the divine message of salvation throughout the world, and in particular in those situations to which only the laity have access (canon 225 §1[^228]). Connected to this is their special obligation to sanctify the temporal order (canon 225 §2[^229]).

> See Pope Benedict's [*Homily at Bellahouston Park, Glasgow*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/homilies/2010/documents/hf_ben-xvi_hom_20100916_glasgow.html), on 16 September 2010, in which he called upon the lay faithful "in accordance with your baptismal calling and mission, not only to be examples of faith in public, but also to put the case for the promotion of faith's wisdom and vision in the public forum".

Canon 226[^230] sets out the rights and duties of Christian spouses and parents; while canon 229[^231] deals with the rights and duties of the laity as regards formation and teaching.

Canon 227[^232] affirms the freedom of Christ's faithful in secular affairs, which is a basic human right, but also a right as before the hierarchy and the other faithful.

> In this connection [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 36, says: ""Because of the very economy of salvation the faithful should learn how to distinguish carefully between those rights and duties which are theirs as members of the Church, and those which they have as members of human society. Let them strive to reconcile the two, remembering that in every temporal affair they must be guided by a Christian conscience, since even in secular business there is no human activity which can be withdrawn from God\'s dominion".
>
> Canon 747 §2 affirms the Church's right "always and everywhere to proclaim moral principles, even in respect of the social order, and to make judgements about any human matter in so far as this is required by fundamental human rights or the salvation of souls".

**4. Other capacities of lay people**

Canons 228[^233], 230[^234] and 231[^235] may be regarded as referring to "capacities" of lay people to carry out tasks and functions which are not strictly speaking proper to the lay (secular) state as such, e.g. acting as experts and advisers to the hierarchy; fulfilling the ministry of lector, acolyte, or extraordinary minister of Holy Communion; or providing other special services to the Church.

> See the Holy See's Interdicasterial [*Instruction on Certain Questions Regarding the Collaboration of the Non-Ordained Faithful in the Sacred Ministry of the Priest*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cclergy/documents/rc_con_interdic_doc_15081997_en.html), 15 August 1997, which begins by presenting some fundamental theological principles (the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial priesthood; the unity and diversity of ministerial functions; the indispensability of the ordained ministry; and the collaboration of the non-ordained faithful in pastoral ministry), before establishing a number of practical provisions concerning the ministry of the Word, the homily, the parish priest and the parish, the structures of collaboration in the particular Church, liturgical celebrations, Sunday celebrations in the absence of a priest, the extraordinary minister of Holy Communion, the apostolate to the sick, assistance at marriage, the minister of baptism, the leading of the celebration at funerals, and the need for selection and adequate formation.
>
> However, as mentioned earlier, and as repeatedly stressed by Pope Benedict XVI, e.g. in his [*Address at the inauguration of the Ecclesial Convention of the Diocese of Rome*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2009/may/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20090526_convegno-diocesi-rm.html), 26 May 2009, the lay people "must no longer be viewed as 'collaborators' of the clergy" but must be "truly recognised as 'co-responsible' for the Church's being and action, thereby fostering the consolidation of a mature and committed laity".

? QUESTIONS

1\. What is the particular characteristic that is proper to lay persons in the Church, and how is this reflected in the rights and duties of the laity in the 1983 Code?

2\. How are the rights and duties that pertain to the laity as such to be distinguished from other capacities which the laity may have to perform certain tasks and functions in the Church?

**\**
**CHAPTER VIII:\
ASSOCIATIONS OF THE FAITHFUL\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 298-329.
>
> John Paul II, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Christifideles Laici*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_30121988_christifideles-laici.html), 30 December 1988, no. 30.
>
> Pontifical Council for the Laity, [*Directory on International Associations of the Faithful*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/laity/documents/rc_pc_laity_doc_20051114_associazioni_en.html#:~:text=This%20Directory%20of%20the%20associations,it%20is%20also%20designed%20for), 2006, with Preface by Cardinal Stanisław Ryłko.
>
> Benedict XVI, Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* [*Intima Ecclesiae Natura*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/motu_proprio/documents/hf_ben-xvi_motu-proprio_20121111_caritas.html), 11 November 2012.

**1. The fundamental right of association**

Associations are moral bodies which are formed through the voluntary union of faithful, for the purposes mentioned in canon 298 §1: "to foster a more perfect life, or to promote public worship or Christian teaching. They may also devote themselves to other works of the apostolate, such as initiatives for evangelisation, works of piety or charity, and those which animate the temporal order with the Christian spirit".

> The right of association is based on: a) the human person's social nature, and b) the specific provision in canon 215 that "Christ's faithful may freely establish and direct associations which serve charitable or pious purposes or which foster the Christian vocation in the world".
>
> A distinction is to be drawn between associations of the faithful on the one hand, and "institutionalised" associative phenomena such as religious institutes on the other; the latter will be dealt with in the next chapter.

**2. Associations in the Code of Canon Law**

> The norms common to all associations are given in canons 298-311[^236].

According to their membership and purposes, associations in the Church may be **clerical** (canon 302), **lay** (canons 327-329[^237]), or **third orders** (in which the members "live in the world but share in the spirit of some religious institute": canon 303).

According to their relationship with the hierarchy, associations may be **public** or **private:**

- **public associations** are established by ecclesiastical authority (the Holy See, the Episcopal Conference, or the diocesan bishop);

- **private associations** are established by agreements among the faithful.

A "public" nature is necessary for associations imparting Christian teaching in the name of the Church, promoting public worship, or which have other ends reserved by their nature to the ecclesiastical authority (canon 301 §1[^238]).

> The [*Directory on International Associations of the Faithful*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/laity/documents/rc_pc_laity_doc_20051114_associazioni_en.html#:~:text=This%20Directory%20of%20the%20associations,it%20is%20also%20designed%20for) issued by the Pontifical Council for the Laity in 2006 provides details of 122 associations which have received official recognition and explicit approval from the Holy See.
