The Preface to the Directory by Cardinal Stanisław Ryłko, then President of the Pontifical Council for the Laity, provides a summary of the place and importance of lay associations in the life of the Church.
>
> Concerning lay associations, Pope John Paul II laid down a number of what he called "criteria of ecclesiality" in [*Christifideles Laici*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_30121988_christifideles-laici.html), no. 30, including the primacy given to the call of every Christian to holiness; the responsibility of professing the Catholic faith, embracing and proclaiming the truth about Christ, the Church and humanity, in obedience to the Church's Magisterium; the witness to a strong and authentic communion in filial relationship to the Pope, in total adherence to the belief that he is the perpetual and visible centre of unity of the universal Church, and with the local Bishop in the particular Church, and in "mutual esteem for all forms of the Church\'s apostolate"; the readiness to embrace the doctrinal teachings and pastoral initiatives of both Pope and Bishop; and conformity to and participation in the Church's apostolic goals; the commitment to a presence in human society, which in light of the Church\'s social doctrine, places it at the service of the total dignity of the person.
>
> On the right to establish charitable agencies, and foundations to fund charitable initiatives, see Benedict XVI's Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* [*Intima Ecclesiae Natura*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/motu_proprio/documents/hf_ben-xvi_motu-proprio_20121111_caritas.html), 11 November 2012, which lays down norms to ensure that such activities are managed in accordance with the Church's teaching and the faithful's intention, and that they respect the legitimate norms of the civil authorities.

? QUESTION

To what extent do the faithful require the consent of the ecclesiastical authority in order to form a private association?

**\**
**CHAPTER IX:\
CONSECRATED LIFE\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 573-746.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 39-42.
>
> John Paul II, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), 25 March 1996, nos. 7, 9-12, 36, 60, 62.
>
> Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life, Instruction [*The Service of Authority and Obedience -- "Faciem tuam, Domine, requiram"*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccscrlife/documents/rc_con_ccscrlife_doc_20080511_autorita-obbedienza_en.html), 11 May 2008.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Homily on the occasion of the 15th Day of Consecrated Life*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/homilies/2011/documents/hf_ben-xvi_hom_20110202_vita-consacrata.html), 2 February 2011.
>
> Francis, [*Message* *to consecrated people gathered in the Basilica of S. Maria Maggiore on the occasion of world day for consecrated life*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/messages/consecrated_life/documents/20230202-messaggio-gm-vitaconsacrata.html), 2 February 2023.

**1. Notion of consecrated life: its function in the Church**

Canon 573 §1 establishes that "Life consecrated through profession of the evangelical counsels is a stable form of living, in which the faithful follow Christ more closely under the action of the Holy Spirit, and are totally dedicated to God, who is supremely loved. By a new and special title they are dedicated to seek the perfection of charity in the service of God's Kingdom, for the honour of God, the building up of the Church and the salvation of the world. They are a splendid sign in the Church, as they foretell the heavenly glory."

> This provision needs to be read in the light of [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), nos. 39-42, on the universal call to holiness: "all the faithful of Christ of whatever rank or status, are called to the fullness of the Christian life and to the perfection of charity" (no. 40); "Every person must walk unhesitatingly according to his own personal gifts and duties in the path of living faith" (no. 41); "all the faithful of Christ are invited to strive for the holiness and perfection of their own proper state. Indeed they have an obligation to so strive" (no. 42).
>
> In relation to consecrated life, "the holiness of the Church is fostered in a special way by the observance of the counsels proposed in the Gospel by Our Lord to His disciples" (no. 42).
>
> Pope John Paul II, in his post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), 25 March 1996, deals with the origins of the consecrated life in the mystery of Christ and of the Trinity; consecrated life as a sign of communion in the Church; and as a manifestation of God's love in the world.
>
> In a [*homily on the occasion of the 15th Day of Consecrated Life*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/homilies/2011/documents/hf_ben-xvi_hom_20110202_vita-consacrata.html), 2 February 2011, Pope Benedict XVI said that the consecrated life expresses the spiritual journey as *philokalia* -- love of the divine beauty, a reflection of God's goodness. At the same time it is a call to bear prophetic witness, linked to its twofold contemplative and active approach. Consecrated life in the world and in the Church is a visible sign of the search for the face of the Lord.
>
> Pope Francis, addressing consecrated men and women, has said: "you consecrated persons have a specific role, that derives from the particular gift you have received: a gift that gives your witness a special character and value, for the very fact that you are fully dedicated to God and to his Kingdom, in poverty, virginity and obedience. If each person is a mission in the Church, then each and every one of you is a mission with a grace of your own, as a consecrated person. Beyond this fundamental gift, your mission is enriched by the charisms of your institutes and societies, the charisms of your founders. In their remarkable variety, they are all given for the edification of the Church and for her mission. All charisms are for the mission, and they are precisely so with the incalculable richness of their variety; so that the Church may bear witness to and proclaim the Gospel to everyone and in every situation" ([*Message* *to consecrated people gathered in the Basilica of S. Maria Maggiore on the occasion of world day for consecrated life*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/messages/consecrated_life/documents/20230202-messaggio-gm-vitaconsacrata.html), 2 February 2023).

Consecrated life thus involves a special divine vocation; it fulfils a specific mission in the Church, as well as having social importance. It is normally lived within an institute of consecrated life, but it can take the form of eremitic life (canon 603[^239]) or an order of consecrated virgins (canon 604[^240]).

**2. Institutes of consecrated life**

Institutes of consecrated life are canonically established by the Church authority.

In them the faithful freely assume the consecrated life, professing the evangelical counsels of chastity, poverty and obedience, by vows or other bonds, in accordance with the laws of the institute (canon 573 §2[^241]; see the Instruction of Congregation for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life [*The Service of Authority and Obedience -- "Faciem tuam, Domine, requiram"*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccscrlife/documents/rc_con_ccscrlife_doc_20080511_autorita-obbedienza_en.html), 11 May 2008).

Institutes of consecrated life pertain to the Church's life and holiness (canon 574 §1[^242]).

Although they arise out of private initiative, they have a public mission in the Church. It is for the hierarchy to discern their foundational charism (canons 576-577[^243]). Once approved by the Church, the intentions of founder must be preserved (canon 578[^244]).

**3. Religious institutes, secular institutes, and societies of apostolic life**

Institutes of consecrated life may be **religious institutes** (canon 607[^245]) or **secular institutes** (canon 710[^246]). There also exist **societies of apostolic life** (canon 731[^247]), which are not institutes of consecrated life, but are treated as equivalent for the purposes of legal regulation.

> Characteristics of **religious institutes** (see [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), no. 9): the members

- profess the evangelical counsels through **public vows**;

- live **fraternal life in common**; and

- give public witness through **separation from the world**. The main apostolate of a religious institute is the witness of their consecrated life (canon 673[^248]).

> Characteristics of **secular institutes** (see [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), no. 10): the members

- profess the evangelical counsels through **vows** **or other sacred bonds**;

- are **not held to life in common**;

- **live in the world** (although the institutes do not admit married faithful);

- carry out apostolate above all by working in the world by means of the witness of their life (canon 710).

> Characteristics of **societies of apostolic life** (see [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), no. 11): these are treated as juridically equivalent to institutes of consecrated life. The members

- are **not** required to take **vows or other bonds**;

- live **fraternal life in common**;

- strive for perfection by observing their constitutions.

**4. Types of institute of consecrated life**

**a) Clerical institutes and lay institutes**

Although in itself, consecrated life is neither clerical nor lay (canon 588 §1[^249]), there can exist clerical and lay institutes:

- **clerical institutes** are governed by clerics, presuppose the exercise of sacred orders, and are recognised as such by ecclesiastical authority (canon 588 §2[^250]);

- **lay institutes** do not involve the exercise of sacred orders; they are recognised as such by ecclesiastical authority (canon 588 §3[^251]).

> In [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), no. 60, Pope John Paul II, talking of institutes which have a character and tradition which do not entail the exercise of holy orders, expresses a preference for the term "religious institutes of brothers" instead of "lay institutes", to avoid ambiguity and confusion with the secular state of the lay faithful.

**b) Institutes of pontifical right and institutes of diocesan right**

**Institutes of pontifical right** are established or approved by a formal decree of the Apostolic See (canon 589[^252]), to which they are subject directly and exclusively (canon 593[^253]).

**Institutes of diocesan right** are established by the diocesan bishop and have not obtained a decree of approval from the Apostolic See (canon 589[^254]); they are subject to the special care of the diocesan bishop (canon 594[^255]).

**5. Other forms of consecrated life**

**a) The eremitic life (hermits)**

"Hermits are recognised by law as dedicated to God in consecrated life if, in the hands of the diocesan bishop, they publicly profess, by a vow or some other sacred bond, the three evangelical counsels, and then lead their particular form of life under the guidance of the diocesan bishop" (canon 603 §2).

**b) Consecrated virgins**

These are consecrated by the bishop according to the appropriate rite, and constitute another individual form of consecrated life (canon 604[^256]).

> See [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), nos. 7, 12 and 62.

? QUESTIONS

1\. Describe the ways in which consecrated life may be lived within and outside an institute of consecrated life.

2\. What are the features common to religious institutes, secular institutes, and societies of apostolic life, and what are the principal differences between them?

**\**
**CHAPTER X:\
ECCLESIASTICAL POWER\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book I, canons 129-196.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, Preliminary Explanatory Note (appended to the end of the document), no. 2.

**1. Power of governance in the Church**

Power of governance (*potestas iurisdictionis*, "power of jurisdiction") in the Church is understood as the power to give binding commands, giving rise to an obligation in justice to observe them, for the purpose of ordering social life towards the common good.

Power is not for the benefit of the one who holds it but for the community. A person has power because he has a function to fulfil in the Church. Power is always to be understood as a service.

Although power of governance refers to legislative, executive, and judicial, it is often used simply to mean executive power.

> An act of legislative power would be, for example, the issuing of a law; an act of executive (or administrative) power might be the granting of a privilege or dispensation, or the removal of faculties from a priest; the primary example of an act of judicial power would be the issuing of a decision in a trial (e.g. the declaration of the nullity of a marriage, after the appropriate procedure has been followed).
>
> The sixth of the Guiding Principles for the Revision of the Code of Canon Law[^257] (see the Appendix to chapter II) recommended that the exercise of authority should appear more clearly as service.

**2. Those who can exercise power**

In order to be able to exercise power there has to be a fundamental ("ontological") capacity to exercise a specific ecclesiastical office (see point 3, below). In many situations this means that the person should have received the sacrament of order, which is what creates the ontological capacity.

> The Preliminary Explanatory Note to [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 2, states: "In his consecration a person is given an ontological participation in the sacred functions \[*munera*\]; this is absolutely clear from Tradition, liturgical tradition included. The word 'functions' \[*munera*\] is used deliberately instead of the word 'powers' \[*potestates*\], because the latter word could be understood as a power fully ready to act. But for this power to be fully ready to act, there must be a further canonical or juridical determination through the hierarchical authority. This determination of power can consist in the granting of a particular office or in the allotment of subjects, and it is done according to the norms approved by the supreme authority."

Canon 129 §1 states: "Those who are in sacred orders are, in accordance with the provisions of law, capable of the power of governance, which belongs to the Church by divine institution. This power is also called the power of jurisdiction."

Paragraph 2 of the same canon says that lay people "can cooperate in the exercise of this same power in accordance with the law". Examples of norms allowing such cooperation in the power of jurisdiction are canons 1421 §2[^258] and 1673 §3[^259], which allow lay people to be appointed as judges.

**3. Ecclesiastical office**

Canon 145 §1[^260] defines an ecclesiastical office as "any post which by divine or ecclesiastical disposition is established in a stable manner to further a spiritual purpose". It consists of a set of rights and duties conferred on an individual in a stable way, whereby that person shares in juridical power.

An ecclesiastical office may be conferred by:

- **free conferral** (canon 157[^261]): this is the normal system;

- **canonical presentation** (canons 158[^262], 163[^263]): a person or college presents one or several candidates; the authority then appoints the one whom it chooses from among them;

- **election** (canons 164-179[^264]), which may or may not require confirmation by a higher authority such as the Pope;

- **postulation** (canons 180-183[^265]): this involves the election of a candidate who has some impediment to being elected, the request for confirmation of the appointment being accompanied by a request for dispensation from the impediment.

> "An ecclesiastical office is lost on the expiry of a predetermined time; on reaching the age limit defined by law; by resignation; by transfer; by removal; by deprivation" (canon 184 §1; canons 187-196 define these terms in greater detail). An office is not lost through the death of the person conferring it: canon 184 §2[^266].

**4. Types of power in the Church**

**a) Ordinary power and delegated power**

Power can be conferred in two ways (see canon 131[^267]):

- it can be attached to the ecclesiastical office, so that the person receives it on taking office: this is known as **ordinary power**;

- it can be granted directly to the person, without that person necessarily holding an office: this is called **delegated power**.

> Normally it is only ordinary executive power that can be delegated (see canon 137[^268]).

**b) Proper and vicarious ordinary power:**

Ordinary power -- that is, power annexed to an ecclesiastical office (canon 131) -- may be

- **proper ordinary power**, exercised in the person's own name; or

- **vicarious ordinary power**, exercised in the name of another.

**c) Distinction of functions: legislative, executive and judicial power**

Canon 135 §1 states: "The power of governance is divided into legislative, executive and judicial power".

These functions are exercised personally by the bishop (or by the Pope for the universal Church), or else through vicarious bodies:

- **legislative power** is normally exercised by the holder of power, e.g. the bishop (it is only the supreme authority of the Church that can delegate legislative power: canon 135 §2[^269]);

- **executive power** (canon 135 §4[^270]; see canons 136-144[^271]) can be ordinary (proper or vicarious) or delegated;

- **judicial power** is that possessed by judges and judicial colleges (canon 135 §3[^272]).

**d) Ordinaries and local Ordinaries**

According to canon 134 §1[^273], "Ordinary" is the name given to the one who exercises the **executive** functions that pertain to the one in charge of the diocese or equivalent structure (see canon 368[^274]).

Apart from the bishop himself, the term includes those who have executive power in the diocese, such as the vicar general or episcopal vicar (see chapter XIII on the Diocesan Organisation).

The bishop, the vicar general, the episcopal vicar, etc., are also referred to as "local Ordinaries".

> The main difference between an "Ordinary" and a "local Ordinary" is that the former term includes superiors of religious institutes and societies of apostolic life, while the latter does not.

**e) The "supplying" of power**

By virtue of canon 144 §1[^275], the Church "supplies" executive power of governance in certain situations in which such power is mistakenly thought to exist, but in fact does not do so:

- where there is a "common error" of fact or law (that is, an error on the part of the community, not on that of the individual);

- where there is a "positive and probable doubt" of fact or law (that is, there are well-founded reasons for thinking that, in a situation in which the doubt cannot be resolved, the power probably does exist).

The same rules apply in the case of the faculty of the priest to administer confirmation and penance, and in the case of delegation to assist at marriages (canon 144 §2[^276]).

For these provisions to be applicable, the person acting must have ontological capacity to act. Thus no "supply" of power can take place if the person hearing confessions, administering confirmation or marrying a couple turns out not to be a validly ordained minister.

*\*

? QUESTIONS

1\. Why is it necessary to give attention to the question of "power" in the Church?

2\. What is the significance of reception of the sacrament of order in relation to the exercise of power?

**\**
**CHAPTER XI:\
GOVERNMENT OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 330-367.
>
> Catholic Encyclopedia: [*Infallibility*](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07790a.htm).
>
> [*Historical Notes*](https://www.vatican.va/news_services/press/documentazione/documents/cardinali_documentazione/cardinali_documentazione_generale_en.html#The%20College%20of%20Cardinals) section of the "Holy See Press Office, College of Cardinals General Documentation" on Vatican website.
>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P29.HTM), nos. 832-835, 880-887.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 2, 8, 23, and Preliminary Explanatory Note (appended to the end of the document).
>
> Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Letter [*Communionis Notio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_28051992_communionis-notio_en.html), 28 May 1992, nos. 7-9.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Universi Dominici Gregis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_22021996_universi-dominici-gregis.html), 22 February 1996.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Constitution [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html#Secretariat_of_State), 19 March 2022.

**1. Relationship between the universal Church and particular Churches**

The one Church founded by Jesus Christ, "constituted and organised as a society in the present world, subsists in the Catholic Church, which is governed by the successor of Peter and by the bishops in communion with him" ([*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 8).

Within this unity there exist "particular Churches", the principal example of which is the diocese (canon 368[^277]). A diocese is defined as "a portion of the People of God, which is entrusted to a bishop to be nurtured by him, with the cooperation of the *presbyterium*, in such a way that, remaining close to its pastor and gathered by him through the Gospel and the Eucharist in the Holy Spirit, it constitutes a particular Church. In this Church, the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of Christ truly exists and functions" (canon 369[^278]; see also [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 23).

> In the particular Church there is the mystery of the "whole" present in the "part". The [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P29.HTM), nos. 832-835, describing the nature of the relationship between particular Churches and the universal Church, states that particular Churches are fully "Catholic" through their communion with the Church of Rome, which "presides in charity".
>
> The Letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith [*Communionis Notio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_28051992_communionis-notio_en.html), 28 May 1992, clarifies that the universal Church precedes and gives birth to the particular Churches as daughters: She expresses herself in them, and is a mother to them, not a product of them (nos. 7-9).

Other structures similar to dioceses (mentioned in canon 368) share in these fundamental features, each of them constituting a specified "portion of the People of God", entrusted to a bishop (or in some cases a priest with episcopal functions), helped by the priests assigned to that structure.

**2. Primacy and collegiality**

The Roman Pontiff, the Successor of Peter, together with the bishops as successors of the Apostles, form a single "college", which has supreme and full authority over the Church (canons 330-331[^279]). The College of Bishops succeeds the College of the Apostles in matters of Magisterium and the pastoral governance of the Church, always acting in union with its head, the Roman Pontiff.

"The Roman Pontiff, in fulfilling his office as supreme Pastor of the Church, is always joined in full communion with the other bishops, and indeed with the universal Church. He has the right, however, to determine, according to the needs of the Church, whether this office is to be exercised in a personal or in a collegial manner" (canon 333 §2).

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P2A.HTM), nos. 880-883. See also the Preliminary Explanatory Note appended to [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html).

**3. Holders of supreme power in the Church**

**a) The Roman Pontiff**

Canon 331 makes clear that the Pope, as head of the College of Bishops, the Vicar of Christ, and Pastor of the universal Church, "has supreme, full, immediate and universal ordinary power in the Church", which he can always freely exercise.

The Bishop of Rome differs from other bishops by virtue of his jurisdiction (supreme, full power), and also his charism (indefectibility and infallibility).

> See the entry [*Infallibility*](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07790a.htm) in the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, which not only refers to the dogmatic definition of infallibility formulated by the First Vatican Council, but also supplies proofs from Scripture and Tradition. The promise to Peter in *Mt* 16:8 ("And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it") provides the source of the Church's indefectibility, of which the successor of Peter is the visible foundation.

**b) The College of Bishops**

The College of Bishops, "by virtue of their sacramental consecration and hierarchical communion with the head of the College and its members" (canon 336[^280]), also holds supreme and full power over all the Church, although this power may only be exercised with the consent of the Roman Pontiff.

> "Communion" here is not to be understood as "some kind of vague disposition, but as an organic reality which requires a juridical form and is animated by charity" (Preliminary Explanatory Note to [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 2).
>
> As a member of the College of Bishops, the bishop participates in the "solicitude for the whole Church" (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 23), which is manifested in the first place by the good governance of his own diocese.
>
> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P2A.HTM), no. 886.

The College exercises its supreme power in a solemn way in an ecumenical council (canon 337 §1[^281]; see also canon 341 §1[^282]). The same collegial power may also be exercised by the bishops dispersed throughout the world, in union with the Pope, "when this action is as such proclaimed or freely accepted by the Roman Pontiff, so that it becomes a truly collegial act" (canon 337 §2[^283]).

> Examples might include the canonisation of a saint, or a universal petition for and proclamation of a dogma of faith, such as occurred prior to the declaration by Pope Pius XII on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

**4. Auxiliary institutions**

**a) The synod of bishops**

In exercising his power the Pope may be assisted by the synod of bishops, which is "a group of bishops selected from different parts of the world, who meet together at specified times to promote the close relationship between the Roman Pontiff and the bishops" (canon 342[^284]). This synod is of a "consultative" nature only, and is not a form of exercising collegiality in the government of the Church, but rather provides a way of helping the Pope in his own task.

> Canon 345[^285] lists 3 types of synodal assemblies (ordinary general, extraordinary general, and special), which are described in canon 346[^286]. Synodal assemblies have frequently given rise to post-synodal Apostolic Exhortations from the Holy Father, examples being [*Amoris Laetitia*](https://www.vatican.va/content/dam/francesco/pdf/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20160319_amoris-laetitia_en.pdf), on Love in the Family, 19 March 2016; [*Verbum Domini*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_ben-xvi_exh_20100930_verbum-domini.html), on the Word of God in the Life and Mission of the Church, 30 September 2010, [*Sacramentum Caritatis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_ben-xvi_exh_20070222_sacramentum-caritatis.html), on the Eucharist as the Source and Summit of the Church's Life and Mission, 22 February 2007; [*Pastores Gregis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_20031016_pastores-gregis.html), on the Bishop, Servant of the Gospel of Jesus Christ for the Hope of the World, 16 October 2003; [*Vita Consecrata*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031996_vita-consecrata.html), on the Consecrated Life and its Mission in the Church and in the World, 25 March 1996; [*Pastores Dabo Vobis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_25031992_pastores-dabo-vobis.html), on the Formation of Priests in the Circumstances of the Present Day, 25 March 1992; among many others.

**b) The College of Cardinals**

> For the historical origins of the College of Cardinals see the [*Historical Notes*](https://www.vatican.va/news_services/press/documentazione/documents/cardinali_documentazione/cardinali_documentazione_generale_en.html#The%20College%20of%20Cardinals) section of the "Holy See Press Office, College of Cardinals General Documentation" on the Vatican website.

This College assists and advises the Pope in the government of the Church. It has a dual function:

- to elect the Pope in accordance with particular law (currently John Paul II's Apostolic Constitution [*Universi Dominici Gregis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_22021996_universi-dominici-gregis.html) of 22 February 1996);

- to assist the Holy Father in his task as universal Pastor, both collegially and individually (canon 349[^287]).

> The number of Cardinals has varied over the centuries, but [*Universi Dominici Gregis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_22021996_universi-dominici-gregis.html), no. 33, restricts the number of Cardinals electing the Pope to 120. In addition, Cardinals reaching the age of 80 before the day when the Apostolic See becomes vacant cannot participate in the election.

Cardinals take part in the resolution of the most important matters. A Cardinal may also be asked by the Pope to represent him "in some solemn celebration or assembly of persons as a *legatus a latere*, that is, as his alter ego; or he may, as a special emissary, be entrusted with a particular pastoral task" (canon 358[^288]).

**c) The Roman Curia**

Canon 360 states: "The Supreme Pontiff usually conducts the business of the universal Church through the Roman Curia, which acts in his name and with his authority for the good and for the service of the Churches". The Curia must act in accordance with the intentions of the Pope, and in the case of the more important acts must obtain the Pope's approval.

> The main components of the Roman Curia, following the Apostolic Constitution [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html#Secretariat_of_State) of 19 March 2022, are:

- the **Secretariat of State**, consisting of a Section for General Affairs (current affairs of the Papal secretariat and the relations between the different departments of the Curia); and the Section of Relations with the States and International Organisations (foreign affairs); and the Section for Diplomatic Personnel of the Holy See;

- sixteen departments known as **Dicasteries**:

  - for Evangelisation

  - for the Doctrine of the Faith

  - for the Service of Charity

  - for the Eastern Churches

  - for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments

  - for the Causes of Saints

  - for Bishops

  - for the Clergy

  - for Institutes of Consecrated Life and Societies of Apostolic Life

  - for the Laity, the Family and Life

  - for Promoting Christian Unity

  - for Interreligious Dialogue

  - for Culture and Education

  - for Promoting Integral Human Development

  - for Legislative Texts

  - for Communication

- three **Institutions of Justice**

  - the Apostolic Penitentiary

  - the Supreme Tribunal of the Apostolic Signatura

  - the Tribunal of the Roman Rota

- six **Institutions of Finance**

  - the Council for the Economy

  - the Secretariat for the Economy

  - the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See

  - the Office of the Auditor General

  - the Commission for Confidential Matters

  - the Committee for Investments

- three **Offices**

  - the Prefecture of the Papal Household

  - the Office for the Liturgical Celebrations of the Supreme Pontiff

  - the Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church

- **Advocates**

  - the Register of Advocates at the Roman Curia, including Advocates of the Rota and others authorised to appear before the Supreme Tribunal of the Apostolic Signatura and other curial institutions

  - the Corps of Advocated of the Holy See who act before ecclesiastical or civil tribunals in the name of the Holy See or of curial institutions

- **other institutions** associated with but not forming part of the Holy See

  - the Vatican Apostolic Archive

  - the Vatican Apostolic Library

  - the Fabric of Saint Peter's, dealing with everything that concerns the Papal Basilica of Saint Peter

  - the Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology

  - various academies including the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences, and the Pontifical Academy for Life

  - the Agency for the Evaluation and Promotion of Quality in Ecclesiastical Universities and Faculties

  - the Supervisory and Financial Information Authority

**d) Papal legates**

The main role of the Papal legates (nuncios, apostolic delegates, etc.) is to ensure close cooperation between the Roman Pontiff and the bishops in the different territories. These legates also usually have a diplomatic function before the civil authorities, so as to foster understanding and cooperation between Church and State. Many States in their turn have diplomats accredited to the Holy See, usually with the rank of ambassadors.

> The various functions of the legates are listed especially in canons 364[^289] and 365[^290]

? QUESTIONS

1\. What is the relationship of the Pope to the College of Bishops?

2\. How does the Roman Curia assist the Pope in his task of governing the Church?

**\**
**CHAPTER XII:\
THE DIOCESE AND OTHER HIERARCHICAL STRUCTURES\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 294-297, 368-372.
>
> Vatican II, Decree concerning the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), 28 October 1965, no. 11.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Ut Sit*](https://opusdei.org/en/article/apostolic-constitution-ut-sit/), 28 November 1982.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Spirituali Militum Curae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/la/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_19860421_spirituali-militum-curae.html), 21 April 1986.
>
> Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Letter [*Communionis Notio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_28051992_communionis-notio_en.html), 28 May 1992, nos. 7-9, 11-14.
>
> Benedict XVI, Apostolic Constitution [*Anglicanorum Coetibus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apc_20091104_anglicanorum-coetibus.html), 4 November 2009.
>
> Francis, *motu proprio [Ad charisma tuendum](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20220714-motu-proprio-ad-charisma-tuendum.html)*, 14 July 2022.

**1. Juridical configuration of the portions of the People of God: the principle of territoriality**

In order to define the extent of a particular Church, the Church needs to delineate the sphere of competence of the bishop who heads a particular "portion of the People of God". The normal criterion used is that of "territoriality", meaning that dioceses are defined by geographical boundaries (see canon 372 §1[^291]).

> The possibility of a diocese being determined by a "personal" criterion is envisaged in canon 372 §2[^292], but to date no such diocese has been erected.
>
> In relation to territory, the canonical concepts of domicile and quasi-domicile (see canons 101-102[^293], 107[^294]) are important, since they determine one's parish priest and diocesan bishop.

**2. Ecclesiastical circumscriptions and their structure**

The term "ecclesiastical circumscription" is used to describe a structure consisting of

- a bishop (or in some cases a priest with episcopal powers);

- his *presbyterium* (priests);

- the people.

These are the constitutive elements of any ecclesiastical circumscription. Canon 368[^295] states that the principal canonical form of the particular Church is the diocese.

Among the various types of ecclesiastical circumscription there is both a **common element**, in that they each reproduce the structure proper to the Church (the interaction between the common priesthood and ministerial priesthood: the bishop-priests-people relationship), and a **distinguishing element**, in that they may lack the full range of the sacraments, or be subject to some special law. Canons 370[^296] and 371[^297] list a number of structures other than dioceses which constitute particular Churches.

> NB the concept of "particular Church" is a theological one, which canon law merely translates into certain juridical forms for practical purposes. These canonical forms are thus to be considered creations of ecclesiastical law. See Vatican II, Decree [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), no. 11.

**3. "Complementary" ecclesiastical circumscriptions**

The term "complementary ecclesiastical circumscriptions" has been used by some authors to describe those which arise out of the desire to complement the pastoral function carried out by the particular Church. A characteristic of complementary structures is that, while they have the same bishop-priests-people structure as in the particular Churches, their members do not cease to belong to the particular Church of which they already form part.

Such circumscriptions may be defined by a *personal* criterion, such as rite, profession, or nationality, instead of by domicile.

It is for the supreme authority of the Church to make a judgement concerning the need to create these structures and to issue the corresponding norms so that there is proper coordination with other jurisdictions.

Complementary circumscriptions have been considered to include personal Prelatures, military Ordinariates, Latin Ordinariates for faithful of Eastern rite, and personal Ordinariates for former Anglicans.

**a) Personal Prelatures**

These are governed by canons 294-297[^298], which provide a framework for many different possible forms of personal prelature. To date only one personal Prelature has been established, that of the Holy Cross and Opus Dei.

> The Personal Prelature of the Holy Cross and Opus Dei was established by the Apostolic Constitution [*Ut Sit*](https://opusdei.org/en/article/apostolic-constitution-ut-sit/), 28 November 1982, and at the same time received its statutes or "particular law". Its purpose is "to put into practice the teaching of the universal call to sanctity, and to promote at all levels of society the sanctification of ordinary work, and by means of ordinary work" (*Ut Sit*, Preamble).
>
> Art. III of *Ut sit* establishes that "The jurisdiction of the personal Prelature extends to the clergy incardinated in it, and also only in what refers to the fulfilment of the specific obligations undertaken through the juridical bond, by means of a contract with the Prelature to the laity who dedicate themselves to the apostolic activities of the Prelature: both clergy and laity are under the authority of the Prelate in carrying out the pastoral task of the Prelature..."

The Prelate is "endowed with the faculties of an Ordinary" (canon 295 §1) and may establish a national or an international seminary and incardinate students and promote them to orders. He may thus be seen as holding quasi-episcopal powers and to be the head of a community of faithful, helped by his *presbyterium*. The faithful of the prelature also belong to the local Churches in which they have their domicile.

> The existing statutes of Opus Dei, as set out in *Ut Sit*, are currently being revised as a result of the *motu proprio [Ad charisma tuendum](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20220714-motu-proprio-ad-charisma-tuendum.html)* of 14 July 2022.

**b) Military Ordinariates**

Military Ordinariates, established for the spiritual care of military personnel", are governed by the Apostolic Constitution [*Spirituali Militum Curae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/la/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_19860421_spirituali-militum-curae.html) of 21 April 1986. They are defined by a personal criterion (the members are those who belong to the Armed Forces, and their families).

The military Ordinary may be a non-bishop. His jurisdiction is described as being "cumulative" with that of the diocesan bishop, since the faithful remain members of the local Church, and are therefore simultaneously under the jurisdiction of both the military Ordinary and the local bishop.

**c) Latin Ordinariates for faithful of Eastern rite**

These Ordinariates are ecclesiastical circumscriptions which came into being in the twentieth century, to cater for the pastoral needs of faithful of Eastern rite living in territories of Latin rite. The Ordinary is a Latin-rite bishop. Jurisdiction may be either cumulative or non-cumulative with that of the diocesan bishop.

> These Ordinariates exist in Argentina, Austria (for faithful of Byzantine rite), Brazil, France and Poland.
>
> There are other Ordinariates entrusted to Eastern-rite Ordinaries.

**d) Personal Ordinariates**

Personal Ordinariates were established in response to requests from groups of Anglicans who had been moved by the Holy Spirit "to petition repeatedly and insistently to be received into full Catholic communion individually as well as corporately" (Apostolic Constitution [*Anglicanorum Coetibus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apc_20091104_anglicanorum-coetibus.html), 4 November 2009).

The power of the Ordinary, who may be a priest or bishop, is *vicarious* (i.e. it is exercised in the name of the Roman Pontiff).

> From the documents issued to date it is not entirely certain whether his power is cumulative with that of the diocesan bishop.
>
> So far three Ordinariates have been erected: the Personal Ordinariate of Our Lady of Walsingham, for England and Wales (established on 15 January 2011); the Personal Ordinariate of the Chair of St Peter, for the United States (established on 1 January 2012); and the Personal Ordinariate of Our Lady of the Southern Cross, for the territory of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference (established on 15 June 2012).

**4. Ecclesiastical circumscriptions and the "communion of the Churches"**

The Church is one and universal, and among the particular Churches there exists a "communion". The particular Churches are "Church" in so far as the one, universal Church of Christ exists in them. All the Churches are characterised by "openness": the "solicitude for the whole Church" of the sacred ministers.

> See the Letter of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith [*Communionis Notio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_28051992_communionis-notio_en.html), 28 May 1992, nos. 7-9. Nos. 11-14 of the same document explain the basis of this communion of the Churches as being the Eucharist and the episcopate. All the particular Churches are dependent on the Roman Pontiff, who is the guarantor of the communion of the Churches.

**5. Ecclesiastical structures of Eastern law: eparchies and exarchates**

In the Eastern Catholic Churches the equivalent of the diocese is the **eparchy** ([*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf), canon 177 §1).

An **exarchate** on the other hand is defined as "a portion of the people of God which, because of special circumstances, is not erected as an eparchy, and which is established within territorial or other kinds of limits and is committed to an exarch" ([*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf), canon 311 §1).

> In Britain, the Apostolic Exarchate for Ukrainians was erected in 1957, with jurisdiction over Ukrainian Catholics in England and Wales. In 2013 it became an Eparchy in 2013, acquiring jurisdiction for Scotland as well as England and Wales.
>
> The Syro-Malabar Catholic Eparchy of Great Britain was established in 2016, with jurisdiction over Syro-Malabar Catholics in England, Scotland, and Wales.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What is the normal criterion for determining the extent of a particular Church? What exceptions might there be?

2\. What is the purpose of the various "complementary" personal jurisdictions established by the supreme authority of the Church?

**\**
**CHAPTER XIII:\
THE DIOCESAN ORGANISATION\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 374, 381-411, 469-494, 515-572; Book VII, canon 1420.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 23.
>
> Vatican II, Decree concerning the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), 28 October 1965, no. 11.
>
> Congregation for the Clergy, Instruction [*The pastoral conversion of the Parish community in the service of the evangelising mission of the Church*](https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2020/07/20/200720a.html), 20 July 2020.

**1. The diocesan bishop**

Canon 381 §1 states: "In the diocese entrusted to his care, the diocesan bishop has all the ordinary, proper and immediate power required for the exercise of his pastoral office, except in those matters which the law or a decree of the Supreme Pontiff reserves to the supreme or to some other ecclesiastical authority."

> See Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 23, and Decree *[Christus Dom](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html)inus*, no. 11. The heads of the other structures mentioned in canon 368 are treated as equivalent in law to the diocesan bishop (canon 381 §2[^299]).
>
> In exercising his pastoral office, the diocesan bishop is to be solicitous for all Christ's faithful entrusted to his care (canon 383 §1[^300]).
>
> The bishop is the representative of the diocese (canon 393[^301]).

**2. Auxiliary and coadjutor bishops**

An **auxiliary bishop** may be requested by the diocesan bishop, e.g. because of the size of diocese).

A **cooadjutor bishop** is appointed to the diocese by the Holy See. He has special faculties, and automatic right of succession.

**3. Offices of the diocesan curia which assist in the bishop's governing function**

**a) The vicar general**

The bishop is to appoint a vicar general to assist him in the governance of the diocese. The vicar general has ordinary executive power (canon 475 §1[^302]); that is, power for executive (non-legislative, non-judicial) matters (see canon 131 §§1-2[^303]).

Normally the vicar general's executive power extends to the whole diocese (canon 479 §1[^304]).

The vicar general is a "local Ordinary" in the sense of canon 134[^305], and therefore has the powers attributed to local Ordinaries throughout the Code.

**b) The episcopal vicar**

Canon 476[^306] allows the diocesan bishop to appoint one or more episcopal vicars for the good governance of the diocese.

The episcopal vicar is a local Ordinary and has the same powers as the vicar general, but these are normally restricted to a specific part of the diocese, or to specific matters (canons 476, 479 §2[^307]).

> The diocesan bishop freely appoints and revokes the appointment of the vicar general and episcopal vicars.

**c) Other offices which cooperate in the bishop's executive function**

Also assisting in the bishop's executive function are:

- the **administrative curia**, which consists of three principal offices: the **moderator of the curia** (canon 473 §2[^308]: the vicar general normally performs this role: §3[^309]), the **chancellor** (canon 482[^310]), who ensures "that the acts of the curia are drawn up and dispatched, and that they are kept safe in the archive of the curia"; and the **notary** (canon 483[^311]): one or more notaries may be appointed in addition to the chancellor, to authenticate public documents;

&nbsp;

- the **financial curia**, which consists especially of the **finance committee** (canon 492[^312]) and the **financial administrator**, who is "to administer the goods of the diocese in accordance with the plan of the finance committee" (canon 494 §3[^313]).

**d) The judicial vicar**

Canon 1420 §1[^314] states that "Each diocesan bishop is obliged to appoint a judicial vicar, or *officialis*, with ordinary power to judge".

The judicial vicar therefore has ordinary vicarious *judicial* power, and constitutes a single tribunal with the bishop (canon 1420 §2[^315]).

> Normally the judicial vicar is someone other than the vicar general (canon 1420 §1).

**e) Offices which assist in the bishop's pastoral function**

There are other offices which do not share in executive power, but dispense the Word of God and the sacraments. They include:

- the **parish priest**, defined in canon 519 as "the proper pastor of the parish entrusted to him. He exercises the pastoral care of the community entrusted to him under the authority of the diocesan bishop, whose ministry of Christ he is called to share, so that for this community he may carry out the offices of teaching, sanctifying and ruling with the cooperation of other priests or deacons and with the assistance of lay members of Christ's faithful, in accordance with the law".

> Canon 521[^316] sets out the requirements regarding the parish priest's suitability for office. Canons 528[^317] and 530[^318] set out the parish priest's duties and functions.

- the **parish**: see canons 374[^319], 515.[^320]

- the **assistant priest (**or **curate**): see canon 545[^321].

- the **parish pastoral council** (if the bishop wants it): see canon 536[^322].

- the **parish finance committee** (obligatory): see canon 537[^323].

- the **dean** or **vicar forane**: see canons 553-555[^324]. His duties are in respect of a group of parishes grouped together into a "deanery" or vicariate; they include promoting and coordinating common pastoral action in the vicariate; seeing that the clerics of the deanery lead a life befitting their state and discharge their obligations carefully; watching over how the liturgy is celebrated, how the churches are maintained, the parish registers kept up to date, the parish goods administered, and the parish priest's living quarters looked after (canon 555).

> Other figures in the pastoral organisation include **rectorates** (canons 556[^325]-563) and **chaplaincies** (canons 564[^326]-572).
>
> On the role of the parish in the evangelising mission of the Church see the Congregation for the Clergy's Instruction [*The pastoral conversion of the Parish community in the service of the evangelising mission of the Church*](https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2020/07/20/200720a.html), 20 July 2020.

**\**
**CHAPTER XIV:\
THE *PRESBYTERIUM* AND ITS COOPERATION\
IN THE TASK OF THE DIOCESAN BISHOP\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book II, canons 265-272, 495-510.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 28-29.
>
> Vatican II, Decree concerning the Pastoral Office of Bishops in the Church [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), 28 October 1965, nos. 11, 28.
>
> Vatican II, Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), 7 December 1965, nos. 7, 10.

**1. The nature and functions of the *presbyterium***

The *presbyterium*, consisting of the clerics who cooperate with the diocesan bishop in the pastoral care of the portion of the People of God entrusted to him, is a constitutive element of the diocese (see Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 28, and Decree [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), no. 11).

The theological documents on the *presbyterium* state that on being ordained, priests receive a universal function (see Vatican II, Decree [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 10), participating with the bishops in the one priesthood of Christ. The "very unity of their consecration and mission requires their hierarchical union with the order of bishops" (*Presbyterorum Ordinis*, no. 7), since all priests are cooperators of the episcopal order and must bear in their hearts the concern for the universal Church (see *Christus Dominus*, no. 28; *Presbyterorum Ordinis*, no. 10).

> Note that priests are cooperators with the episcopal *order*, not just with their own bishop. Among all the priests in the world there is a special fraternity (*communio*) through their sharing the same sacrament and mission, by means of which they form the "order of presbyters".
>
> At a lower level of the hierarchy are the deacons (see *Lumen Gentium*, no. 29).

**2. Incardination of sacred ministers**

Incardination of clerics is the juridical relationship of ministerial service linking a cleric to a specific ecclesiastical structure, giving rise to rights and duties as regards that structure.

Canon 265[^327] establishes the absolute necessity for incardination. This may take place within

- particular Churches as in canon 368[^328];

- personal Prelatures as in canon 295 §1[^329];

- institutes of consecrated life and societies of apostolic life endowed with the faculty of incardinating;

- a public clerical association endowed with this faculty (see canon 302[^330]; the Dicastery for the Clergy has the privilege, granted by Pope Benedict in 2008 and confirmed by Pope Francis in 2017, of allowing such associations to incardinate).

Clerics already incardinated can pass to another diocese (permanently or temporarily) and are encouraged to show themselves willing to go to places suffering a shortage of clerics (see canon 257 §1[^331]).

> Canons 265-272[^332] set out the rules for incardination and excardination. Canons 269-271 encourage diocesan bishops to be generous, and to make do without the services of some priests, to enable them to help in areas suffering a shortage of clergy.

**3. Juridical forms of cooperation of priests in the functions of the bishop**

**a) The council of priests**

"In each diocese there is to be established a council of priests, that is, a group of priests who represent the *presbyterium* and who are to be, as it were, the bishop's senate. The council's role is to assist the bishop, in accordance with the law, in the governance of the diocese, so that the pastoral welfare of that portion of the people of God entrusted to the bishop may be most effectively promoted" (canon 495 §1[^333]; see also [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 7).

As regards matters of government in the diocese, the council of priests takes over the role formerly carried out by the cathedral chapter (see below), advising the bishop on pastoral matters.

> The bishop must request advice of the council of priests in matters of great importance for the governance of the diocese. However, in most cases the vote of the council of priests is "consultative", and therefore not binding on the bishop.
>
> Canons 497-501[^334] deal with the membership and convening of the council of priests.

**b) The college of consultors**

The college of consultors is a new figure in canon law (see canon 502[^335]). In general its function is a consultative one. Because of the small number of its members (between 6 and 12), it is easy to convene for giving advice to the bishop.

> The bishop must consult the college of consultors before appointing or removing a financial administrator, or carrying out acts of administration of major importance.
>
> The college of consultors has an important role when the see is vacant.

**c) The chapter of canons**

The chapter of canons "is a college of priests, whose role is to celebrate the more solemn liturgical functions in a cathedral or collegiate church" (canon 503[^336]). (A "canon" in this context means a member of a chapter.)

> The chapter of canons of a cathedral church is the cathedral chapter; that of a collegiate church the collegial chapter. Cathedral chapters arose in the eighth century: the clergy of the cathedral lived together in community and followed a common rule. Other large churches followed the same pattern and were referred to as "collegiate" (one such example was Darlington, which flourished up to the time of the Reformation). Chapters were established in England at the restoration of the hierarchy (1850), but the canons were exempt from residence and attendance at the divine offices in the cathedral. They were bound, however, to be present once a month (wearing canonical dress).
>
> Under the 1917 Code the cathedral chapter not only participated in the more solemn liturgical worship of the cathedral, but also assisted the bishop as his "senate and counsel". The 1983 Code, following [*Christus Dominus*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651028_christus-dominus_en.html), no. 27, and [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 7, has transferred the latter function to the council of priests (and more particularly to the college of consultors when the see becomes vacant).
>
> Canon 508[^337] gives the "canon penitentiary" ordinary, non-delegable, faculties to absolve from *latae sententiae* censures that have not been declared and are not reserved to the Apostolic See.

**\**
**CHAPTER XV:\
THE COOPERATION OF THE DIOCESAN PEOPLE\
IN THE TASK OF THE BISHOP\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book I, canon 129; Book II, canons 204-231, 460-468, 492-494, 511-514.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 32.

**1. The juridical condition of the faithful of a diocese**

Canon 204 §1[^338] states that all the faithful are called to carry out the mission of the Church according to their own condition. The Second Vatican Council saw a rediscovery of the role of the ordinary faithful in relation to the Church's mission.

> See also canon 208[^339], which reproduces part of [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 32.

**a) Active juridical condition of the faithful**

The role of faithful of the diocese in developing the Church's mission is made specific in a series of rights and duties.

From an "active" point of view, these rights and duties include:

- "the obligation and the right to strive so that the divine message of salvation may more and more reach all people of all times and all places" (canon 211[^340]);

- the "liberty to make known their needs, especially their spiritual needs, and their wishes to the Pastors of the Church" (canon 212 §2[^341]);

- "the right, indeed at times the duty ... to manifest to the sacred Pastors their views on matters which concern the good of the Church" and "to make their views known to others of Christ's faithful", while respecting the integrity of faith and morals, showing due reverence to the Pastors and taking into account the common good and the dignity of individuals (canon 212 §3[^342]);

- the right to "establish and direct associations which serve charitable or pious purposes or which foster the Christian vocation in the world" (canon 215[^343]);

- "the right to promote and support apostolic action, by their own initiative" (canon 216[^344]);

- the right to "vindicate and defend the rights they enjoy in the Church, before the competent ecclesiastical forum" (canon 221[^345]);

- "the obligation to provide for the needs of the Church, so that the Church has available to it those things which are necessary for divine worship, for apostolic and charitable work and for the worthy support of its ministers" and to promote social justice and help the poor (canon 222 §§1-2[^346]).

Each of these rights and duties is to be exercised according to whether the individual is a cleric, lay person or religious.

**b) Passive juridical condition of the faithful**

From a "passive" point of view, the following rights and duties apply:

- the right to receive the action of the hierarchy, and the duty of obedience to the hierarchy (canon 212 §1[^347]);

- the duty of union with the bishop (as well as with the Pope) (canon 209[^348]);

- the right to receive the means of salvation from the Pastors (canon 213[^349]).

Within the diocese the bishop cannot violate these rights or ignore them, since otherwise he would not be allowing the Holy Spirit to work.

**2. Cooperation of the people in the government of the diocese**

While government does not pertain to the people, nevertheless there is the possibility of helping with advice, and also in certain cases of exercising the power of jurisdiction (see canon 129 §2[^350]).

**a) The diocesan synod**

"The diocesan synod is an assembly of selected priests and other members of Christ's faithful of a particular Church which, for the good of the whole diocesan community, assists the diocesan bishop" (canon 460). It is a consultative body by means of which the bishop, making use of the help and advice of the different components of the diocesan community, exercises in solemn fashion the office and ministry of pasturing the flock, adapting the laws and norms of the universal Church to the particular situation of the diocese.

> Canon 462[^351] deals with the convening of the diocesan synod; canons 463-464[^352] with membership. Canon 466[^353] makes clear that the bishop remains the sole legislator in the diocese, so that other components of the synod have only a consultative role.

**b) The diocesan pastoral council**

Canon 511 states that a diocesan pastoral council is to be established "in so far as pastoral circumstances suggest" -- hence it is not obligatory. "Its function, under the authority of the bishop, is to study and weigh those matters which concern the pastoral works in the diocese, and to propose practical conclusions concerning them" (canon 511).

> Canon 512[^354] deals with membership. Canon 514 §1[^355] specifies that it has only a consultative vote.

**c) The diocesan finance committee**

The diocesan finance committee is dealt with in canons 492-494. It must be established in each diocese, the members being appointed for a renewable five-year term (canon 492[^356]). Its task is to prepare a budget of income and expenditure each year, and to present an account at the end of the year (canon 493[^357]). A diocesan financial administrator is also to be appointed to administer the goods of the diocese in accordance with the plan of the finance committee, and to present an account of income and expenditure at the end of the year (canon 494[^358]).

**3. Involvement of the faithful in other offices**

Canon 129 §2, mentioned earlier, states that the laity can cooperate in the exercise of power of government; there can for example be lay judges (canons 1421 §2[^359] and 1673 §3[^360]); the laity can also exercise other offices such as those of notary (for some cases: see canon 483[^361]) or financial administrator, as referred to above.

However, the principal and most authentic cooperation of the faithful in the diocese is to "contribute, each according to his or her own condition and office, to the building up of the Body of Christ" (canon 208[^362]).
