>
> Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, [*Doctrinal Note on Some Aspects of Evangelisation*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20071203_nota-evangelizzazione_en.html),\
> 3 December 2007.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Exhortation [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), 24 November 2013.

**1. Evangelisation as a right and duty of the Church**

"The joy of the Gospel fills the hearts and lives of all who encounter Jesus. For those who accept his offer of salvation are set free from sin, sorrow, inner emptiness and loneliness" (Pope Francis, [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), 24 November 2013, no. 1).

> See the Vatican II Decree on the missionary activity of the Church [*Ad Gentes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_ad-gentes_en.html), no. 1, which talks of the urgent need for evangelisation. See also Paul VI's Apostolic Exhortation [*Evangelii Nuntiandi*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_p-vi_exh_19751208_evangelii-nuntiandi.html), 8 December 1975, which describes evangelisation as the essential mission of the Church.

**a) The evangelising mission**

Evangelisation is the announcing of Christ to those who do not know him, and involves preaching, catechesis and the administration of Baptism and the other sacraments.

It is "first and foremost about preaching the Gospel to *those who do not know Jesus Christ or who have always rejected him*. Many of them are quietly seeking God, led by a yearning to see his face, even in countries of ancient Christian tradition. All of them have a right to receive the Gospel. Christians have the duty to proclaim the Gospel without excluding anyone. Instead of seeming to impose new obligations, they should appear as people who wish to share their joy, who point to a horizon of beauty and who invite others to a delicious banquet" ([*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), no. 15).

Canon 747[^383] considers the *munus docendi* as an activity aimed at bringing to the faith those who do not yet have it, keeping in it those who already form part of the People of God, and showing the perfection of all that is human in Christ.

> NB no human definition is wholly adequate, since evangelisation is also a supernatural action (see [*Evangelii Nuntiandi*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_p-vi_exh_19751208_evangelii-nuntiandi.html), nos. 17-18). As Pope Francis says, "there is no greater freedom than that of allowing oneself to be guided by the Holy Spirit, renouncing the attempt to plan and control everything to the last detail, and instead letting him enlighten, guide and direct us, leading us wherever he wills. The Holy Spirit knows what is needed in every time and place": [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), no. 280).
>
> The supernatural and human aspects of the teaching office are reflected in various canons of the Code, e.g. canons 768,[^384] 787,[^385] and especially canon 795.[^386]

The Church carries out her evangelising mission through the ministry of the Word and the sacraments. Preaching alone is not sufficient, because although preaching leads to true Christian life, such life finds its living expression in the sacraments. The teaching function is never the mere communication of ideas or of information.

**b) The right to evangelise**

"It is the obligation and inherent right of the Church, independently of any human authority, to preach the Gospel to all peoples": canon 747 §1. However, those who come into and submit to the authority of the Church must do so freely. Consequently, even when the Catholic faith is in harmony with an individual's conscience he or she cannot be forced to embrace that faith (see canon 748 §2[^387] and the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__PX.HTM), no. 160).

> On 3 December 2007 the Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for the Doctrine of the Faith issued a [*Doctrinal Note on Some Aspects of Evangelisation*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20071203_nota-evangelizzazione_en.html), setting out some of the anthropological, ecclesiological and ecumenical implications of evangelisation, and concluding that "\[t\]he relativism and irenicism prevalent today in the area of religion are not valid reasons for failing to respond to the difficult, but awe-inspiring commitment which belongs to the nature of the Church herself and is indeed the Church's 'primary task'."
>
> In [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), nos. 52-75 and 102-107, Pope Francis sets out a number of challenges posed by today's world, as well as by a lack of vocations, concluding (in no. 109): "Challenges exist to be overcome! Let us be realists, but without losing our joy, our boldness and our hope-filled commitment. Let us not allow ourselves to be robbed of missionary vigour!"

**2. Evangelisation as a task of the whole Church**

It is the whole Church that evangelises, continuing the mission of Christ, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit (canon 747 §1; cf. [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), no. 111-134). "Being Church means being God's people, in accordance with the great plan of his fatherly love. This means that we are to be God's leaven in the midst of humanity. It means proclaiming and bringing God's salvation into our world, which often goes astray and needs to be encouraged, given hope and strengthened on the way. The Church must be a place of mercy freely given, where everyone can feel welcomed, loved, forgiven and encouraged to live the good life of the Gospel" ([*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), no. 114).

Hence the Code sometimes considers the function of the People of God as a whole; while at other times it looks at the different responsibilities of the Roman Pontiff, the College of Bishops, the diocesan bishop, the priests and the faithful. These different functions do not imply independence or exclusiveness, but are complementary to one another.

> At times the Code calls on some of the faithful to perform functions which are not being performed by those primarily responsible for them: e.g. pastors of souls may have to make up for the failure or incapacity of parents to form their children in the faith (see canons 773-774)[^388]; or the laity may in certain circumstances preach in a church or oratory (see canon 766).[^389]

**3. The role of the Magisterium**

> See canons 749-754[^390].

The power of Magisterium is the authority to teach publicly in the name of the Church.

The Vatican II Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation [*Dei Verbum*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651118_dei-verbum_en.html) states that "the task of authentically interpreting the word of God, whether written or handed on, has been entrusted exclusively to the living teaching office of the Church, whose authority is exercised in the name of Jesus Christ. This teaching office is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on, listening to it devoutly, guarding it scrupulously and explaining it faithfully in accord with a divine commission and with the help of the Holy Spirit" (no. 10).

> Magisterium may be:

- **authentic**: that is, set forth as coming from Christ, by those endowed with his authority;

- **private**: when given by a private teacher;

- **merely authentic**: when it is taught for the whole Church by the Pope or College of Bishops, without being declared in a definitive manner (the teaching of bishops in communion with the Roman Pontiff also falls within this category);

- **infallible**: this includes not only the specific formulations proclaimed by a definitive act of the Supreme Pontiff with the intention of defining it as a matter of faith, but also authentic Magisterium taken as a whole;

- **solemn** (or **extraordinary**): when a teaching is expressed in a solemn way or by means of solemn formulas;

- **ordinary**: when customary forms are used;

- **universal**: containing teaching for the whole Church;

- **particular**: containing teaching for a particular section of the faithful.

> As for its **content**, it may refer to truths to be believed (dogmas of faith), customs to be followed, moral judgements on temporal matters, exhortations regarding Christian life, and so on.

**a) Those who exercise Magisterium**

Canon 749[^391] specifies those who exercise infallible authority:

- the Pope and the Ecumenical Council (solemn/extraordinary Magisterium);

- the College of Bishops, dispersed throughout the world but remaining in communion among themselves and with the Pope, when they are agreed that a particular teaching is definitively to be held (ordinary Magisterium);

> Under the sure guidance of the ordinary and universal Magisterium, the *sensus fidei* of the People of God is also infallible (see Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 12).
>
> Although relatively few *ex cathedra* pronouncements have been made, much of the Church's Magisterium is in fact infallible because it restates ordinary and universal Magisterium.

**b) How the faithful are bound by the Magisterium**

The infallible Magisterium of the Pope and College of Bishops may

- propose a divinely revealed truth, which requires the assent of "divine and Catholic faith" (canon 750 §1);[^392] or

- propose a truth in a definitive manner because of its connection with divine revelation; the faithful are to "accept and hold" such teachings, denial of which would constitute opposition to the Church's teaching (canon 750 §2).[^393]

The authentic Magisterium of the Pope or College of Bishops which is not proclaimed by a definitive act demands a "religious submission of intellect and will" on the part of the faithful (canon 752);[^394] while a "religious submission of mind" is required for the authentic Magisterium of Bishops (canon 753).[^395]

> Violation of these various obligations may involve heresy, apostasy, or schism (canon 751),[^396] punishable according to canon 1364 §1;[^397] or the crime dealt with in canon 1365.[^398]
>
> Pope John Paul II's Apostolic Letter *motu proprio [Ad Tuendam Fidem](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/motu_proprio/documents/hf_jp-ii_motu-proprio_30061998_ad-tuendam-fidem.html)*, 18 May 1998, filled a gap in the legislation of the 1983 Code regarding the assent to be given to teachings definitively proposed by the Church's Magisterium regarding faith or morals (now dealt with in canon 750 §2).

**c) Examination and judgement of teachings**

Pastors should consider and judge the teachings that are put forward to guide the faithful, determining whether or not those teachings are compatible with revealed truths and in conformity with the authentic Magisterium.

> This role is generally carried out by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, for the universal Church, and the local Ordinary for his own diocese.
>
> Theologians have the right to free investigation and research, but not the right to spread error among the faithful while at the same time wishing to be regarded as Catholic theologians.
>
> The faithful have the corresponding right to receive the faith unaltered.

**4. Different ways of participating in the ministry of the word of God**

"Ministry of the word" is a technical expression referring mainly to preaching and catechesis, and in a looser sense to any type of Christian instruction.

> [*Dei Verbum*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651118_dei-verbum_en.html), no. 24, refers to the ministry of the word as including "pastoral preaching, catechetics and all Christian instruction".

While all the faithful share in the responsibility for the Church's mission (see Vatican II, Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity [*Apostolicam Actuositatem*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651118_apostolicam-actuositatem_en.html), no. 2), they have different functions:

- **bishops** announce the word in authoritative way, and exercise control over the initiatives arising in their dioceses;

- **priests** exercise their ministry in communion with the bishops, and have special responsibility for explaining the word of God in a public manner to the group of faithful entrusted to them;

- the **lay faithful** have the task of imbuing temporal structures with Christian meaning; in so doing, they will transmit and explain the word of God, acting with personal freedom and responsibility;

> The lay faithful may also be invited by the hierarchy to collaborate in some aspect of the (public) mission of evangelising;

- the **religious** "bear particular witness to the Gospel" (canon 758).[^399]

> The hierarchy may call on the cooperation of the religious, while respecting their personal freedom and vows, and the fidelity they must show to their own vocation and spirit.
>
> See also canon 761[^400] on the different ways of proclaiming Christian doctrine, and canons 762-772[^401] on "Preaching the Word of God"; see also [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), nos. 110-175.

**4. Catechetical formation**

> See canons 773-780[^402], and John Paul II, Apostolic Exhortation [*Catechesi Tradendae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_16101979_catechesi-tradendae.html), 16 October 1979.

Catechetical instruction refers to the teaching of Christian doctrine with a view to initiation into the fullness of Christian life (see [*Catechesi* *Tradendae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_16101979_catechesi-tradendae.html), no. 18)

As opposed to preaching, which is intended to expound some aspect of the Christian message by moving the listeners to adhere sincerely to the Lord and to live according to the law of Christ, catechesis presents Christian teaching in a manner that is, above all, systematic and organic.

Catechesis brings together several essential elements:[^403]

- *knowledge of the faith*, to help bring about an ever greater understanding of the Christian message;

- *liturgical education*, which prepares the faithful for full, conscious and active participation in the celebration of the Church;

- *moral formation*, fostering an attitude of conversion and interior transformation so as to lead a life marked by Gospel values and by the practical exercise of mercy;

- *initiation into the apostolate*, by which Christians commit themselves to society and to cooperating in the various ecclesial services, and to living out the mission to which they are called by Baptism;

- *a life of prayer*, because without growth in contemplation one cannot be Christian in today's world;

- *education for community life*, promoting concern for the little ones, fraternal correction, and mutual forgiveness.

> The Second Extraordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops in 1985 called for "a catechism or compendium of all Catholic doctrine regarding both faith and morals". In 1986 John Paul II established a commission with the mandate of preparing the text of what would eventually be promulgated as the *Catechism of the Catholic Church* (see Apostolic Constitution [*Fidei Depositum*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_19921011_fidei-depositum.html), 11 October 1992).

Canons 773[^404] and 774[^405] establish that while it is the pastors of souls who have the primary duty of catechising, all have a share in the responsibility for catechesis, beginning with family catechesis.

> The Encyclical [*Redemptor Hominis*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_jp-ii_enc_04031979_redemptor-hominis.html), 4 March 1979, no. 19, states that "increasing care must be taken that the various forms of catechesis and its various fields -- beginning with the fundamental field, family catechesis, that is the catechesis by parents of their children -- should give evidence of the universal sharing by the whole of the People of God in the prophetic office of Christ himself".
>
> The parish priest should give catechesis on the sacraments, so that the faithful may receive them validly, lawfully and fruitfully.
>
> Religious can also participate in parish catechesis, and ensure that in their churches and schools proper catechetical formation is provided (see canons 776-779,[^406] and the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P2A.HTM), no. 906).
>
> Catechisms and catechetical texts are regulated at universal level by the Apostolic See and at the particular level by the bishops. The Episcopal Conference also has certain competences (see canon 775).[^407]
>
> See [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), nos. 163-168.

**6. The ecumenical movement**

The Second Vatican Council devoted the Decree [*Unitatis Redintegratio*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19641121_unitatis-redintegratio_en.html), 21 November 1964, to the topic of ecumenism. See also the Encyclical of John Paul II [*Ut Unum Sint*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_jp-ii_enc_25051995_ut-unum-sint.html), 25 May 1995, dealing with the Church's commitment to ecumenism, the fruits of ecumenical dialogue, and the ways in which further progress may be made; and [*Evangelii Gaudium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20131124_evangelii-gaudium.html), nos. 244-246 on ecumenical dialogue.

Canon 755[^408] of the 1983 Code states that is primarily the responsibility of the College of Bishops and the Holy See to promote and direct the participation of Catholics in the ecumenical movement. The bishops are to issue practical norms in accordance with the provisions laid down by the College of Bishops and the Holy See, i.e. those in the Code itself, and in the 1993 [*Directory for the Application of Principles and Norms on Ecumenism*](http://www.christianunity.va/content/unitacristiani/en/documenti/testo-in-inglese.html), issued by the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity.

The [Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf) also deals with ecumenism in canons 902-908. The Eastern Catholic Churches are particularly entrusted with fostering unity among all the Eastern Churches (Catholic and Orthodox) by prayers, their example of life, faithfulness to the ancient traditions of the Eastern Churches, mutual knowledge, cooperation and fraternal appreciation. Non-Catholic Christians who attend Catholic institutions can receive spiritual and sacramental assistance there from their own ministers.

Canons 896-901 of the Eastern Code are dedicated to the non-Catholic baptised who spontaneously come from an Eastern Church or other Church or community into full communion with the Catholic Church. If their baptism is already valid, the profession of faith will suffice to receive them into the Catholic Church.

> In the Latin Church the question of *communicatio in sacris* -- the reception by Catholics of sacraments administered by non-Catholic ministers, and by non-Catholics of sacraments administered by Catholic ministers -- is addressed in canon 844, which will be dealt with later.

**7. Catechumens**

Catechumens are those who, moved by the Holy Spirit, ask to be incorporated in the Church. "By this very desire, as well as by the life of faith, hope and charity which they lead, they are joined to the Church which already cherishes them as its own" (canon 206). Through the manifestation of this desire, a juridical relationship arises, with rights and duties.

> See canons 788[^409] (formation of catechumens); 1170[^410] (entitlement to blessings); 1183 §1[^411] (right to a Christian burial); and 1476[^412] (the right to take part in a process).

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the responsibilities of the Roman Pontiff, the College of Bishops, the diocesan bishop, the priests and the faithful regarding the ministry of the Word?

2\. How is preaching to be distinguished from catechesis?

**\**
**CHAPTER XIX:\
CATHOLIC EDUCATION\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book III, canons 793-821.
>
> Vatican II, Declaration on Christian Education [*Gravissimum Educationis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651028_gravissimum-educationis_en.html), 28 October 1965.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Sapientia Christiana*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_15041979_sapientia-christiana.html), 15 April 1979.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Ex Corde Ecclesiae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_15081990_ex-corde-ecclesiae.html), 15 August 1990.
>
> Dicastery for Culture and Education, Decrees [2 September 2002](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccatheduc/documents/rc_con_ccatheduc_doc_20021114_decree-canon-law_en.html) and [28 January 2011](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccatheduc/documents/rc_con_ccatheduc_doc_20110128_dec-rif-filosofia_en.html).

**1. Meaning of Catholic education**

Catholic education involves imparting various areas of learning, and at the same time teaching ways of behaving and acting. It aims not only at human maturity, but also at development according to the measure of the fullness of Christ (see the Vatican II Declaration on Christian Education [*Gravissimum Educationis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651028_gravissimum-educationis_en.html), no. 2).

For education to be Catholic it must not only transmit religious truths in accordance with the Magisterium, but must also ensure the formation of the whole person (canon 795[^413]), which includes human and supernatural aspects -- the order of nature and the order of grace. Hence the need to develop the physical, moral and intellectual qualities of the students.

"Catholic education" is therefore a much wider term than "catechesis". There is no true Catholic education if does not show the human person's relationship to God, and the divine demands of Revelation. Therefore "Catholic" education refers essentially to the *content* of what is taught, independently of whether it is given by an official Church institution or privately by individuals.

> An educational institution can use the name "Catholic" in a formal way only if it is given approval by the Church authorities (see canon 216[^414]).

The primary right and duty to educate belongs to the parents. The civil authority has responsibility secondarily, in a subsidiary manner. The State should not have a monopoly of education, which is against natural law (see [*Gravissimum Educationis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651028_gravissimum-educationis_en.html), nos. 3 and 6).

The Church has a share in this right and duty, both "as a human society capable of imparting education" ([*Gravissimum Educationis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651028_gravissimum-educationis_en.html), no. 3), and also in so far as "it has a divine mission of helping all to arrive at the fullness of Christian life" (canon 794 §1[^415]).

> The first of these two titles is held in common with other societies, while the second is an exclusively supernatural title regarding religious formation.

In the case both of schools (canon 803[^416]) and of higher institutes of education (canon 808[^417]) two kinds of institute may bear the name "Catholic":

- those run by the Church authorities or an ecclesiastical public juridical person;

- those recognised as Catholic by a written document.

In addition to these there are institutions which, while not called "Catholic", are nevertheless Catholic in inspiration.

**2. Schools**

As just mentioned, apart from schools which bear the name Catholic, there are others which are the fruit of the free initiative of the faithful, and for which the faithful themselves are responsible. This is closely bound up with the fundamental right and duty of parents to educate (see canon 796 §1[^418]).

Parents are entitled not only to recognition of their freedom to choose a school for their children, but also to legal protection of the effective exercise of that right (canon 797[^419]).

Parents should send their children whenever possible to schools imbued with a Catholic spirit; otherwise they must ensure the proper Catholic education of their children outside school (canon 798[^420]).

The bishop should watch over the manner in which Catholic doctrine is imparted, taking action if necessary to remove or have removed teachers who are unsuitable. He should also watch over religious education in State schools and schools which remain under the free initiative of the faithful (canon 804 §2[^421]). The bishop does not appoint teachers in these cases, but can lay down general requirements for suitability.

Schools lawfully using the name Catholic are under the more direct control of the bishop, who is responsible for appointing, approving and removing teachers (canon 805[^422]). In the case of schools that have been authorised to call themselves Catholic, the agreement with the ecclesiastical authority will determine how the authority is to intervene in appointments and dismissals.

**3. Catholic universities**

Universities are an institution largely of ecclesiastical origin, although a number were founded by kings and queens. As a result of the Protestant Reformation, the term "Catholic" (as opposed to "Protestant") in relation to a university was used without reference to the origins of its foundation. From the nineteenth century onwards, after the nationalisation of university education, the term "Catholic university" began to be applied to the universities founded by and dependent on the Holy See, as distinct from State universities.

Within the universities founded by the Holy See and dependent on it, a distinction should be made between Catholic universities and ecclesiastical universities. The 1983 Code devotes a separate chapter to each of these two kinds of university, which differ by virtue of the subjects taught and the ends they pursue.

Catholic universities are regulated by canons 807-814[^423] and the Apostolic Constitution [*Ex Corde Ecclesiae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_15081990_ex-corde-ecclesiae.html), 15 August 1990. Ecclesiastical universities and faculties (dealt with in the following section) are regulated by canons 815-821[^424] and the Apostolic Constitution [*Sapientia Christiana*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_15041979_sapientia-christiana.html), 15 April 1979. Both are regulated by their own statutes. Matters falling within the competence of the Holy See are dealt with by the Dicastery for Catholic Education.

The Catholic university is devoted mainly to secular studies, although canon 811 prescribes that it must include at least one institute or chair of theology. For the most part, those who receive this education are not clerics, and the academic degrees granted have civil recognition.

> The use of the name "Catholic" requires the consent of ecclesiastical authority (canon 808).
>
> Similarly to what has been said in relation to schools, there are three kinds of Catholic university: those inspired by Catholicism, those acknowledged by the authorities as Catholic, and those which the ecclesiastical authority establishes canonically, and which will also be called Catholic. The canonical norms apply differently according to which kind it is: those that are only "materially" (not "officially") Catholic depend on the ecclesiastical authority as regards the teaching of theological disciplines, since they need the appropriate "mandate" (canon 812); those authorised to bear the name Catholic, apart from the requirement of the mandate, also depend on the ecclesiastical authority in accordance with their statutes and act of approval; those formally established as Catholic depend on the ecclesiastical authority as laid down in the act of establishment and in the statutes.

**4. Ecclesiastical universities and faculties**

Ecclesiastical universities are devoted to the study of ecclesiastical disciplines and subjects related to them (canon 815). These studies are divided into three main faculties: theology, philosophy and canon law. To these may be added other institutes and research centres.

Although not intended exclusively for clerics, ecclesiastical universities help clerics in their preparation for ministry.

They may be established by the Apostolic See or with its approval (see canon 816), and are governed by the Congregation for Catholic Education.

> [*Sapientia Christiana*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_15041979_sapientia-christiana.html) establishes that it is only in such institutions that academic degrees can be awarded that are valid in the Church (see canon 817).
>
> Decrees issued by the Congregation for Catholic Education \[now Dicastery for Culture and Education\] on [2 September 2002](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccatheduc/documents/rc_con_ccatheduc_doc_20021114_decree-canon-law_en.html) and [28 January 2011](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccatheduc/documents/rc_con_ccatheduc_doc_20110128_dec-rif-filosofia_en.html) amended the length of time required for certain courses; in particular the canon law licence programme is extended from two to three years.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the essential features of Catholic education?

2\. On what basis can there be schools which, although Catholic in inspiration, are not established or run by the Church authorities?

**\**
**CHAPTER XX:\
THE SANCTIFYING OFFICE OF THE CHURCH\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book IV, canons 834-848.
>
> Pius XII, Encyclical [*Mediator Dei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/pius-xii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-xii_enc_20111947_mediator-dei.html), 20 November 1947, no. 92.
>
> Vatican II, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), 4 December 1963, nos. 7, 26-32, 37-39.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 26, 28-29, 37, 41.
>
> Vatican II, Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), 7 December 1965, no. 5.
>
> Paul VI, Encyclical [*Mysterium Fidei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-vi_enc_03091965_mysterium.html), 3 September 1965, nos. 11 and 32.
>
> John Paul II, post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), 22 November 1981, no. 56.
>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P2A.HTM), nos. 901-903, 1122-1126, 1399-1401.
>
> Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, [*Directory for the Application of Principles and Norms on Ecumenism*](http://www.christianunity.va/content/unitacristiani/en/documenti/testo-in-inglese.html), 25 March 1993.
>
> Dicastery for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments, Instruction [*Redemptionis Sacramentum*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccdds/documents/rc_con_ccdds_doc_20040423_redemptionis-sacramentum_en.html), 25 March 2004, nos. 12, 27, 34, 69, 79, 96, and 126.

**1. Canon law and sacred liturgy**

The canons of Book IV of the Code of Canon Law -- "The Sanctifying Office of the Church" -- deal with subjects that are also of interest to dogmatic theology and other sacred sciences, particularly liturgy.

Canon 2[^425] establishes that while the Code does not for the most part deal with liturgical laws, the canons do prevail over liturgical norms in the case of conflict.

The Code also deals with the juridical situations of the ministers and the rest of the faithful, considering the relationship between those who represent Christ in the sacred acts and those who require the sacraments for entering into the Church or for developing their own vocation within the People of God.

**2. Those who may perform the sanctifying office ("*munus sanctificandi*")**

Canon 835[^426] indicates the variety of offices discharged by the different members of the People of God in the sanctification of the faithful.

In the first place is the **bishop**, who is the "steward of the grace of the supreme priesthood" (Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 26) above all in the Eucharist, which he himself offers or ensures is offered.

> Every lawful celebration of the Eucharist is regulated by the bishop (see canon 838 §4[^427]).
>
> Bishops also "control the conferring of baptism" and "are the original ministers of confirmation; it is they who confer sacred orders and regulate the discipline of penance" ([*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 26).

**Priests** exercise their sacred functions to a supreme degree in the Eucharist. They also carry out a ministry of reconciliation and comfort on behalf of the faithful who are moved to sorrow or are stricken with sickness (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 28; Decree [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 5).

The function of **deacons** is to administer baptism solemnly, to be custodians and distributors of the Eucharist, to assist at and bless marriages, to bring Viaticum to the dying, to preside over the worship and the prayer of the faithful, to administer sacramentals, and to officiate at funeral and burial services (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 29).

According to the Vatican II Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), no. 26, liturgical activities "pertain to the whole body of the Church" (see canon 837[^428]). While all the faithful share in the priestly function of Christ, canon 835 §4[^429] makes special reference to the participation of **married couples** in the sanctifying office (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 41; the post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), 22 November 1981, no. 56; and the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P2A.HTM), nos. 901-903).

**3. Liturgical worship by all the faithful**

> See [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), nos. 26-32.

Liturgical worship is the worship that the Mystical Body of Christ offers to the Father. In it, all the faithful adhere to Christ, the Head of the Church, even though they may not be physically present.

The faithful participate in liturgical activities according to their situation within the Body of Christ.

> Hence to emphasise only the "communal" nature of the liturgy would result in a lack of balance which could lead to serious practical errors, such as those mentioned in Pius XII's Encyclical [*Mediator Dei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/pius-xii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-xii_enc_20111947_mediator-dei.html), 20 November 1947, in which the Pope stresses the need to recognise that the priest acts "as the representative of Christ and not as the representative of the people" (no. 92).
>
> See also Paul VI's Encyclical [*Mysterium Fidei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-vi_enc_03091965_mysterium.html), 3 September 1965, nos. 11 and 32.

**4. Kinds of liturgical act**

Canon 834 §2[^430] establishes that public liturgical worship takes place when 3 conditions are fulfilled:

- it is offered in the name of the Church

- by persons lawfully deputed

- through actions approved by ecclesiastical authority.

Consequently, "every liturgical celebration, because it is an action of Christ the Priest and of his Body, which is the Church, is a sacred action surpassing all others. No other action of the Church can equal its efficacy by the same title and to the same degree" ([*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), no. 7).

> Apart from the seven sacraments, there are also the sacramentals instituted by the Church to be looked at in chapter XXVII, below). These are "sacred signs which in a sense imitate the sacraments. They signify certain effects, especially spiritual ones, and they achieve these effects through the intercession of the Church" (canon 1166[^431]). Their administration is an act of public worship (see canon 834[^432]).
>
> In view of the public nature of all liturgical activities, it is clear that they can be regulated only by the authority of the Church. Indeed, the liturgy is so closely linked to the principles of the doctrine of the Church that it is very difficult to separate the authority of the Magisterium from the responsibilities of the hierarchy of the Church regarding the organisation of liturgical activities: *lex orandi, lex credendi* (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P32.HTM), nos. 1122-1126).
>
> The influence of the different mentalities and traditions of peoples is reflected in liturgical law (see [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), nos. 37-39). The celebrant, however, cannot act with complete freedom but must be aware of what constitute lawful adaptations (see canon 838 §3[^433]). The dicastery of the Holy See with primary responsibility for the liturgy is the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments.

**5. Basic principles of law in relation to the sacraments**

**a) Juridical nature of the sacraments**

"The sacraments of the New Testament were instituted by Christ the Lord and entrusted to the Church. As actions of Christ and of the Church, they are signs and means by which faith is expressed and strengthened, worship is offered to God and our sanctification is brought about. Thus they contribute in the most effective manner to establishing, strengthening and manifesting ecclesiastical communion\...." (canon 840).

By means of the sacraments the Church acquires its juridical structure, and through the sacraments the faithful acquire specific responsibilities: the duties arising out of the sacraments of order and marriage; the specific vocation of those who have received confirmation; etc.

> NB: the definition of the sacrament as a sign "by which faith is expressed" should not be taken to mean that the faith of the minister is necessary for their validity; nor does the lack of the faith which is required of an adult for the fruitful reception of baptism or matrimony necessarily render these sacraments invalid.

**b) Competence for establishing laws regarding the sacraments**

Canon 841[^434] refers to the exclusive responsibility of the supreme authority of the Church -- the Roman Pontiff and the College of Bishops -- to approve and define what is needed for the validity of the sacraments.

> Within the limits of his competence the local Ordinary may lay down liturgical regulations for his own diocese (canon 838 §4[^435]).

**c) The right to receive the sacraments**

Canon 842 §1 states: "A person who has not received baptism cannot validly be admitted to the other sacraments." Canon 843 §1 goes on to say that: "Sacred ministers may not deny the sacraments to those who opportunely ask for them, are properly disposed and are not prohibited by law from receiving them" (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 37).

> Some examples of prohibitions may be found in canon 915[^436] (forbidding reception of the Eucharist); canons 1040-1041[^437] (debarring certain persons from the reception of orders); and canon 1124[^438] (forbidding mixed marriages without special permission). Since each sacrament requires specific evangelisation or catechetical instruction, it follows that the right of the faithful to receive the sacraments also implies the right to the appropriate preparation (see canon 843 §2[^439]). It is also the duty of all the faithful to provide such formation. Parents in particular have the duty of preparing their children (see canons 774 §2[^440] and 776[^441]).

**d) Sacramental sharing or "*communicatio in sacris*"**

Canon 844 §1[^442] establishes the general principle that Catholic ministers may lawfully administer the sacraments only to Catholic members of Christ's faithful, who in their turn may lawfully receive them only from Catholic ministers.

The following paragraphs of canon 844[^443] then consider three situations of fact:

- Catholics physically or morally unable to go to a Catholic minister may receive penance, the Eucharist or anointing of the sick from a non-Catholic minister in whose Church these sacraments are valid; there must be a true need, and all danger of indifferentism must be avoided;

- a Catholic minister may administer penance, the Eucharist or anointing of the sick to Orthodox Christians who spontaneously ask for them and are properly disposed; any prior pressure by the Catholic minister is clearly forbidden;

- a Catholic minister may administer penance, the Eucharist or anointing of the sick to other non-Catholic Christians in danger of death, if they are unable to approach their own minister and spontaneously ask the Catholic minister for these sacraments; they must show Catholic faith in respect of these sacraments and be properly disposed.

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P42.HTM), nos. 1399-1401, and the [*Directory for the Application of Principles and Norms on Ecumenism*](http://www.christianunity.va/content/unitacristiani/en/documenti/testo-in-inglese.html) of the Pontifical Council \[now Dicastery\] for Promoting Christian Unity, 25 March 1993.

**e) Principles followed by the Code in its laws on the sacraments**

The Code treats the sacraments as actions of Christ and of the Church. They are never private actions, but celebrations of the Church herself: the holy People gathered together under the care and guidance of the bishops.

Canon 845[^444] sets out the principle that a sacrament that confers character may not be repeated. Canon 846 §1[^445] establishes that the approved liturgical books are to be followed in the sacraments, and that no one may on a personal initiative amend anything in these books.

> Many of the provisions in the Instruction [*Redemptionis Sacramentum*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/ccdds/documents/rc_con_ccdds_doc_20040423_redemptionis-sacramentum_en.html), issued by the Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments on 25 March 2004 confirm this requirement: see for example nos. 12, 27, 34, 69, 79, 96, and 126.

Canon 846 §2[^446] stipulates that ministers are to celebrate according to their own rite (Latin or Eastern).

? QUESTIONS

1\. How do the different members of the People of God take part in the Church's sanctifying office?

2\. When is it lawful for a Catholic to receive a sacrament from a non-Catholic minister, or for a Catholic minister to administer a sacrament to a non-Catholic?

**\**
**CHAPTER XXI:\
THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book IV, canons 849-878.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 7, 11, 29.
>
> Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Instruction on Infant Baptism [*Pastoralis Actio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_19801020_pastoralis_actio_en.html), 20 October 1980, nos. 3, 15.
>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3G.HTM), nos. 1213-1284.
>
> Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, [*Directory for the Application of Principles and Norms on Ecumenism*](http://www.christianunity.va/content/unitacristiani/en/documenti/testo-in-inglese.html), 25 March 1993.
>
> *[Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults](https://www.liturgyoffice.org.uk/Resources/Rites/RCIA.pdf).*
>
> *[Rite of Baptism for Children](https://www.liturgyoffice.org.uk/Resources/Rites/Baptism-Children.pdf).*

**1. The nature of baptism**

Like every sacrament of the New Law, baptism is a visible sign through which an invisible reality is expressed and caused. The transition from mere signification to effectively producing what is signified comes about through a sacred rite which in the case of baptism consists of washing with real water accompanied by the proper form of words.

> The remote matter of the sacrament is real water, but the visible sign is manifested in the washing.
>
> The form of words is that prescribed in the liturgical books. The words indicate the minister, the person being baptised, the action of baptising, the unity of the divine nature, and the mystery of the Blessed Trinity: "I baptise you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit".
>
> In February 2008 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith [clarified](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20080201_validity-baptism_en.html) that a baptism conferred with the formulas "I baptise you in the name of the Creator, and of the Redeemer, and of the Sanctifier" or "I baptise you in the name of the Creator, and of the Liberator, and of the Sustainer" is invalid, and a new baptism is required using the true Trinitarian formula.

At present there are two possible forms of baptising: immersion and pouring. The former is considered theologically more suitable for signifying the Death and Resurrection of Christ, but it is the Episcopal Conference which determines which form is to be used (canon 854[^447]).

From the point of view of lawfulness (not validity), the water must be blessed in accordance with the prescriptions of the liturgical books (canon 853[^448]).

> The blessing of water takes place within the rite of baptism itself, except in the Easter season when the water blessed during the Easter Vigil should be used.

**2. Theological and juridical effects of baptism**

> See canon 849[^449]; see also the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3G.HTM), nos. 1213, 1263-1274.

As a result of receiving baptism, the baptised person is freed from sin (original sin and, in the case of an adult, personal sins); born again as a child of God; configured to Christ by an indelible character ("In this sacred rite fellowship in Christ's death and resurrection is symbolised and is brought about": Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 7); and incorporated into the Church and its sacramental mystery.

Hence baptism is not only the first sacrament, but also the gateway to all the others. Through the indelible character it imprints, the faithful are appointed to Christian religious worship (Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 11).

Incorporation into the Church as the People of God and a visible society has important juridical consequences:

- the baptised person acquires the condition of a faithful Christian, a member of the Church, and a sharer in the priestly, prophetical and royal office of Christ (canon 204 §1[^450]);

- baptism gives rise to the radical equality of all faithful, their common dignity, their common calling to holiness and their common responsibility in building up the body of Christ (canon 208[^451]);

- since baptism is the gateway to the other sacraments, a person who is not baptised cannot be validly admitted to them (canon 842 §1[^452]);

- baptism is the origin and basis of all the rights and duties of the faithful;

- in view of the necessity of the Church, which a person enters via baptism, baptism becomes a right of every person properly disposed to receive it.

> See also canon 11[^453]: baptism also renders a person subject to merely ecclesiastical laws.
>
> As will be seen below, the theological principle of the necessity of baptism for salvation is the canonical principle inspiring several important aspects of the law on baptism.

**3. Celebration of adult baptism: the catechumenate and other requisites**

"Adult" here means a person who has ceased to be an infant (i.e. is 7 or over: canon 97 §2[^454]) and has use of reason.

> One who, though no longer an infant, does not have use of reason is regarded as an infant (canon 852[^455]). This is important because different laws apply for adults and infants, as set out in the [*Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults*](https://www.liturgyoffice.org.uk/Resources/Rites/RCIA.pdf) and the [*Rite of Baptism for Children*](https://www.liturgyoffice.org.uk/Resources/Rites/Baptism-Children.pdf).

For an adult to be baptised, the desire to receive baptism is required for validity. In danger of death, it is sufficient that the person should have expressed in some way his or her intention to be baptised.

> Other requirements (not for validity but only for lawfulness: see canon 865[^456] and the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3J.HTM), nos. 1233, 1247-1249) are:

- sufficient instruction regarding the truths of the faith and Christian obligations;

- experience of Christian life through the catechumenate;

- sorrow for sins.

> Detailed regulations for the catechumenate are given in the [*Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults*](https://www.liturgyoffice.org.uk/Resources/Rites/RCIA.pdf), adapted to the particular circumstances of each region by the Episcopal Conference (canon 851, 1º [^457]).
>
> Unless there is a grave reason to the contrary, immediately after baptism an adult should receive the other two sacraments of Christian initiation, namely Confirmation and the Eucharist (see canons 866,[^458] 842 §2[^459]).

**4. Celebration of infant baptism**

> See the Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's Instruction on Infant Baptism [*Pastoralis Actio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_19801020_pastoralis_actio_en.html), 20 October 1980, whose purpose "is to recall the principal points of doctrine in this field which justify the Church's constant practice down the centuries and demonstrate its permanent value in spite of the difficulties raised today" (no. 3).

The most frequent objections to infant baptism are based on an appeal to faith and human freedom as necessary conditions for receiving the grace of baptism. Behind these arguments is a more or less explicit rejection of three dogmatic principles:

- the existence of original sin which affects every human person except the Virgin Mary;

- the *ex opere operato* action of the sacraments;

- salvation as a gift of God, not a human achievement.

It is true that baptism is a sacrament of faith, but it is also a cause of faith. Thus the fact that infants are unable to profess their faith personally does not prevent the Church from conferring this sacrament in her own faith (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3K.HTM), nos. 1253-1255). Those who in the name of freedom deny a person baptism, in fact deny that person what is his or hers by right.

> It is equivalent, in the natural order, to denying a baby food, on the ground that the baby's consent has not been obtained.

On these doctrinal principles are based three canonical precepts:

- the duty of baptising without delay an infant in danger of death (canon 867 §2[^460]);

- the lawfulness of baptising an infant in danger of death even against the wishes of its parents (canon 868 §2[^461]);

- the obligation of baptising in the first few weeks, making this compatible with a suitable time of preparation (see canon 867 §1[^462]).

> Certain provisions are given in order to ensure the lawfulness of infant baptism (see [*Pastoralis Actio*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_19801020_pastoralis_actio_en.html), no. 15):

- the parents and those who will act as sponsors must be sufficiently instructed on the meaning of the sacrament and the obligations attaching to it (canon 851, 2º [^463]);

- the consent of at least one of the parents or those who lawfully take their place must be obtained, and there must be a realistic hope that the child will be brought up in the Catholic faith (canon 868 §1[^464]).

**5. The minister of baptism**

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3L.HTM), no. 1256; canons 861-863.[^465]

For the validity of baptism, the minister is any person who performs the sacramental sign with the proper intention.

The provisions regarding the different types of minister therefore affect only the *lawfulness* of the administration of baptism:

- the ordinary minister is one who has been ordained, including a deacon (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 29; canon 861 §1);

- canon 863 states that the baptism of those over 14 should be referred to the bishop so that he can decide whether to confer it personally;

- if the ordinary minister is absent or impeded, the extraordinary minister is a catechist or another person deputed to this office by the local Ordinary (see canon 861 §2, which encourages the priests to ensure that the faithful know how to baptise);

- for the purposes of good order, the administration of baptisms is "entrusted" to the parish priest (canon 530[^466]), although they are not his exclusive competence. However, since they are primarily his responsibility, canon 862 establishes that it is not lawful for anyone, except in case of necessity, to confer baptism outside his own territory, even upon his own subjects, without due permission.

**6. The role of the sponsors**

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3K.HTM), no. 1255; canons 872-874[^467].

As far as possible no one should be admitted to baptism without a sponsor, whose function varies according to whether the baptism is of an infant or an adult.

The sponsor helps an adult in his or her Christian initiation, at least in the last phase of preparation for the sacrament, and after baptism helps that person persevere in the faith and in Christian life.

In the case of children, the sponsor, or sponsors (godfather and godmother) have the mission, together with the parents, of presenting the child for baptism, and helping the child live faithfully as befits the Christian vocation it has received.

To ensure that these roles are properly fulfilled, a list of requirements for sponsors is given in canon 874, including those of being a Catholic and having received confirmation and Eucharist, and leading a life befitting the role to be undertaken.

> Hence a member of a non-Catholic ecclesial community cannot be a sponsor, although he or she can be admitted together with a Catholic sponsor as a witness to the baptism. A member of the Orthodox Churches, however, can be admitted as a sponsor together with a Catholic: see Pontifical Council \[now Dicastery\] for Promoting Christian Unity, [*Directory for the application of principles and norms concerning ecumenism*](http://www.christianunity.va/content/unitacristiani/en/documenti/testo-in-inglese.html), 25 March 1993, no. 98.

**7. The role of the parish in recording baptisms**

The parish is the focal point in the pastoral organisation of baptism; and is entrusted with recording the celebration of the sacramental act, which is of great importance not only for the juridical condition of the faithful, but also because the sacrament cannot be repeated (canon 845[^468]) and is an essential requirement for the validity of the other sacraments (canon 842[^469]).

Consequently some specific requirements arise:

- the parents should go to the parish priest as soon as possible to request the sacrament for their child and to receive proper preparation (canon 867 §1[^470]);

- the parish priest must see to it that the parents receive, whether from himself or from others, adequate instruction concerning the doctrine and liturgy relating to baptism (canon 851, 2º [^471]);

- the parish priest is entrusted specifically with the function of baptising (see above), and is responsible for recording baptism in the register (canon 877[^472]);

- as a general rule, the baptism takes place in the parish church of the adult to be baptised, or the church of the parents of the child to be baptised, which is why all parish churches should have a baptismal font.

> Some exceptional situations are dealt with in canons 857-860[^473].

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the chief juridical effects of receiving the sacrament of baptism?

2\. What special considerations apply in respect of the baptism of infants?

**\**
**CHAPTER XXII:\
THE SACRAMENT OF CONFIRMATION\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book IV, canons 879-896.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, nos. 11, 26.
>
> Paul VI, Apostolic Constitution [*Divinae Consortium Naturae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/la/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_p-vi_apc_19710815_divina-consortium.html), 15 August 1971.
>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3P.HTM), nos. 1285-1321.

**1. Theological and juridical effects of confirmation**

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3P.HTM), no. 1285.

Confirmation is the second sacrament of Christian initiation, which perfects and completes the grace and character of baptism.

The new life to which a person is born in baptism is called grows and becomes stronger through the constant action of the Holy Spirit, but it was the will of Christ that this strengthening of the Holy Spirit should also be channelled sacramentally.

According to the Apostolic Constitution [*Divinae Consortium Naturae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/la/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_p-vi_apc_19710815_divina-consortium.html) of Paul VI, 15 August 1971, and canon 880[^474], in the Latin Church the sacrament is conferred by anointing with chrism on the forehead, which is done by the laying on of the hand, and by the words prescribed (*Accipe signaculum doni Spiritus Sancti*: "Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit").

Whereas real water is the remote matter of baptism, the remote matter of this sacrament is the chrism, i.e. oil mixed with balm or another sweet-smelling or aromatic substance as a sign of the "aroma of Christ" which the Christian should spread through his or her works (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3R.HTM), no. 1294).

The proximate matter of confirmation is the anointing with chrism on the forehead accompanied by the laying on of the hand. Together with the sacramental formula, these are the essentials of the rite by which the sacramental sign is performed (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3R.HTM), no. 1300).

"By the sacrament of confirmation \[the faithful\] are more perfectly bound to the Church and are endowed with the special strength of the Holy Spirit. Hence they are, as true witnesses of Christ, more strictly obliged to spread the faith by word and deed" (Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 11). These words, which form the basis of canon 879[^475], describe the theological and canonical effects of the sacrament of confirmation, i.e. what is signified and produced by the sacramental sign described above

In so far as it perfects the grace of baptism, confirmation is a sacrament of the living which operates efficaciously only when the recipient is in the grace of God. The gift of the Holy Spirit, as the specific grace of the sacrament, is not received by one who is in mortal sin.

Confirmation also completes the character of baptism and all its effects. It is therefore a sacrament which imprints character: an indelible spiritual sign on the soul by which the person is linked more strongly to the Church, and strengthened and urged more forcefully to be a witness of Christ (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3R.HTM), nos. 1295-1296).

> If there is no contrary will in the case of an adult, and if the sacrament is administered validly, these effects inherent in the sacramental character are produced objectively *ex opere operato*, independently of the subjective dispositions (including the state of grace and level of personal faith) of the person concerned.
>
> NB: the effects of the sacrament do not give rise to a new mission which the baptised person did not have previously; nor do they substantially modify the juridical condition of the baptised person. What is specific to confirmation is that it perfects and fortifies the baptismal condition.
>
> In view of the importance of the sacrament, there are a number of situations in canon law where it is a condition of lawfulness (not validity) to have been confirmed. Hence the importance of recording confirmations in the register and of notifying the parish priest of the place of baptism so that it can be noted in the baptismal register (canon 895[^476]).
>
> Although confirmation is not absolutely necessary for salvation, in view of the benefits it confers it is the duty of the faithful to receive it properly, and also the right of the faithful to receive it when it is duly and reasonably requested (canon 885 §1[^477]).

**2. The minister of confirmation**

*Lumen Gentium*, no. 26 refers to the bishop as the "original minister" of confirmation. His power in respect of confirmation is therefore "original", whereas such power as the priests may have is a sharing or participation in that power.

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3U.HTM), nos. 1312-1314; and canons 882-888[^478].

The *ordinary* minister is the Bishop. Therefore confirmation by a bishop is always valid, although there are some requirements for lawfulness:

- the bishop may lawfully administer confirmation to his own subjects inside and outside his own diocese;

- he may lawfully administer to those who are not his subjects, within his own diocese, unless their bishop has expressly forbidden it;

- to administer lawfully to those who are not his subjects, outside his own diocese, he needs the permission (at least reasonably presumed) of the relevant diocesan bishop.

> NB: the term *ordinary* does not conflict with term *original* used by [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 26. The 1983 Code of Canon Law is designed for the Latin Church where the bishop is the "ordinary" as well as the "original" minister. In the Eastern Churches, it is frequent for the priest to confirm immediately after baptism.

A priest may also have the faculty to confirm, either *ipso iure* (by virtue of the law itself) or by a special grant. Those who have it *ipso iure* are

- those equivalent to a bishop according to canons 381 §2[^479] and 368[^480];

- a priest who by virtue of his office or by mandate of the diocesan bishop baptises an adult or receives a baptised person into full communion with the Church (see canon 866[^481]);

- in danger of death, any priest, even if under a censure or other canonical penalty.

A priest may receive a special grant of the faculty enabling him to administer confirmation validly to all the faithful within a given territory. However, no priest (not even one equivalent to diocesan bishop) can validly administer confirmation outside his territory or jurisdiction, except in danger of death.

> Precisely because the diocesan bishop (in the Latin Church) is the ordinary minister, he has the duty of administering the sacrament personally or ensuring that another bishop administers it (canon 884[^482]). Confirmation is an episcopal ministry which should not be delegated to priests except in cases of necessity.

**3. The age for confirmation**

Canon 891[^483] says that confirmation should be conferred on the faithful at about the age of discretion, unless the Episcopal Conference has decided on a different age, or there is danger of death, or in the judgement of the minister a grave reason suggests otherwise.

> The condition regarding age affects the lawfulness but not the validity of the sacrament. According to the tradition of the Church, both infants and those lacking the use of reason can, if they are baptised, be confirmed.
>
> From the canonical point of view there is no problem in delaying confirmation to the age of, for example, 14, but it is necessary to be aware of certain underlying theological problems. Arguments in favour of delaying confirmation often call into question fundamental aspects of sacramental theology, such as the *ex opere operato* effectiveness of the sacrament, and its permanent efficacy through being a sacrament that imprints character. Sometimes so much emphasis is placed on the personal dispositions of the person to be confirmed -- the *ex opere operantis* aspect -- that he or she is regarded as needing to be already "confirmed" in the faith, as though the sacrament were not above all an action of Christ, by whose merits we are objectively granted the gift of the Holy Spirit which confirms us in the faith. Sometimes, too, confirmation is seen as a sacrament whose efficacy depends entirely on the person's ability to appreciate, at the very moment of the ceremony, the richness of the gift and the obligations it entails.
>
> It is necessary to remember that one receives the sacrament *in order to* become an adult in the faith, not because one *is already* an adult (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3T.HTM), no. 1308).
>
> From a pastoral point of view, delays in conferring confirmation are often justified on the grounds of the secularised environment and the resulting need for a longer and more intense preparation. This approach has its merits, but there is the problem of leaving children without the help of the sacrament precisely at the time they most need it. The difficulties of the environment may be precisely a reason for conferring rather than delaying the sacrament.
>
> The practice of delaying confirmation also alters the order of the sacraments of Christian initiation (baptism-confirmation-Eucharist), according to which a person should not receive the Eucharist without being confirmed. Delaying confirmation establishes an inverted order of baptism-Eucharist-confirmation.

**4. The role of the sponsors**

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P3T.HTM), no. 1311; canons 892-893[^484].

The person to be confirmed should if possible have a sponsor, whose function is to take care that the one confirmed behaves as a true witness of Christ and faithfully fulfils the duties inherent in the sacrament (canon 892).

Canon 893 states that the sponsor must fulfil the conditions mentioned in canon 874[^485] for sponsors for baptism (see above), thus expressing the connection between confirmation and baptism, confirmation perfecting the character received in baptism.

**5. Recording confirmations in the diocesan register**

Details of confirmations are to be recorded in the diocesan register, or where appropriate the register kept in the parochial archive. The parish priest must notify the parish priest of the place of baptism so that the confirmation can also be recorded in the baptismal register (canon 895[^486]).

> There is a clear relationship with the provisions regarding the registering of baptisms: in both juridical situations, the public good of the Church and the proper safeguarding of the rights of the person concerned require that there should be a record of the sacrament having been received.

? QUESTIONS

1\. Who may validly and lawfully administer the sacrament of confirmation in the Latin Church?

2\. What factors are to be taken into account in determining the appropriate age for receiving confirmation?

**CHAPTER XXIII:\
THE BLESSED EUCHARIST\**
