**1. Definition of marriage**

"Marriage" can mean conjugal life (the "existential" dimension: marriage in the strict sense); or it can refer to the celebration of marriage (the "causal" dimension: the conjugal pact or covenant).

The "existential" aspect is what canon 1055[^551] calls the *totius vitae consortium* -- "partnership of their whole life".

> Canon 1055 is based on the Vatican II Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 48. Rather than a definition, it provides a *description* of what marriage is; and goes on to add

- what the ends of marriage are: the well-being of the spouses and the procreation and upbringing of children (§1);

- the raising of marriage to the dignity of a sacrament (§1);

- the inseparability of the contract and the sacrament for baptised persons (§2).

> On the question of marriage as a covenant between a man and a woman, see the Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for the Doctrine of the Faith, [*Considerations regarding proposals to give legal recognition to unions between homosexual persons*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20030731_homosexual-unions_en.html), 3 June 2003.
>
> In his Address to the United States bishops on their *ad limina* visit, 9 March 2012, Pope Benedict called for "a reasoned defence of marriage as a natural institution consisting of a specific communion of persons, essentially rooted in the complementarity of the sexes and oriented to procreation. Sexual differences cannot be dismissed as irrelevant to the definition of marriage. Defending the institution of marriage as a social reality is ultimately a question of justice, since it entails safeguarding the good of the entire human community and the rights of parents and children alike".

**2. Marriage as a sacrament of the New Law**

Marriage is a sensible sign producing grace in those who receive it with the proper dispositions (the fundamental Scripture text in this regard is *Eph* 5:22-23: "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Saviour").

> The Second Vatican Council refers to the sacramental character of marriage in [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 48: "our Saviour, the spouse of the Church, now encounters Christian spouses through the sacrament of marriage".
>
> John Paul II, in the Apostolic Exhortation [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), no. 13, states that "the Church has solemnly taught and continues to teach that the marriage of the baptised is one of the seven sacraments of the New Covenant \... By virtue of the sacramentality of their marriage, spouses are bound to one another in the most profoundly indissoluble manner. Their belonging to each other is the real representation, by means of the sacramental sign, of the very relationship of Christ with the Church".
>
> The sacrament is not *added* to marriage: rather, marriage itself -- the whole of it -- has been raised and enriched by a supernatural dimension. Hence we can speak of a "new institution" by Christ the Redeemer, in raising it to the dignity of a sacrament. This is why for the baptised, marriage and sacrament are inseparable.

The **elements** of the sacrament are:

- **the external sign**: the matrimonial covenant or pact;

- **the parties**: the spouses themselves;

- **the ministers**: also the spouses themselves;

- **grace**: entitlement to which arises by virtue of the conjugal bond;

- **that which is signified**: namely the union of Christ with his Church (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P51.HTM), nos. 1616-1617).

> The **sacramentality** of the marriage affects

- **the parties** (in whom grace is produced *ex opere operato*);

- **the bond** (which becomes "sacred");

- **the ends** (which now acquire a supernatural as well as a natural dimension).

> The sacramental nature of marriage depends on whether or not the parties are baptised (or subsequently become baptised, in which case the marriage is thereby converted into a sacrament).

**3. The role of consent**

Canon 1057 §1[^552] states that marriage is brought about by the consent of legally capable persons; and that such consent cannot be supplied by any human power.

Consent is the most decisive element of the marriage covenant and the one that brings it into being. Since marriage contains extremely personal rights which affect the bodies of the spouses, consent cannot be supplied by the legal order itself, or by the parents of the persons entering into marriage, or by any other human power. Consequently, human law cannot recognise the validity of a marriage if there is some defect that renders it void according to natural law on account of some substantial defect in the consent (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P53.HTM), no. 1626).

> Canon 1057 §2[^553] describes the object of consent, namely the man and woman in their "conjugality": the woman gives herself to the man as wife, the man gives himself to the woman as husband; and they mutually accept each other as such (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P53.HTM), no. 1627).

**4. The ends and essential properties of marriage**

Marriage is not a human invention, but is inserted into human nature by the Author of creation: therefore it is ordered *naturally* to certain ends (see the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P51.HTM), nos. 1603-1605).

These are the (objective) ends -- the *fines operis*, as opposed to the subjective reasons for marrying (the *fines operantis*).

> Although the parties may have their own motives for marrying (legitimising children, making good some harm done, a desire for wealth, etc.), the marriage is nevertheless valid, so long as there is no exclusion of any of the objective ends established in canon 1055.

Canon 1055 speaks of the marriage partnership being ordered "of its very own nature" to **the well-being of the spouses** and to **the procreation and upbringing of children. These ends are interrelated** (see Paul VI, Encyclical [*Humanae Vitae*](https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-vi_enc_25071968_humanae-vitae.html), 25 July 1968).

> NB: the fact that marriage is ordered to the procreation of offspring does not mean that there must actually be offspring for the marriage to be valid: otherwise the marriage of a sterile person would not be valid, whereas canon 1084 §3[^554] says otherwise. What is clear, however, is that the exclusion of any end would render the marriage invalid.

The **essential properties** of marriage are dealt with in canon 1056.[^555] These are **unity** and **indissolubility**, which are really two aspects of the same reality. Since these properties are essential, their exclusion from consent renders the marriage null and void.

> "... unity and fidelity. Indeed, these two marital 'assets', in fact, before being, or rather, in order to be, the legal obligations of every conjugal union in Christ, must be the manifestation of baptismal faith. In order for marriage to be valid, each of the future spouses must establish full unity and harmony with the other, so that through the mutual exchange of their respective human, moral and spiritual riches --- almost as if they were communicating vessels --- the two spouses may become as one. Marriage also requires the commitment of fidelity, that lasts throughout life, becoming a stable *consortium totius vitae* (can. 1135[^556])": Pope Francis, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2019/january/documents/papa-francesco_20190129_rota-romana.html), 29 January 2019.
>
> The unity of marriage is affirmed in Scripture and Tradition and was dogmatically proclaimed at Trent. It is based on natural law (especially the personal dignity of the man and the woman) and on the sacramental significance of marriage (see *Eph* 5:22-33). The sacramentality of marriage strengthens unity (canon 1056; see [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P51.HTM), nos. 1610-1611, 2387; also Pope John Paul II, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/speeches/2003/january/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_20030130_roman-rota.html#:~:text=After%20having%20dealt%20in%20past,the%20dignity%20of%20a%20sacrament.), 30 January 2003).
>
> Indissolubility is also based on the natural law (marriage is indissoluble because of the end of the upbringing of children, as well as that of the good of the spouses themselves: see canon 1055); and on Christ's command: "what therefore God has joined together, let no man put asunder" (*Mt* 19:6; see [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P51.HTM), nos. 1614-1617, 2364; also Pope John Paul II, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/speeches/2002/january/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_20020128_roman-rota.html), 28 January 2002; Pope Benedict XVI, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2007/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20070127_roman-rota.html#:~:text=To%20the%20Prelate%20Auditors%2C%20Officials,27%2C%202007)%20%7C%20BENEDICT%20XVI&text=Dear%20Prelate%20Auditors%2C,inauguration%20of%20the%20judicial%20year.), 27 January 2007; Pope Francis, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2016/january/documents/papa-francesco_20160122_anno-giudiziario-rota-romana.html), 22 January 2016). The sacramentality of marriage, in which the union of Christ with his Church is symbolised, gives added strength to indissolubility (see canon 1056; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P86.HTM), no. 2365), making it absolutely indissoluble.

**5. Marriage and the favour of law**

Canon 1060[^557] states that marriage enjoys the favour of law, and that as a general principle a marriage is presumed to be valid until the contrary is proven.

> The presumption arises where there is both the appearance of marriage, and a doubt as to its validity. The presumption stands until the opposite is proved, i.e. until the judge is morally certainty of the nullity of the marriage (see canon 1608[^558]), the burden of proof resting on the one alleging nullity. See Pope John Paul II's [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/speeches/2004/january/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_20040129_roman-rota.html), 29 January 2004.
>
> The one exception to the principle is the so-called "favour of faith" (see canon 1150[^559]). This applies where there is doubt as to the validity of a marriage between two non-baptised persons, of whom one is later baptised. In such circumstances it is presumed that the marriage is invalid, so that the baptised person may then marry a Christian. This is not a dissolution of the marriage, but a *presumption* of invalidity *in case of doubt*.

**6. The jurisdiction of the Church over Catholic marriages**

Canon 1059[^560] reaffirms the exclusive jurisdiction of the Church over canonical marriage, except for effects of a merely civil nature, which are the competence of the civil authority.

> According to correct legal principles, the State ought to recognise canonical marriage as a marriage system in its own right, and not merely as a "method" of contracting marriage. The system of "compulsory civil marriage" in force in many countries often results from a desire on the part of the State to impose its own secular tenets.

**7. The *ius connubii* and matrimonial impediments**

The term *ius connubii* ("the right to marry") comes from Roman law. It is a natural right, although there is no obligation on any particular individual to exercise it. In the 1983 Code it is formally recognised in canon 1058: "All can contract marriage who are not prohibited by law".

Limitations on the *ius connubii* must therefore be exceptional. They take the form of **impediments**: a term covering a series of juridical situations affecting one or both of the spouses and constituting an obstacle to the validity of marriage.

**a) Kinds of impediment**

In the 1917 Code a distinction was drawn between "diriment" impediments (affecting validity) and "impedient" impediments (affecting lawfulness). The 1983 Code does away with impedient impediments, although it keeps the term "diriment" in some rubrics and in canon 1073. All impediments are now diriment.

> Canon 1073 states: "A diriment impediment renders a person incapable of validly contracting a marriage".
>
> An impediment may be public (externally provable) or occult (not externally provable): see canon 1074[^561].

**b) The competent authority for declaring or establishing impediments**

Canon 1075[^562] distinguishes between "declaring" an impediment that exists by virtue of divine law (§1) and "establishing" other impediments (§2): both are the exclusive competence of the supreme authority of the Church.

> Canon 1076[^563] reproves customs introducing new impediments, or going against existing ones. Canon 1077[^564] deals with the competence of the local Ordinary, who can forbid a marriage of his own subjects, or of any person actually present in his territory, for a time; but it is only the supreme authority that can attach an invalidating clause to such a prohibition.

**c) Individual impediments**

The impediments listed in the Code (canons 1083-1094) are:

- **age** (canon 1083[^565]): 16 for a man, 14 for a woman.

> The Episcopal Conference can establish a higher age, but only for lawfulness. The impediment is of human law, and therefore a dispensation may be obtained.
>
> \[According to the civil law in England and Wales, as from 27 February 2023 the legal minimum age to enter into a marriage is now 18.\]

- **impotence** (canon 1084[^566]): antecedent (pre-existing the marriage) and perpetual (incurable) impotence to have sexual intercourse.

> The impediment is of divine natural law, and does not allow of dispensation.

- **bond** (canon 1085[^567]): the bond of a previous marriage is an impediment of divine natural law.

> It cannot be dispensed from. It ends by the death of one of the spouses or by one of the forms of dissolution allowed for in canon law (to be looked at later).

- **disparity of cult** (canon 1086[^568]): this applies when one of the parties is a Catholic and the other is not baptised.

> The former exception in cases where the Catholic party had defected from the Catholic faith by a formal act has been removed by Pope Benedict's Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* [*Omnium in Mentem*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_letters/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apl_20091026_codex-iuris-canonici.html), 26 October 2009. The reason for the impediment is the danger to the faith of the Catholic party and the offspring. However, a dispensation is possible.

- **sacred orders** (canon 1087[^569]): the impediment applies to the orders of diaconate, priesthood and episcopate.

> This impediment has its roots in ecclesiastical celibacy which, while not belonging to the constitutional structure of priesthood, is based on Holy Scripture and the long tradition of the Church. A dispensation can be granted, but is reserved to the Roman Pontiff.

- **public vow** (canon 1088[^570]): this applies to a public perpetual vow of chastity in a religious institute.

> The impediment does not apply to other sacred bonds such as promises or oaths. The vow must be public (that is, received in the name of the Church by the lawful superior). It may be dispensed from, but dispensation is reserved to the Roman Pontiff.

- **abduction** (canon 1089[^571]): the elements constituting the impediment are that the abductor must be male; that the woman is either taken away against her will, or kept against her will in the place where she is already; and that this is done with a view to contracting marriage with her.

> The impediment ceases when the woman is both separated from her abductor and established in a safe and free place. Theoretically a dispensation can be granted, but such a dispensation while the woman is still under the power of the abductor would be absurd.

- **crime** (canon 1090[^572]): this impediment arises from certain cases involving the death of a spouse: murder of one's own spouse in order to marry another; murder of the spouse of another in order to marry that other; murder of a spouse by mutual cooperation.

> Dispensation is reserved to the Roman Pontiff.

- **kinship** (canons 1091-1094[^573]): various impediments (**consanguinity**, **affinity**, **public propriety**, and **legal relationship**) are aimed at protecting the dignity of the family so that the intimate relations developed naturally within the life of the family do not go beyond their proper boundaries. They also have the object of helping the Christian family -- and consequently the Church community -- to grow through marriages between members of different families. These impediments are in some cases of natural divine law (certainly between parents and children; very probably between other ascendants or descendants, as well as between brothers and sisters), while in other cases, they depend upon the discretion of the legislator, who takes into account the biological and cultural factors that influence the family structure:

> Dispensations may in some cases be obtained.
>
> In the Eastern Code, there is also the impediment of spiritual relationship (between a godparent and godchild).[^574] This however no longer applies in the Latin Church.

**d) Dispensation from impediments**

"The local Ordinary can dispense his own subjects wherever they are residing, and all who are actually present in his territory, from all impediments of ecclesiastical law, except for those whose dispensation is reserved to the Apostolic See" (canon 1078 §1).

> Dispensations reserved to the Holy See are those from sacred orders (including the diaconate), a public perpetual vow of chastity in a religious institute of pontifical right, and crime.
>
> In danger of death, special provisions apply (canon 1079[^575]).
>
> See also canon 1080[^576] on the so-called *casus perplexus*, where the impediment is discovered by the parish priest or Ordinary after everything is prepared for the wedding, and the marriage cannot be postponed without the probable danger of great harm.

**8. Capacity to consent**

"A marriage is brought into being by the lawfully manifested consent of persons who are legally capable. This consent cannot be supplied by any human power": canon 1057 §1.

By means of their consent the parties contracting marriage make a perpetual and exclusive gift of themselves to each other (see canon 1057 §2[^577]), as the husband of this woman and the wife of this man, with a reciprocal right and a reciprocal duty regarding community of life and love due in justice.

Marriage consent, therefore, in so far as it is a psychological human act, must not only be free, full and responsible, but also sufficiently proportionate to the object of marriage.

A person who, at the time of exchanging consent, does not have sufficient use of reason and will, nor sufficient maturity of judgement to assess -- in understanding and will -- the essential rights and duties entailed in the mutual spousal surrender and acceptance, or who is incapable of assuming the essential conjugal obligations, lacks the capacity necessary to give true matrimonial consent.

> The requirement of this sufficient proportionate capacity is of natural law.
>
> **Consensual incapacity should not be confused with impediments**: consensual incapacity concerns the **internal act of consent**, and involves a serious anomaly in the psychic structure of a person. Such an anomaly prevents the act of will from being a free, full and responsible human act sufficiently proportionate to marriage. An internal act of a person who suffers from an anomaly of the psychic structure is necessarily defective.

**a) Kinds of incapacity to consent**

Canon 1095[^578] refers to three kinds of incapacity to consent:

- **lack of sufficient use of reason** (canon 1095 1º): those persons are considered to lack sufficient use of reason who are affected by mental illness and who, at the moment of exchanging consent, lack the effective use of their intellect and will -- faculties which are absolutely necessary for a human act.

> This includes those who, at the moment of exchanging consent, are affected by other psychic disturbances (e.g. intoxication, drug addiction, alcoholism, somnambulism, hypnosis, etc.), which may not constitute a mental illness from the medical point of view, but nevertheless produce a lack of self-control and of the use of the intellectual and volitional faculties. Such psychological states are legally comparable to a lack of sufficient use of reason, so that the actions of a person in such a state cannot be considered to be fully responsible human acts.

- **grave lack of discretion of judgement** (canon 1095 2º): the parties must have a degree of maturity that is greater not only than simple use of reason, but also than that necessary for many other affairs in life.

> The expression "discretionary judgement" (or "discretion of judgement") refers above all to the degree of personal maturity which enables the contracting parties to discern, understand and desire the essential rights and duties of marriage adequately.
>
> The cause of consensual incapacity is not the gravity of the psychic anomaly, which is a medical concept, but the gravity of the lack of discretion of judgement, which is a juridical concept. The decisive factor is not the mental illness or disturbance giving rise to the serious lack of judgement, but the fact that it effectively deprived the person of discretion of judgement, and thus resulted in incapacity.

- **impossibility of assuming the essential obligations of marriage** (canon 1095 3º): the Code recognises, as a consensual incapacity and a cause of nullity of marriage, a complex series of psychic anomalies (especially psychosexual disorders, although these are not the only conditions) which affect the personality structure of the individual, and while perhaps not depriving him or her of sufficient use of reason, or directly and clearly impeding his or her discretion of judgement, nevertheless produce a psychological incapacity to assume the essential obligations of marriage.

> The nullity must result from causes of a psychological nature. This implies that difficulties concerning the essential matrimonial obligations which are not caused by psychological anomalies, or those which, in spite of being produced by a psychological anomaly, can be overcome by means of ordinary moral efforts, are juridically irrelevant.
>
> In determining this cause of nullity it is important to prove not so much the seriousness of the psychological anomaly as the incapacity of the contracting party to assume the essential obligations of marriage. While expert testimony may indicate the precise psychological anomaly, the task of determining whether there is true incapacity falls to the ecclesiastical judge in each case.
>
> Important in this regard are the [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/it/speeches/1987/february/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_19870205_roman-rota.html) of Pope John Paul II, 5 February 1987[^579]; also his [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/speeches/1988/january/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_19880125_roman-rota.html), 25 January 1988, and Pope Benedict XVI's [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2009/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20090129_rota-romana.html), 29 January 2009.

**b) Lack of consent**

The consent given by a person who is legally capable may be affected by the following factors:

- **ignorance concerning the nature of marriage**: canon 1096 provides that "For matrimonial consent to exist, it is necessary that the contracting parties be at least not ignorant of the fact that marriage is a permanent partnership between a man and a woman, ordered to the procreation of children through some form of sexual cooperation".

> It is rare but not impossible for such a situation to exist. Canon 1096 §2 states that such ignorance is not presumed after puberty.

- **error of fact and of law** (canon 1097[^580]): there is lack of consent when there is an error concerning the person (error of fact: e.g. a person intends to marry A but in fact marries B). Such an error renders a marriage invalid, as there is clearly no consent.

> If the object of the error is a *quality* of the other party, then even if the reason for contracting marriage was a false estimation of that quality, the marriage is valid, unless the quality is "directly and principally intended" (canon 1097 §2). Thus if A is motivated to marry B because B appears to be wealthy, but it turns out that in fact that is not the case, then even though A might afterwards say, "I wouldn't have married B if I had known the true situation", the reality was that A chose to marry the "person" B, while the quality of "B's wealth" was not directly and principally intended. However, if A in marrying B not only believes that B is wealthy but also makes B's (supposed but in fact non-existent) wealth *part of the object of the act of will* at the moment of contracting marriage, then the error invalidates consent.
>
> Concerning "error of law", a person may marry thinking, for example, that marriage is dissoluble. The marriage is nevertheless valid, so long as the error remains in the realm of the intellect and does not enter into the act of expression of consent (see canon 1099[^581]).

- **deceit** (canon 1098[^582]): where deceit has been perpetrated in order to secure matrimonial consent, and has actually misled the other party into agreeing to the marriage, this can be a cause of nullity.

> The object of the deceit must be "some quality of the other party, which of its very nature can seriously disrupt the partnership of conjugal life". See for example canon 1084 §3[^583] (sterility): sterility in itself is not an impediment, but if the other party's consent is obtained through deceit over this quality, then the marriage is invalid. Other examples might be a false claim of pregnancy (in order to obtain consent); deceit concerning a medical condition rendering the woman incapable of having children; or the determination on the part of one of the spouses to remain in a Protestant sect, despite assurances to the contrary.
>
> Deceit for a motive other than obtaining consent is not relevant.
>
> (In a marriage nullity trial, in the absence of an admission by the deceiving party, the reaction of the deceived person on discovery of the deceit is an indirect proof.)

- **simulation of consent** (canon 1101[^584]): in general terms "simulation" refers to a deliberate discrepancy between the internal will of the contracting party and the outward manifestation of that will. Outward consent is given which in reality does not exist (**total simulation**); or it exists but is directed to a juridical relationship which is not properly marriage, since one of the essential elements of the conjugal bond has been excluded (**partial simulation**).

> Partial simulation may consist of

- exclusion of the right to the conjugal act;

- exclusion of the right to community of life;

- exclusion of the right and duty to accept and bring up offspring within the context of marriage;

- exclusion of unity or of the corresponding duty of fidelity;

- exclusion of indissolubility.

> It would appear that all these situations fit within the three "goods" of marriage of St Augustine: exclusion of offspring, exclusion of unity/fidelity; and exclusion of indissolubility.
>
> It is important to distinguish between an intention not to contract marriage (total simulation), and an intention to contract marriage but not be juridically bound (partial simulation).
>
> An intention to contract marriage *and* to be juridically bound, but not to fulfil certain obligations, does *not* invalidate the marriage.

- **force and grave fear** (canon 1103[^585]): a marriage is invalid if it is entered into by reason of force (physical violence) or grave fear imposed from outside.

> Fear can either vitiate consent, or it can be the cause of simulation: these are two completely different situations. Canon 1103 deals with it in so far as it vitiates consent.
>
> The fear must be grave, external (from an outside, human and free cause), antecedent (the fear has to be the principal motivating cause of the marriage), and unavoidable (the victim sees no escape other than by choosing marriage).

- **conditional consent** (canon 1102[^586]): a marriage contracted subject to a future condition is invalid; a marriage contracted subject to a past or present condition is valid or not, according to whether or not the condition is fulfilled.

> Canon 1102 §3 deals with the lawfulness of such a condition: the written permission of the Ordinary is required.

**9. The canonical form of the celebration of marriage**

Marriage has been set forth by the Church as a formal as well as a consensual juridical act ever since the publication in 1563 of the Decree [*Tametsi*](http://www.law.harvard.edu/faculty/cdonahue/courses/CLH/mats/MAT13CLH.16AB.pdf) of the Council of Trent. This document instituted a compulsory canonical form for the valid celebration of marriage, but was modified somewhat in the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Council [*Ne Temere*](https://www.ewtn.com/catholicism/library/decree-on-betrothal-and-marriage-2299) of 2 August 1907, and was largely adopted by the 1917 Code.

Canon 1108 of the 1983 Code lays down that as a general rule the validity of marriage is subject to the presence, at the moment of celebration, of the parish priest or local Ordinary or of a priest or deacon delegated by one of these, and of two witnesses (see [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P53.HTM), no. 1631).

> The ministers of the sacrament are the contracting parties themselves. The role of the sacred minister is to be a witness, along with the other ordinary witnesses, and to ensure that the act of contracting marriage is a public legally confirmed act.
>
> Canons 1108-1111[^587] and 1114-1115[^588] deal with the requirements for the validity and lawfulness of the assistance of the sacred minister.
>
> Canon 1118-1120[^589] set out the requirements concerning the place of the celebration and the liturgical form.
>
> Canon 1116[^590] deals with the extraordinary form of marriage, in cases where the sacred minister competent to assist cannot be present or approached without grave inconvenience. In such situations, "those who intend to enter a true marriage can validly and lawfully contract in the presence of witnesses only: 1º in danger of death; 2º apart from danger of death, provided it is reasonably foreseen that this state of affairs will continue for a month." Canon 1116 §2 adds, but only for lawfulness, that in such a case, if there is another priest or deacon at hand he must be called upon and, together with the witnesses, be present at the celebration of the marriage.
>
> A "secret" marriage (see canons 1130-1133[^591]) is not an extraordinary form of marriage, but a special way of celebrating marriage according to the ordinary form.
>
> Canons 1104-1105[^592] set out the rules for "marriage by proxy" (where a contracting party is unable to be physically present), including the requirements for the validity of the proxy mandate and of the acts of the proxy.

**10. Those who are bound to observe the canonical form**

The canonical form "is to be observed if at least one of the parties contracting marriage was baptised in the Catholic Church or received into it" (canon 1117[^593]).

> The previous exception for those who had abandoned the Church by means of a "formal act" was removed by the *motu proprio [Omnium in Mentem](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/apost_letters/documents/hf_ben-xvi_apl_20091026_codex-iuris-canonici.html)*.
>
> Canon 1117 is binding on a Catholic who celebrates marriage with an unbaptised person, or with a baptised non-Catholic who is not of an Eastern Church, even in the event of a dispensation having been received from the impediment of disparity of cult or from the prohibition on celebrating a mixed marriage.
>
> In a mixed marriage between a Catholic and a baptised non-Catholic of Eastern rite, the canonical form is required only for lawfulness, although for validity the intervention of a sacred minister is required (canon 1127 §1).
>
> For other mixed marriages (between a Catholic and a baptised non-Catholic), see canons 1124-1129[^594]. Canons 1126 and 1127 §2 give the Episcopal Conference competences relating to the necessary declarations and promises and the granting of dispensations. See also [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), nos. 80-84.

**11. Declaration of nullity of marriage**

A marriage may be null because of

- an impediment;

- lack of consent or defective consent;

- lack of form or defective form

> .

The nullity of marriage is *declared* after the corresponding matrimonial process: hence it is not a question of *annulling* the marriage, but of declaring that an apparent marriage is in fact null, and that the conjugal bond has never arisen. The marriage nullity process will be looked at later.

**12. Convalidation of marriage**

In the event of an invalid marriage, the possible steps are:

- to have the marriage declared invalid via the appropriate process;

- to have recourse to the exceptional solution of the man and woman living together "as brother and sister", provided that there is no danger of incontinence or scandal, and the proper authorisation has been obtained;

- to celebrate the marriage again;

- to convalidate the marriage by simple convalidation or *sanatio in radice*

> Simple convalidation is dealt with in canons 1156-1160[^595]. It is the convalidation of a marriage which is null either because of an occult impediment (provided this has ceased either naturally or via dispensation), or because of defective or non-existent consent which cannot be proved. It requires:

- the appearance of marriage, the proper form having been observed;

- the cessation of the cause of nullity (by time, dispensation, etc.);

- the persistence of the consent of the other party;

- a renewal of consent by one or both parties, according to the circumstances.

> No intervention by the ecclesiastical authority is required, unless it is to dispense from an impediment.
>
> NB a new celebration is required if the impediment is public, or if the non-consent can be proved, or if there is lack of form.
>
> *Sanatio in radice* (or *retroactive convalidation*: see canons 1161-1165[^596]) is an act of the ecclesiastical authority whereby a marriage is convalidated -- for example, where one party desires the convalidation of a marriage which is invalid because of an impediment or lack of form, while the other, although persevering in the consent previously given, refuses to renew consent according to the canonical form. It involves a dispensation from an impediment, and a dispensation from the canonical form, if this was not observed. Renewal of consent is not required.

**13. Dissolution of a ratified but non-consummated marriage**

A "ratified" marriage (one which has been celebrated in accordance with the canonical form) becomes absolutely indissoluble once it has been consummated. Canon 1141[^597] bases this absolute indissolubility of marriage on its sacramentality and consummation (see [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P54.HTM), nos. 1640, 2382; Pope John Paul II, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/speeches/2000/jan-mar/documents/hf_jp-ii_spe_20000121_rota-romana.html), 21 January 2000).

If one or other of these elements is missing, dissolution is possible through the exercise by the Roman Pontiff of his vicarious power.

> This power is proper only to God, who is the principal cause. The Pope has power vicariously and is the instrumental cause.
>
> Through this power the Pope makes the conjugal bond "disappear". This may apply in the case of a non-consummated marriage between two baptised parties, or between one baptised party and one non-baptised, at the request of both or of one, even if the other party opposes it (see canon 1142[^598]).
>
> For the validity of the Roman Pontiff's act there must be a just cause.
>
> The process is governed by canons 1697-1706[^599].

**14. Dissolution of a marriage in favour of the faith**

Canon 1143[^600] states that a marriage between two non-baptised parties is dissolved in favour of the faith of the party baptised by the very fact of a new marriage, provided the other party "departs" (see §2).

> This is the so-called "Pauline privilege", based on the text in *1 Cor* 7:12-15: "To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy. But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace."
>
> It involves:

- a marriage between two non-baptised parties;

- the baptism of one of them;

- separation by the one who is not baptised (this could consist of a refusal to cohabit physically, or to cohabit peacefully without offence to the Creator);

- the "interpellations" of the unbaptised party (see canons 1144-1145[^601]).

> The effect is to dissolve the first marriage and to entitle the baptised party to contract a new marriage with another Catholic (or for a grave reason a non-Catholic: see canons 1146-1147[^602]).
>
> For other situations involving the dissolution of non-sacramental marriages on the basis of the vicarious or ministerial power of the Roman Pontiff, see canons 1148-1149[^603], as well as the Norms issued by the Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for the Doctrine of the Faith [*De conficiendo processu pro solutione vinculi matrimonialis in favorem fidei*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20010430_favor-fidei_lt.html), 30 April 2001.

**15. Separation of the spouses**

> See the [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P87.HTM), no. 2383.

Separation of the spouses is dealt with in canons 1151-1155[^604]. Here the conjugal bond remains, but the conjugal rights and duties are suspended.

Canon 1151 states that the spouses have the obligation and right to maintain common conjugal life unless a lawful reason excuses them.

> Since the rights and duties are merely suspended, they reacquire their force as soon as the lawful reason disappears.
>
> Lawful reasons include situations going against the fundamental principles of marriage, such as adultery, or grave bodily or spiritual danger to the spouse or children.
>
> The procedures are given in canons 1692-1696.[^605]

**16. Preparation for marriage**

The documents of the Second Vatican Council and subsequent Magisterium make clear that marriage is a way of holiness: see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 41; [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), nos. 47-52; [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), no. 34.

Canons 1063-1065[^606] deal with the pastoral attention of the future spouses, canon 1063 referring to the obligation on pastors of souls to ensure that their own church community provides the assistance by which the married state is preserved in its Christian character and develops in perfection.

This assistance includes preaching and catechetical instruction, including making use of the means of social communication; personal preparation for entering marriage; the fruitful celebration of the marriage liturgy; and the help given to those who are married to enable them to grow in holiness and the fulness of family life (see [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P53.HTM), no. 1632, and the 2016 [*Ordo Celebrandi Matrimonium*](https://archseattle.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Order-of-Celebration-for-Matrimony-min.pdf), nos. 12-27).

Canon 1065 §1 states that the parties should be confirmed if this is possible without grave inconvenience. Canon 1065 §2 earnestly recommends the parties to go to confession and receive communion.

Pastoral attention should maintain a delicate balance between the *ius connubii* of all the faithful (canon 1058[^607]) and the necessary preparation to ensure they receive the sacrament fruitfully (canon 1065 §2).

> In this connection see the reflections of Pope Benedict XVI in his [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2011/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20110122_rota-romana.html#:~:text=Dear%20Members%20of%20the%20Tribunal,thank%20for%20his%20courteous%20words.), 22 January 2011, and of Pope Francis in his [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/speeches/2019/january/documents/papa-francesco_20190129_rota-romana.html), 29 January 2019; also Pope Francis's post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation [*Amoris Laetitia*](https://www.vatican.va/content/dam/francesco/pdf/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20160319_amoris-laetitia_en.pdf), nos. 205-216.
>
> For pastoral directives concerning more difficult cases and irregular unions, see [*Familiaris Consortio*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_exhortations/documents/hf_jp-ii_exh_19811122_familiaris-consortio.html), nos. 80-84; Pope Francis, [*Amoris Laetitia*](https://www.vatican.va/content/dam/francesco/pdf/apost_exhortations/documents/papa-francesco_esortazione-ap_20160319_amoris-laetitia_en.pdf), nos. 296-300.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What is meant by the objective ends and the essential properties of marriage?

2\. What is the difference between an impediment and a defect in consent?

3\. Why does the Church insist on a canonical form of marriage?**\**


**\
CHAPTER XXVIII:\
OTHER ACTS OF DIVINE WORSHIP. SACRED PLACES AND TIMES\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>

>

>

>
> [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P38.HTM), nos. 1159-1162, 1174-1178, 1667-1673, 1680-1690, 2101-2103, 2150-2155.
>

>

>
