**1. Sacramentals**

> See canons 1166-1172[^608]; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P58.HTM), nos. 1667-1673; Vatican II Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), no. 60.

Sacramentals are sacred signs which signify, and through the intercession of the Church achieve, certain effects, especially spiritual ones. They are similar to the sacraments, but differ in that they are of ecclesiastical institution; they do not produce grace *ex opere operato* but only *obtain* it; they are signs of the prayer of the Church rather than of grace; and they are instituted not to produce grace but rather to prepare people to receive it and to sanctify the different circumstances of life.

> Since they are of ecclesiastical institution and are linked to the intercession of the universal Church, it is only the Apostolic See that can establish new sacramentals, or authentically interpret, suppress or change existing ones (canon 1167 §1).

As a rule only clerics are the ordinary ministers of sacramentals, although according to canon 1168 the Ordinary can allow lay people with the requisite qualities to administer some sacramentals.

The cleric's power of order is not sufficient in itself: he must also have power given by the law itself or by the competent authority. In this respect the Code establishes certain general rules:

- **consecrations** (generally of persons) and **dedications** (of things, such as an altar or a church) must be administered by a bishop or by a priest permitted to do so by law or by a legitimate grant of power;

- **blessings**: all things or places destined for divine worship that do not require a dedication should be blessed in order to become sacred things or places.

> Priests can give all kinds of blessings not reserved to the Pope or bishops. Deacons cannot carry out consecrations or dedications, and can only give those blessings which the law expressly allows them to. On the pastoral meaning of blessings, see Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, Declaration [*Fiducia Supplicans*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_ddf_doc_20231218_fiducia-supplicans_en.html), 18 December 2023.

- **exorcisms** -- the invocation of the name of God by a lawful minister with the purpose of removing the devil in an imperative way from a person, animal, place or thing -- are strictly governed by canon 1172. The special and express permission of the local Ordinary is necessary; and the Ordinary will only grant such permission to a priest with piety, knowledge, prudence and integrity of life.

**2. Liturgy of the hours**

> See canons 1173-1175[^609]; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P39.HTM), nos. 1174-1178; Vatican II, Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy [*Sacrosanctum Concilium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19631204_sacrosanctum-concilium_en.html), no. 84; Vatican II, Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 5.

"In fulfilment of the priestly office of Christ, the Church celebrates the liturgy of the hours, wherein it listens to God speaking to his people and recalls the mystery of salvation. In this way, the Church praises God without ceasing, in song and prayer, and it intercedes with him for the salvation of the whole world" (canon 1173)

In view of its nature as an act of public worship, those primarily obliged to celebrate the liturgy of the hours each day are deacons preparing for the priesthood, and all priests and bishops: (canons 276 §2[^610]; 1174 §1).

Permanent deacons are obliged to pray that part of the Office which the Episcopal Conference determines (canon 276 §2, 3º).

Members of institutes of religious life and societies of apostolic life are obliged to pray the Office in accordance with their constitutions (canon 1174 §1).

The celebration of the liturgy of the hours is a function entrusted to the cathedral and collegiate chapters of canons, in accordance with their own statutes (canons 503-505[^611]).

**3. Church funerals**

> See canons 1176-1185[^612]; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P5A.HTM), nos. 1680-1690.

In Church funerals, celebrated according to the norms of the liturgical books, "the Church prays for the spiritual support of the dead, it honours their bodies, and at the same time it brings to the living the comfort of hope" (canon 1176 §2).

The basis of funerals is the belief in Purgatory, the resurrection of the body, and the Paschal significance of Christian death.

"Christ's faithful who have died are to be given a Church funeral according to the norms of law" (canon 1176 §1).

"The Church earnestly recommends that the pious custom of burial be retained; but it does not forbid cremation, unless this is chosen for reasons which are contrary to Christian teaching" (canon 1176 §3).

> NB: it is not permitted to celebrate the funeral in a church in the presence of an urn containing the ashes: it is the body, not the ashes, that receives liturgical honour. See also Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for the Doctrine of the Faith, Instruction [*Ad resurgendum cum Christo*](https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2016/10/25/161025c.html), 15 August 2016, regarding the burial of the deceased and the conservation of the ashes in the case of cremation; and Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, *Two questions about the preservation of the ashes of the deceased following cremation*, 9 December 2023\]
>
> Canons 1177-1182 refer to the places in which funerals may be celebrated, the offerings that can be received, and the registering of burials.
>
> Canons 1183-1185 specify who may be allowed or denied a church funeral.

**4. Veneration of the saints, sacred images and relics**

> See canons 1186-1190[^613]; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P38.HTM), nos. 1159-1162.

Veneration of the saints is based on the dogma of the Communion of Saints: on the powerful intercession of those already in the glory of heaven (see [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 49), and on the example they give to the faithful.

> Public veneration can only be given to those servants of God whom the ecclesiastical authority has numbered among the Saints or the Blessed (canon 1187). Special veneration is given to "the Mother of God, whom Christ constituted the Mother of all" (canon 1186).

"The practice of exposing sacred images in churches for the veneration of the faithful is to be retained. However, these images are to be displayed in moderate numbers and in suitable fashion, so that the Christian people are not disturbed, nor is occasion given for less than appropriate devotion" (canon 1188).

> For the restoration of precious images, canon 1189 requires the written permission of the Ordinary, who is to consult experts beforehand.
>
> See Congregation \[now Dicastery\] for the Causes of the Saints, Instruction [*Relics in the Church: authenticity and preservation*](https://www.causesanti.va/it/documenti/relics-in-the-church-authenticity-and-preservation.html), 8 December 2017, on the canonical procedure to follow in order to verify the authenticity of relics and mortal remains, to guarantee their preservation and to promote the veneration of relics.

As regards sacred relics, canon 1190 §1 says that it is absolutely wrong to sell sacred relics. If they are "distinguished" or held in great veneration, the permission of the Apostolic See is necessary before they can be validly transferred on a permanent basis (§2).

**5. Vows and oaths**

> See canons 1191-1204[^614]; [*Catechism of the Catholic Church*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P7D.HTM), nos. 2101-2103, 2150-2155.

A vow is "a deliberate and free promise made to God, concerning some good which is possible and better. The virtue of religion requires that it be fulfilled" (canon 1191 §1).

> The different kinds of vow are set out in canon 1192.
>
> All who have suitable use of reason can make a vow unless the law forbids it. For example, those under 18 do not have the capacity to make temporary vows in a religious institute; and those under 21 cannot make perpetual vows (see canons 656[^615], 658[^616]). But outside a religious institute, if they have use of reason, they can make vows.
>
> As a general rule, acts performed out of grave and unjust fear or deceit are valid unless the law determines otherwise (see canon 125 §2[^617]). One of the exceptions to this general rule is precisely the making of a vow: see canon 1191 §3.
>
> Canons 1194-1198 deal with the ways in which a vow may cease.

"An oath is the invocation of the divine Name as witness to the truth. It cannot be taken except in truth, judgement and justice" (canon 1199 §1).

> An oath is **assertory** when God is called to witness the truth of an affirmation regarding past or present events.
>
> It is **promissory** when the divine Name is invoked as a witness to the promise made. In this case, to the obligation of fulfilling the promise is added a new obligation based on the virtue of religion (canon 1200 §1), without altering the nature of the promise, so that if the promise was bad, the oath in no way reinforces it (canon 1201).
>
> An oath must be a fully free act. If it is extorted by deceit, force or grave fear it is invalid by virtue of the law itself (canon 1200 §2).
>
> A promissory oath may cease in the same ways as a vow, except that in the case of an oath it is also possible for the obligation to be remitted by the person in whose favour the oath was sworn.

**6. Sacred places**

> See canons 1205-1243.[^618]

Sacred places are "those places which are assigned to divine worship or to the burial of the faithful by the dedication or blessing which the liturgical books prescribe for this purpose" (canon 1205).

> The **dedication** -- formerly called consecration -- is the responsibility primarily of the diocesan bishop or equivalent. Exceptionally the task can be delegated to a priest (canon 1206).\
> The **blessing** is the responsibility of the Ordinary, although the blessing of churches is reserved to the diocesan bishop. Another priest can be delegated for the purpose (canon 1207).\
> (As seen earlier, churches should in principle be dedicated rather than blessed, but there are some circumstances in which liturgical law prevents dedication.)

**a) Churches**

"The term church means a sacred building intended for divine worship, to which the faithful have right of access for the exercise, especially the public exercise, of divine worship" (canon 1214).

> The characteristic feature is free access by the public.

**b) Oratories and private chapels**

"An oratory means a place which, by permission of the Ordinary, is set aside for divine worship, for the convenience of some community or group of the faithful who assemble there, to which however other members of the faithful may, with the consent of the competent Superior, have access" (canon 1223).

> Oratories differ from churches in that there is restricted access, and also in that churches cannot be built without the express written consent of the diocesan bishop (canon 1215), whereas an oratory merely needs the permission of the Ordinary. In addition, churches must be dedicated (or at least blessed) before any act of worship can be celebrated there. Oratories are not dedicated, although it is fitting for them to be blessed. In any case, they should be used exclusively for divine worship.

"The term private chapel means a place which, by permission of the local Ordinary, is set aside for divine worship, for the convenience of one or more individuals" (canon 1226).

> As opposed to oratories, private chapels are for one or more individuals, and the permission must be from the *local* Ordinary (in the case of oratories it is sufficient to have the permission of the Ordinary, i.e. the one who personally holds executive power, e.g. the major superior in a clerical religious institute of pontifical right).
>
> Like oratories, private chapels are not dedicated, but it is advisable for them to be blessed: otherwise they would not be sacred places (although in view of their being used only for divine worship they would be pious places: see canon 1229).

**c) Shrines**

"The term shrine means a church or other sacred place which, with the approval of the local Ordinary, is by reason of special devotion frequented by the faithful as pilgrims" (canon 1230).

> Shrines can be diocesan, national or international (see canons 1231-1232).

**d) Altars**

The altar is the table on which the Eucharistic sacrifice is celebrated (canon 1235). For it to be a sacred place it must be a table reserved for that function, and dedicated or at least blessed (canon 1237 §1).

> It is called **fixed** if it is so constructed that it is attached to the floor and cannot be moved. It should normally be of stone, although the Episcopal Conference can decide on some other worthy and solid material. (The support can be of any material).
>
> If it can be removed, it is called **movable**, and can be of any solid material suitable for liturgical use (canon 1236 §2).
>
> A fixed altar should be dedicated; a movable altar can be dedicated or blessed (canon 1237 §1).
>
> No secular usage of the altar is allowed (canon 1239).

**e) Cemeteries**

Where possible the Church should have its own cemeteries, or at least an area in a public cemetery which is blessed and reserved for the faithful. If this is not possible, each individual grave must be blessed.

Parishes and religious institutes may have their own cemeteries.

> Bodies (other than those of Popes, Cardinals and, in their proper churches, diocesan bishops, including retired bishops) should not be buried in churches.

**7. Sacred times**

> See canons 1244-1253.[^619]

Only the supreme authority can establish, transfer or suppress holydays or days of penance applicable to the universal Church (see canon 1244 §1)

Diocesan bishops can proclaim special holydays or days of penance for their territories, for individual occasions (canon 1244 §2).

> Canons 1246-1253 set out the provisions on feast days and days of penance.
>
> Faculties for dispensing are dealt with in canon 1245.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the chief kinds of sacramental, and who may administer them?

2\. What is meant by a "sacred place" in canon law?

**\**
**CHAPTER XXIX:\
TEMPORAL GOODS AND THE MISSION OF THE CHURCH\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book V, canons 1254-1310.
>
> Vatican II, Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), 7 December 1965, no. 76.
>
> Vatican II, Decree on the Ministry and Life of Priests [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), 7 December 1965, no. 20.

**1. The Church's right to temporal goods**

The Church, as an earthly and spiritual society, requires temporal goods for her mission. According to canon 1254[^620], this is an inherent right of the Church.

> The Vatican II Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 76, speaks of the Church making use of temporal goods "in so far as her own mission requires it".

**2. Ecclesiastical goods**

Canon 1257 §1[^621] lays down the principle that "All temporal goods belonging to the universal Church, to the Apostolic See or to other public juridical persons in the Church, are ecclesiastical goods". Such goods may result from donations, taxes, and so on. All ecclesiastical goods are under the supreme authority of the Roman Pontiff (canon 1256[^622]).

The purpose of ecclesiastical goods is to serve the specific objectives of each public juridical person, the more general aims mentioned in canon 1254 §2, and the ultimate goal of the salvation of souls.

Ecclesiastical goods are governed both by the relevant provisions of the Code of Canon Law, and by the statutes of the public juridical person.

> A private juridical person may own goods, but they are not "ecclesiastical" (canon 1255[^623]), and they are governed only by the statutes of the private juridical person itself.
>
> In the Eastern Code there are no private juridical persons. Hence the goods of any juridical person are "ecclesiastical": [*Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches*](https://orthocath.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/1990_code_of_canons_of_the_eastern_churches.pdf), canon 1009 §2[^624].

**3. Sacred and precious objects**

**Sacred objects** are those goods (places or things) set aside for divine worship by means of a dedication or blessing (canon 1171[^625]). They are not necessarily "ecclesiastical goods", but the law gives them special protection (see canons 1171, 1210[^626], 1269[^627]).

**Precious objects** are "ecclesiastical goods" of special value (artistic, historical, material, venerational, etc.): see canons 1189[^628], 1190[^629], 1292 §2[^630]. They are also given special protection by the law (see canons 1270[^631], 1283[^632], 1292 §2).

**4. Ownership and jurisdictional powers over ecclesiastical goods**

In canon law the Roman Pontiff is considered to have "competence" over ecclesiastical goods, but is not their "owner".

> This subordination of ecclesiastical goods to the competence of the ecclesiastical authority arises from the public nature of ownership by public juridical persons. Their goods are "public" and therefore subject to the administrative rules laid down by the competent authority.

There are three levels of patrimonial organisation: supreme administration (the Roman Pontiff); intermediate administration (the Ordinary or the Episcopal Conference); and immediate administration (the owner).

> **The Roman Pontiff** (canon 1273[^633]) can establish laws and make judgements regarding ecclesiastical goods. He can also make specific acts of administration of the goods of public juridical persons, although he normally acts through other bodies.
>
> **The Ordinary** (cf. canon 1276[^634]): is not a vicar of the Pope. His competences arise from the fact that he is the one who establishes the public juridical persons which own the goods. He has general competences regarding vigilance and organisation; and specific competences regarding acts of extraordinary administration, permissions for civil proceedings, and receiving the oath of the administrators.
>
> **The Episcopal Conference** has competences for unifying regulations at the supradiocesan level.
>
> Immediate ownership of ecclesiastical goods is that of the public juridical person, although a juridical person can only act through a representative (canon 1256[^635]). Every juridical person, therefore, must have an **administrator** -- not only the "inherent administrator" e.g. the parish priest in the case of a parish), but also a person appointed by the juridical person itself or by the Ordinary to fulfil the office of administrator. Every juridical person should have a finance committee, or at least two counsellors to help the administrator (canon 1280[^636]).
>
> Although private juridical persons do not have ecclesiastical goods (canon 1257[^637]), nevertheless these private goods have an "ecclesial" aim, and consequently they come within the scope of the ecclesiastical authority's right and duty of vigilance. They are governed principally, not by Book V of the Code (except for a small number of matters, e.g. canon 1280), but by their statutes.

**5. Pious causes**

A "pious cause" arises where a person disposes of his or her goods in favour of the Church, determining that those goods should be used for worship or charity. There should always be a juridical person to receive the goods, and to take responsibility for ensuring that the will of the donor is complied with (canon 1300[^638]).

The goods donated will be public or private according to whether the juridical person receiving them is public or private.

A pious cause that is longer-lasting is called a foundation, and consists of an endowment that produces income which is used to accomplish the ends of the foundation.

> It is called "autonomous" if the foundation itself is a public juridical person.
>
> If it is integrated into an already existing public juridical person it is called "non-autonomous"

The aim of the foundation must be consistent with the mission of the Church (see canons 1305-1310[^639]).

**6. Acquisition of goods by the Church**

The general principle outlined in canon 1259 is that "The Church may acquire temporal goods in any way in which, by either natural or positive law, it is lawful for others to do this".

All the Church's faithful (not just the hierarchy) need to work towards achieving the Church's aim, although in general the Church prefers to promote generosity rather than impose obligations (thus avoiding the appearance of material interest).

> See [*Presbyterorum Ordinis*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decree_19651207_presbyterorum-ordinis_en.html), no. 20, and canon 222 §1[^640] on the duty of the faithful to provide for the needs of the Church.
>
> The ways in which fulfilment of this duty may be organised include:

- voluntary offerings in response to appeals by the Church;

- voluntary offerings in response to appeals for alms by private persons (these need the permission of the Ordinary);

- spontaneous offerings;

- offerings made on the occasion of pastoral services (although all appearance of trading or "payment" should be avoided);

- fees for acts of the administrative or judicial authority where these have been requested;

- taxes on public juridical persons for the needs of the diocese;

- extraordinary taxes on private juridical persons and physical persons in cases of grave financial need;

- the levy for the seminary, imposed on public and private juridical persons.

**7. Administration of ecclesiastical goods**

The Code draws a distinction between acts of "ordinary" and "extraordinary" administration.

In broad terms, acts of ordinary administration are those which are aimed at preserving and making effective use of the patrimony, without putting it at risk; while acts of extraordinary administration are those which "go beyond the limits and manner of ordinary administration" (canon 1281[^641]); they affect the substance and stability of the patrimony in a significant way (see canon 1295[^642]).

> What constitutes an extraordinary act is determined by the statutes of the juridical person, the bishop and the Episcopal Conference (canons 1277[^643], 1281). The Episcopal Conference establishes the values for which permission for the act of administration is required. If an administrator carries out an extraordinary act without due permission, he acts invalidly.
>
> Regarding the competences and obligations of administrators of goods, see canons 1282-1287[^644].

**8. Alienation of ecclesiastical goods**

> See canons 1290-1298.[^645]

"Alienation" of ecclesiastical goods involves disposing of the goods in some way. Since it includes any transaction whereby the patrimonial condition of the juridical person may be jeopardised (sales, contracts, leasing, etc.) it constitutes an act of extraordinary administration.

To dispose validly of goods pertaining to the stable patrimony of the juridical person, it is necessary to obtain the permission of the relevant authority and the agreement of the college of consultors and the finance committee.

> In some cases the Holy See's permission is needed (see canon 1292 §2).
>
> Canon 1296 deals with situations where an act of alienation is invalid canonically but valid in civil law.

? QUESTIONS

1\. What is the justification for the Church's making use of temporal goods?

2\. What is meant by the terms "ordinary" and "extraordinary" administration?

**\**
**CHAPTER XXX:\
CANONICAL OFFENCES AND PUNISHMENTS\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book VI, canons 1311-1399.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Constitution [*Pascite gregem Dei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/papa-francesco_costituzione-ap_20210523_pascite-gregem-dei.html), 23 May 2021.
>
> *Other readings:*
>
> *- John A. Renken: "Delicts of Financial Malfeasance in the Revised Penal Law", in Studies in Church Law, vol. XVI (2021), pp. 15-30*
>
> *- Valère Nkouaya Mbandji: "The Revised Book VI of the CIC/83: Major Changes and Issues Not Addressed", in Studies in Church Law, vol. XVI (2021), pp. 31-69*
>
> *- Juan Ignacio Arrieta: "The return of Penal Discipline in the pastoral field of Government", in Canon Law Society Newsletter no. 204 (2023), pp. 27-44*
>
> *- Juan Ignacio Arrieta: "A Presentation of the New Penal System of Canon Law", in The Jurist, 77/2 (2021), pp. 245-267*
>
> *John Paul Kimes: "Reclaiming 'Pastoral': Pascite gregem Dei and Its Vision of Penal Law", in The Jurist, 77/2 (2021), pp. 269-289*

**1. Penal law in the Church: general principles**

Book VI of the Code of Canon Law deals with canonical penal law, which sets out how the Church responds to certain serious and harmful external sins, called "offences".

The whole of Book VI (canons 1311-1399) was reformed by Pope Francis's Apostolic Constitution [*Pascite gregem Dei*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/papa-francesco_costituzione-ap_20210523_pascite-gregem-dei.html) of 23 May 2021.

The Church is a visible assembly and spiritual community (Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 8), and to fulfil her mission she has not only the right but also the duty to protect the faithful -- including those faithful who commit offences -- from the consequences flowing from certain external sins. To do this the Church makes use of means suitable to her nature and purpose: prayer and other spiritual means; then fraternal correction, warnings, and if necessary, canonical sanctions.

Can. 1311 §1 states: "The Church has its own inherent right to constrain with penal sanctions Christ's faithful who commit offences."

And §2 of the same canon goes on to say: "The one who is at the head of a Church must safeguard and promote the good of the community itself and of each of Christ's faithful, through pastoral charity, example of life, advice and exhortation and, if necessary, also through the imposition or declaration of penalties, in accordance with the provisions of the law, which are always to be applied with canonical equity and having in mind the restoration of justice, the reform of the offender, and the repair of scandal."

Penal law governs the various means for obtaining those purposes of restoring justice, reforming the offender, and repairing scandal (see also canon 1341[^646]).

> It should not be forgotten that the salvation of (all) souls is present in all the Church's actions, including those actions of a juridical/legal nature.

**2. Notion of an offence**

An offence is an external sin of particular seriousness.

From canon 1321[^647] three necessary elements can be identified:

- **an objective element**: that is, the external sinful behaviour.

> The sin must consist of an action or omission perceivable by an outside observer (even if in fact no one actually witnesses it). Internal sins are therefore excluded, since they do not directly cause objectively-assessable social harm, even though they are an offence against God and wound the Church. Also, only God sees within the conscience of a person.

- **a subjective element**: this is called **imputability** and requires two conditions: a) that the person be at least 16 years of age and capable of understanding and willing; and b) that he have an "offensive" will, i.e. he knows that his conduct constitutes an offence and wishes to commit it (it is not sufficient that he knows it to be sinful: he must know that the Church considers it to be an offence).

> This "offensive will" is called *dolus* or malice. In certain cases, which must be expressly stated (e.g. canon 1378 §2[^648]) the "offensive will" takes the form of *culpa* or culpability, that is, grave negligence causing harm to others.

- **a legal element**: a law or precept stipulating that the external sinful conduct is an offence.

> All of these elements must be simultaneously present for there to be an offence.

**3. Circumstances which modify imputability**

**Excusing circumstances** are circumstances which altogether exclude imputability, and hence they exclude punishability. They are listed in canon 1323[^649].

> Some refer to the objective element (lawful self-defence; state of necessity, etc.), some to the subjective element (not having reached the age of 16; not having use of reason; ignorance of the penal law; acting under the impetus of a chance occurrence; etc.).

**Extenuating circumstances** are circumstances which affect the subjective or objective element of the offence. While not removing punishability, they render it less serious. They are given in canon 1324[^650].

> An important consequence of the presence of an extenuating circumstance is that the person who has committed a crime for which a *latae sententiae* penalty is prescribed does not receive that penalty (although he may be given another penalty after a judicial or administrative process).

**Aggravating circumstances** are circumstances increasing punishability. These are listed in canon 1326.

**4. Notion and purpose of canonical penalties**

Canonical penalties are sanctions imposed because of the commission of an offence. They consist of the privation of some good or right in the Church, and have the aim of bringing about the reform of the offender, the repair of scandal and the re-establishment of justice (see canon 1341[^651]).

The two major categories are

- **medicinal penalties or censures** (canons 1312 §1, 1º [^652]; 1331-1335[^653]);

- **expiatory penalties** (canons 1312 §1, 2º [^654]; 1336-1338[^655]).

The difference between them is that medicinal penalties aim at the reform of the offender, and are applied only until the "patient" is cured -- that is, until such time as the offender has repented and repaired the scandal (canon 1347 §2[^656]); while expiatory penalties are aimed principally at repairing the scandal and re-establishing justice. Their duration is independent of the reform of the offender.

> For example, if the penalty is for a month and the offender does not repent in that time, the penalty still ends; it also lasts for a month even if he repents within, say, a week.

Medicinal penalties can be of three types:

- **excommunication**: this is the most serious canonical penalty. Its effects are given in canon 1331, 1º [^657];

- **interdict**: this shares some of the characteristics of excommunication (see canon 1332[^658]);

- **suspension**: this can be applied only to clerics (see canon 1333[^659]).

Expiatory penalties can be of various types (canon 1336[^660]). The most serious is dismissal from the clerical state.

> Both medicinal penalties (censures) and expiatory penalties may be *latae sententiae* or *ferendae sententiae. Latae sententiae* means the offender automatically incurs the penalty, without the need for any process. *Ferendae sententiae* means the penalty is imposed after a judicial or administrative process.
>
> The Code sets out six *latae sententiae* excommunications for which remission is reserved to the Holy See:

- physical violence against the Roman Pontiff (canon 1370 §1[^661]);

- attempting to confer sacred ordination on a woman, or attempting to receive ordination as a woman (canon 1379 §3[^662]);

- profanation of the sacred species (canon 1382 §1[^663]);

- attempting to absolve an accomplice in a sin against the sixth commandment (canon 1384[^664]);

- direct violation of the sacramental seal (canon 1386 §1[^665]);

- episcopal ordination without pontifical mandate (canon 1387[^666]).

> NB: in the Eastern Code there are no *latae sententiae* penalties: all are *ferendae sententiae*.

In addition to penal sanctions properly so-called there are also **penal remedies and penances**, dealt with in canons 1339-1340[^667].

Penal remedies consist of warnings and corrections; penal precepts where warnings and corrections prove ineffective; and vigilance.

Penances take the form of an order to perform some act of religion, piety or charity. They can be used to replace a penalty when the dispositions of the guilty party and the circumstances so warrant (canons 1343[^668], 1344 2º [^669]). In some circumstances they may actually be added to a penalty (cf. canon 1326 §2[^670]).

**5. Types of offence**

Offences are grouped by the Code into the following categories:

- **offences against the faith and the unity of the Church** (canons 1364-1369):

  - apostasy, heresy and schism (canon 1364[^671])

  - teaching a condemned doctrine or rejecting teachings that are definitively proposed (canon 1365[^672])

  - appealing against an act of the Roman Pontiff to an Ecumenical Council or the College of Bishops (canon 1366[^673])

  - parents handing over their children to be baptised or brought up in a non-Catholic religion (canon 1367[^674])

  - publicly uttering blasphemy, or gravely harming public morals, or railing at or exciting hatred of or contempt for religion or the Church (canon 1368[^675])

  - profaning a sacred object (canon 1369[^676])

- **offences against Church authorities and the exercise of duties** (canons 1370-1378):

  - using physical force against the Roman Pontiff or a bishop, or against a cleric or religious or another of Christ's faithful out of contempt for the faith (canon 1370[^677])

  - disobeying a lawful command, violating obligations imposed by a penalty, committing perjury, violating the pontifical secret, failing to execute an executive sentence, neglecting to report an offence when required to do so (canon 1371[^678])

  - hindering the exercise of certain powers, ministries, or right of election (canon 1372[^679])

  - publicly inciting hatred or animosity against the Apostolic See or the Ordinary (canon 1373[^680])

  - joining or taking part in an association which plots against the Church (canon 1374[^681])

  - usurpation or unlawful retention of office (canon 1375[^682])

  - dishonest actions in relation to ecclesiastical goods (canon 1376[^683]): these include stealing ecclesiastical goods, impeding ecclesiastical goods so that their benefits are not realised; alienating ecclesiastical goods without the necessary consulation

  - bribery and corruption on the part of someone having an office or function in the Church (canon 1377[^684])

  - other abuses of ecclesiastical power (canon 1378[^685])

- **offences against the sacraments** (canons 1379-1389):

  - attempting to administer a sacrament when unable to do so (canon 1379[^686])

  - simony in relation to the sacraments (canon 1380[^687])

  - prohibited participation in religious rites (canon 1381[^688])

  - sacrilege in relation to the Eucharist (canon 1382[^689])

  - trafficking in Mass offerings (canon 1383[^690])

  - a priest absolving a partner in sin against the sixth commandment (canon 1384[^691])

  - solicitation in confession (canon 1385[^692])

  - violating the seal of confession (canon 1386[^693])

  - consecration of a bishop without a pontifical mandate (canon 1387[^694])

  - ordination without dimissorial letters, or concealing some censure irregularity or (canon 1388[^695])

  - unlawful exercise of the office of priest or some other ministry (canon 1389[^696])

- **offences against reputation and the offence of falsehood** (canons 1390-1391):

  - false denunciation to an ecclesiastical superior (canon 1390[^697])

  - forgery (canon 1391[^698])

- **offences against special obligations** (canons 1392-1396):

  - cleric voluntarily and unlawfully abandoning the sacred ministry (canon 1392[^699])

  - cleric or religious unlawfully engaging in business or trading (canon 1393[^700])

  - cleric or religious attempting marriage (canon 1394[^701])

  - cleric violating the sixth commandment (canon 1395[^702])

  - cleric violating the obligation of residence (canon 1396[^703])

- **offences against human life, dignity and liberty** (canons 1397-1398):

  - homicide, mutilation, abortion, etc. (canon 1397[^704])

  - abuse of minors or those who habitually have an imperfect use of reason (canon 1398[^705])

- **a grave violation of divine or canon law not included in the above** (canon 1399[^706]):

**\**
**CHAPTER XXXI:\
THE PROTECTION OF RIGHTS IN THE CHURCH\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> [Code of Canon Law](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dBfZuE0O4NTYPiaEdeUtdegdSEyK5YQM/view): Book VII, canons 1400-1752.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 10.
>
> John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution [*Divinus Perfectionis Magister*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_25011983_divinus-perfectionis-magister.html), 25 January 1983.
>
> Pontifical Council for Legal Texts, Instruction [*Dignitas Connubii*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/intrptxt/documents/rc_pc_intrptxt_doc_20050125_dignitas-connubii_en.html), 25 January 2005.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20060128_roman-rota.html), 28 January 2006.
>
> Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, Instruction [*Sanctorum Mater*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/csaints/documents/rc_con_csaints_doc_20070517_sanctorum-mater_en.html), 17 May 2007.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Letter *motu proprio* [*Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20150815_mitis-iudex-dominus-iesus.html), 15 August 2015.
>
> [*Norms regarding delicts reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20211011_norme-delittiriservati-cfaith_en.html), 2021 revision.
>
> Francis, Apostolic Letter [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html), 19 March 2022, nos. 197 §2, 200 §§2-3.

**1. Protection of individual rights in the Church**

The Church as an earthly society lays down laws to protect rights -- some of which are fundamental and exist prior to any law. Since rights may be violated, leading to a situation of injustice, there need to be mechanisms for guaranteeing practical justice and avoiding private defence, personal revenge, etc.

The Church is a communion, and needs to defend the bonds of communion. Accordingly she recognises the inviolable right of the faithful to take action in order to protect their rights by means of the structures and bodies established for that purpose (see canons 1491-1495[^707]).

> Canon 1476[^708] also recognises this right to those who are not baptised.

**2. Ecclesiastical power and the judicial function**

The ministerial priesthood involves the conferral of "sacred power" (see Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 10). The bishop governs his particular Church as a "vicar of Christ", with the legislative, executive and judicial power that he needs in order to fulfil that role.

He exercises his judicial power either personally or through others (canon 1419 §1[^709]). As was seen in chapter XIII, the bishop is to appoint a judicial vicar (*officialis*) with ordinary power to judge; he may also appoint assistant judicial vicars (canon 1420[^710]). In addition, he should appoint a promoter of justice and a defender of the bond (canons 1430-1437[^711]).

The diocesan tribunal may sometimes consist of a sole judge; at other times it will be a collegiate tribunal of three or five judges (these are used for causes of matrimonial nullity, holy orders, removal from the clerical state, and excommunication).

> The judges are to be clerics, although the Episcopal Conference may allow a lay judge in a collegiate tribunal (canons 1421[^712]); in marriage nullity cases the bishop can appoint two lay judges to a college of three judges, with a cleric heading the college (canon 1673 §3[^713]).
>
> The Code of Canon Law contains a number of provisions designed to help the parties reach agreement other than through a formal trial: see canon 1446[^714], and the specific examples in canons 1659 §1[^715] and 1733[^716].

**3. Canonical processes or trials**

A canonical process or trial (the terms are used interchangeably) may be defined as a series of formal juridical acts carried out before a tribunal, in respect of a legal claim presented in the form prescribed by law, with a view to obtaining a binding decision or declaration.

The main parties in the trial are the "petitioner" (plaintiff) and the "respondent" (defendant): see canons 1476-1480[^717]. In most cases the parties can act either in person or through a legal representative (advocate). A party who lacks the capacity to take part in a trial (e.g. a minor) needs to act through a procurator.

> On the purpose of the trial, see Pope Benedict XVI's [*Address to the Roman Rota*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/january/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20060128_roman-rota.html), 28 January 2006.
>
> The rules on procurators and advocates are given in canons 1481-1490[^718].

**4. Kinds of trial**

**a) Ordinary contentious trials**

These are based primarily on written documentation, and are dealt with in the extensive section of the Code from canon 1501 to canon 1655.

The main phases in the trial are:

- the introductory phase (canons 1501-1517);

- the "instruction" phase, including the obtaining of proofs and declarations from the parties and witnesses (canons 1526-1586);

- publication of the acts and discussion of the case (canons 1598-1606);

- the pronouncements of the judge (canons 1607-1618).

> Canons 1619-1648 set out the various ways in which the judgment may be challenged.

**b) Oral contentious trials**

These are dealt with in canons 1656-1670. They may be used in simpler cases, such as those involving the separation of spouses (canon 1693); however, they may not be used for cases concerning the bond of sacred ordination or nullity of marriage.

> The focal point in such trials is the hearing (canons 1661-1668) in which evidence is collected and the case immediately discussed. Several of the formalities of the ordinary contentious trial are omitted.

**c) Special processes:**

- **matrimonial processes**: canons 1671-1706.

> In practice these form the vast majority of cases dealt with by the tribunals. At first sight there appear to be relatively few canons devoted to them; however, they are governed by the canons on ordinary contentious trials, with certain particular features of their own, including:

- the necessary participation of the defender of the bond;

- the right of advocates, the defender of the bond and the promoter of justice to be present at the examination of the parties and witnesses and to inspect the documents and acts;

- the expert testimony that is required in some cases;

- the possibility of an abbreviated process in certain circumstances;

- in the case of an appeal, the possibility of the second instance tribunal confirming the first instance decision by decree if the appeal clearly appears merely dilatory; otherwise the second instance tribunal proceeds in the same manner as the first instance with the appropriate adjustments;

- the possibility of adding a new ground at appeal stage "as at first instance".

> In 2015, Pope Francis, by means of the *motu proprio* [*Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20150815_mitis-iudex-dominus-iesus.html), reformed canons 1671-1691[^719] in order to achieve -- as he stated in that document -- "a more streamlined and readily accessible judicial process".
>
> Canons 1688-1690 allow the possibility of a more rapid documentary matrimonial process, where it can be proved with certainty on the basis of documents that the marriage is invalid because of impediment, lack of form or lack of proxy mandate (see canon 1105[^720]).
>
> A summary of the entire law on matrimonial processes is provided in the Pontifical Council for Legal Texts' Instruction *[Dignitas Connubii](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/pontifical_councils/intrptxt/documents/rc_pc_intrptxt_doc_20050125_dignitas-connubii_en.html)* of 25 January 2005 (as amended by *[Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/papa-francesco-motu-proprio_20150815_mitis-iudex-dominus-iesus.html))*.

- **processes for the nullity of sacred ordination**: canons 1708-1712[^721].

> These follow the ordinary contentious process, but require the presence of the defender of the bond. A process of this kind requires the prior consent of the Congregation for the Clergy.
>
> During the trial the cleric is prohibited from exercising orders.
>
> The Apostolic Letter [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html), 19 March 2022, no. 200 §3, provides that these cases are to be dealt with by a new office within the Roman Rota.

- **penal processes**: canons 1717-1731[^722].

> Before a penal process begins there must be a preliminary investigation (canons 1717-1719). The bishop then needs to decide whether to proceed in a judicial or extra-judicial manner:

- the extra-judicial process involves notifying the accused of the accusation, and giving him the possibility of defence. The bishop is assisted by two assessors in weighing up the proofs and arguments. The outcome of the process may be a penal decree;

- the judicial process follows the canons on ordinary trials, except that it is only the promoter of justice who may initiate a penal action; an advocate is always obligatory, and the accused is entitled to write or speak last. Canons 1729-1731 deal with the possibility of an action for damages;

- specific provisions apply in respect of the "more serious offences" ("*graviora delicta*") included in the 2021 revision of the [*Norms regarding delicts reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/cfaith/documents/rc_con_cfaith_doc_20211011_norme-delittiriservati-cfaith_en.html).

- **other kinds of (non-contentious) process**: the Code contains provisions for:

- *processes for the separation of spouses:* canons 1692-1696[^723];

- *processes for dispensation from a ratified and non-consummated marriage:* canons 1697-1706[^724]; these cases are to be dealt with by the new office of the Roman Rota (see [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html), no. 200 §2);

- *processes for the declaration of the death of a spouse:* canon 1707[^725];

- *processes for causes of canonisation of servants of God:* canon 1403[^726].

> The last category is not regulated by the Code, but by particular pontifical law, namely the Apostolic Constitution [*Divinus Perfectionis Magister*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_25011983_divinus-perfectionis-magister.html) (25 January 1983) and the Instruction [*Sanctorum Mater*](https://www.vatican.va/roman_curia/congregations/csaints/documents/rc_con_csaints_doc_20070517_sanctorum-mater_en.html) (17 May 2007).

**5. Competence and plurality of instances**

The first hearing of a case ("first instance") normally takes place at the diocesan tribunal.

> In some cases dioceses may share a tribunal (canon 1423[^727]); it is also possible for a case to be heard at first instance by the Roman Rota or the Roman Pontiff (canon 1405[^728]).

The second instance or appeal tribunal is the one above that of first instance. If a case is heard at first instance by a diocesan tribunal, the Metropolitan tribunal is the second instance tribunal. Cases heard at first instance by the Metropolitan tribunal go to the second instance tribunal which has been designated for that purpose with the approval of the Holy See.

> A tribunal cannot act at first and second instance in same case. An exception to this is the Roman Rota, in which a different set of judges (or *turnus*) can hear the same case at a higher instance.

The Apostolic Tribunals (the Roman Rota and Apostolic Signatura) can also hear cases at third or higher instance.

In order to be able to hear a case, a tribunal must be "competent" (see canons 1404-1416[^729]). If a judge hears a case which is the competence of another, the sentence may be null: see canon 1620[^730].

> A distinction is drawn between "absolute" and "relative" competence. A case heard by a judge with absolute lack of competence (see for example canons 1404-1405) is irremediably null (canon 1620, 1º).
>
> In cases of relative incompetence (e.g. a marriage case being heard by a tribunal not listed in canon 1672[^731]; see canon 1407 §2) the judgment is not rendered null.

**6. Administrative justice in the Church**

"Administrative justice" is the name given to the system of reviewing acts of the administrative power in order to see whether they are in accordance with justice.

A party who feels harmed or aggrieved by an administrative act may, so long as he or she has a "just motive", challenge the act before the person who issued it, or before that person's superior (this is an *administrative* procedure known as "hierarchical recourse", details of which are set out in canons 1732-1739[^732]).

Once the hierarchical recourse has been exhausted (i.e. when a decision has been given by the appropriate Dicastery of the Holy See) there is then the possibility of a *judicial* action before the Apostolic Signatura (see [*Praedicate Evangelium*](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/apost_constitutions/documents/20220319-costituzione-ap-praedicate-evangelium.html), no. 197 §2; canon 1445 §2).

> The Apostolic Signatura judges as to whether the act being impugned violated some law, either in the decision-making process or in the procedure employed. At the request of the plaintiff, it can also judge concerning the reparation of possible damages incurred through the act in question.

**\**
**CHAPTER XXXII:\
THE CHURCH AND THE POLITICAL COMMUNITY\**

> READINGS FOR THIS CHAPTER
>
> Boniface III, Bull [*Unam Sanctam*](https://www.papalencyclicals.net/bon08/b8unam.htm), 18 November 1302.
>
> John XXIII, Encyclical [*Pacem in Terris*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-xxiii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_j-xxiii_enc_11041963_pacem.html), 11 April 1963.
>
> Vatican II, Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), 7 December 1965, nos. 36, 76.
>
> Vatican II, Dogmatic Constitution on the Church [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), 21 November 1964, no. 36.
>
> Vatican II, Decree on Religious Freedom [*Dignitatis Humanae*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651207_dignitatis-humanae_en.html), 7 December 1965.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Address to the President of the Italian Republic*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/november/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20061120_italian-president.html), 20 November 2006.
>
> Benedict XVI, *[General Audience](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/audiences/2008/documents/hf_ben-xvi_aud_20080917.html#:~:text=The%20Visit%20began%20in%20Paris,played%20a%20fundamental%20civilizing%20role.)* 17 September 2008.
>
> Benedict XVI, [*Address to the representatives of British society, Westminster Hall*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2010/september/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20100917_societa-civile.html), 17 September 2010.

**1. Christian dualism**

The topic of the relationship between the Catholic Church and the political community is hardly a new one, as twenty centuries of history demonstrate.

For a correct understanding of the question, the starting point needs to be that of "Christian dualism", which asserts that the Church, in so far as it claims to be an external and visible society in this world, with its own hierarchy for the attainment of purely spiritual ends, breaks away from the ancient "monism" which would place all public matters, including religious matters, under the authority of a single power. With Christianity there arises the notion of a society which considers itself to be different from the political society, and therefore not subject to the political society as far as its own proper ends are concerned. Hence we see how in the early Church, Christians would refuse to comply with the religious duties imposed by the Emperor.

Christian dualism is based on various New Testament texts, most notably that in *Mt* 22:21: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (see also *Mk* 12:17; *Lk* 20:25).

Other texts in the writings of St Peter and St Paul indicate the Christian duty to obey the lawful authority (see *Rom* 13:1-7; *1 Pet* 2:13-14). There is also the statement of Peter and John before the Sanhedrin: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge" (*Acts* 4:20).

Thus there exist two different societies -- that of the Church and that of the political community -- each with its own ends and means, and each with autonomy and independence in its own sphere. The human person, however, is not divided, but belongs simultaneously to both societies. Accordingly there needs to be a harmonious relationship between them.

The first theoretical exposition of Christian dualism is found in a number of documents written by Pope Gelasius I to the Eastern Roman Emperor Anastasius I, in which he explains that there are two societies, two powers, one relating to ecclesiastical life and its own proper ends (the salvation of souls), the other with competences relating to the temporal common good. In spiritual matters the ecclesiastical authority was superior to the civil authority; and in what pertained to the temporal authority, the Pastors of the Church owed obedience to the lawful authority.

To achieve this balance has not proved easy; and throughout history there have been deviations from the principle and attempts to install "monism" of different sorts -- the notion that there should be only one principle of power, whether ecclesiastical or political.

An example of this is "Caesaropapism", of which the Emperor Constantine is one of the clearest exponents. After granting the Church her freedom in 313AD, by the Edict of Milan, he imposed himself as her protector and assumed functions and competences of a religious nature (appointment of bishops, interference in the internal organisation of Church life and even in matters of doctrine) which in practice constituted a denial of the Church's independence.

The Caesaropapist model remained in force in the East until the invasion of the Turks in the fifteenth century. In the West, the tendency was in the opposite direction: with the fall of the Roman Empire it was bishops and clergy who acquired a fundamental role in political life, since the Church was effectively the only respectable and respected authority. This however did not prevent the emergence of new forms of Caesaropapism, especially under Charlemagne and the Holy Roman Empire. In this context the Church fought for freedom to exercise her spiritual mission without interference by the secular powers, giving rise to the famous investiture controversy, in which the Popes challenged the monarchs' authority to appoint bishops. The controversy was resolved by means of the Concordat of Worms between Pope Calixtus II and the Emperor Henry V (1122) which laid the foundations for more harmonious relations between the two powers.

> The Concordat of Worms did not prevent the conflict between St Thomas Becket and King Henry II of England over the rights and privileges of the Church, leading ultimately to the Saint's assassination in 1170.

Of great significance in this regard is the Bull *[Unam Sanctam](https://www.papalencyclicals.net/bon08/b8unam.htm)* of Pope Boniface III in 1302, in which the superiority of the spiritual power over the temporal is asserted, so that the power of monarchs was subject to the jurisdiction of the Church, in so far as it was for the ecclesiastical power to judge concerning sins and absolve them. This competence *ratione peccati --* in view of the possible "sinfulness" of political actions -- was taken to mean that the Church could enter into an analysis of governmental acts that might appear unjust, and put forward the correct solution.

There is no recognition here of what we would call today the "autonomy of earthly affairs". Nevertheless, St Thomas Aquinas -- even amid the high prestige which the Church enjoyed in the earthly realm -- expounded the existence and autonomy of the natural law, and this was to provide the basis for subsequent developments.

The dominant influence of the Church in political matters was thrown into crisis by the emergence of national States, the Papacy's loss of prestige, the exile at Avignon, the Eastern schism, "conciliarist" doctrines (which taught that the Pope was subject to the decisions of councils), and the secularisation of political power. All of these factors favoured the return of interference by the political power in ecclesiastical matters.

**2. The Protestant view of Church-State relations**

One of the chief principles of the reforming Protestants (Luther, Calvin, Zwingli, etc.) was that of *sola Scriptura*, which affirmed that only the Bible was the source of knowledge of God's will. Since it was for each one to ponder over the Bible freely, the idea of a Church with unity of faith and worship, governed by a hierarchy with the Pope at its head, was rejected. Such rejection of the juridical and hierarchical Church was symbolised by Luther's burning of the *[Corpus Iuris Canonici](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04391a.htm)* along with the bull by which he was excommunicated.

As a result, the notion of Christian dualism lost its meaning; and those countries which embraced the Reformation fell into radical "monism", whereby the monarch was supreme even in spiritual matters.

The principle *cuius regio eius religio*, according to which the people followed the religion of their ruler (Peace of Augsburg, 1555; Peace of Westphalia, 1648), and which was established as a solution to the wars of religion, helped forge the idea of the confessional State, whether Protestant or Catholic.

**3. Regalism in Catholic countries**

Although in theory their Catholic identity obliged them to respect Christian dualism, in practice the rulers of Catholic countries intervened to a notable extent in ecclesiastical affairs. Under different names, this system took hold in Spain ("Regalism"), France ("Gallicanism"), Italy ("Jurisdictionalism"), Germany ("Febronianism") Austria ("Josephinism"), etc.

The foundation for these systems was the teaching that all power comes ultimately from God. This however was taken to the extreme of affirming that such power was entrusted directly and immediately by God to the Sovereign, thus not only reinforcing the Sovereign's temporal authority but also giving rise to the notion of the "divine right of kings" to intervene in ecclesiastical affairs.

Nevertheless, in addition to what St Thomas Aquinas had written in the thirteenth century, the teachings of theologians and jurists such as Francisco de Vitoria, Robert Bellarmine and Francisco Suárez helped to form the doctrine of the indirect power of the Church in temporal matters, with a clearer distinction being drawn between the spiritual and temporal orders.

**4. The Enlightenment and liberalism**

The Enlightenment period saw the emergence of ideas of tolerance in religious affairs in the face of absolutist regimes, leading to "Declarations of Rights" as formulations of individual freedoms before the political authority. The most famous of these declarations are those that followed the American and French Revolutions, although there are important differences between them.

The Declaration of Virginia (1776) considered religion as something positive and aimed to provide protection for the different manifestations of religious belief, so as to overcome the intolerances of the old Continent, the State declaring itself incompetent to intervene in religious matters. The French "Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen" (1789), on the other hand, aimed to overcome the absolutist and confessional Catholic State and proposed the "laicity" of the State, with a negative view of religion and a positive view of agnosticism. The consequence was a sort of special law of religion issuing from the State, that often did violence to the structure -- and in some cases the very existence -- of religious groups.

Not surprisingly this caused the Roman Pontiffs to oppose the concept of liberalism, which (quite apart from the religious persecutions to which it gave rise) "relativised" the idea of truth and of religious dogmas, denying the existence of an objective moral order. For liberalism, the religious aspect was restricted solely to the interior of the person.

Thus there were doctrinal as well as practical reasons for the Church's initial opposition to the separation of Church and State. Nevertheless, when the doctrine of separation shed its markedly anti-ecclesiastical and doctrinally belligerent characteristics, the Church's attitude softened, as can be seen in the case of the Belgian Constitution of 1831, and Pope Leo XIII's favourable attitude to the separation of Church and State in the USA.

Amid these developments, the Popes from the time of Leo XIII developed the doctrine of the Christian notion of the State. One of its first principles was the reaffirmation of Christian dualism, with the consequent defence of the Church's independence as before the State. At the same time, it stressed the duties of the State towards religion and the need to respect the right and duty to give worship to God (including public worship) and to influence laws and State activity in a Christian manner. Leo XIII was aware that many countries were very distant from these principles, and called on Catholics to make themselves present in political life and thus attempt to imbue the workings of the State with Christian values.

In this context the Church reaffirmed the traditional doctrine which considered the ideal to be the confessional State, understood as the conception of public life as being based on the existence of God and on his Revelation of a number of truths which cannot be ignored or set aside. Man and society have the duty to give worship to God; and this worship should be the true worship, as contained in the one true Catholic religion.

This concept of the confessional State was to be tempered by a consideration of the concrete circumstances in which the doctrine was to be applied. As regards the juridical position of non-Catholic religious groups, recourse was to be had to the doctrine of tolerance (without however renouncing the difference between truth and error). For proportionate reasons erroneous opinions might be tolerated, without in any way approving error, since it might be prudent not to impede error, in order that a greater good might follow.

**5. The Church's Magisterium leading up to Vatican II**

In the first half of the twentieth century Pope Leo XIII's doctrine was substantially ratified by his successors up to Pius XII. The prevailing totalitarian ideologies and the damage they caused led the Magisterium to look more deeply into the dignity and rights of the human person, using arguments from Revelation and from natural law which were understood and accepted by all. At the same time the importance of the lay apostolate in order to Christianise a secularised and pluralist society was becoming ever more clear.

The pontificate of Pope John XXIII marked an important turning point in Church-State relations. In his Encyclical [*Pacem in Terris*](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-xxiii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_j-xxiii_enc_11041963_pacem.html) (1963) he gave a positive evaluation of human rights, which are based on the fact that each human being is a person, that is, a nature endowed with intellect and free will. Among the rights listed in the Encyclical are those of honouring God according to the dictates of an upright conscience, and therefore the right to honour God in private and in public. Religious freedom is thus based on natural rights, and not on liberal relativism.

> These arguments are based on natural law and not on Revelation, but it should not be forgotten that the traditional Christian dualism is based not only on natural law but also on divine-positive law.

**6. The teaching of Vatican II**

The Second Vatican Council devoted a significant degree of attention to the question of the relationship of the Church to political communities. On the one hand it delved more deeply into the nature of the Church, and on the other it took very much into account the reality of a society which was increasingly sensitive to the rights of the person. On these premises it once more set out the principles of Christian dualism, from a number of perspectives.

**a) The autonomy of earthly affairs**

The Pastoral Constitution [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 36, sets out the principles of the autonomy of earthly affairs and the responsibility of Catholics in building up the political community: "If by the autonomy of earthly affairs we mean that created things and societies themselves enjoy their own laws and values which must be gradually deciphered, put to use, and regulated by men, then it is entirely right to demand that autonomy. Such is not merely required by modern man, but harmonises also with the will of the Creator. For by the very circumstance of their having been created, all things are endowed with their own stability, truth, goodness, proper laws and order. Man must respect these as he isolates them by the appropriate methods of the individual sciences or arts".

**b) Distinction and cooperation between the Church and the political community**

From the Dogmatic Constitution [*Lumen Gentium*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19641121_lumen-gentium_en.html), no. 36, and [*Gaudium et Spes*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_const_19651207_gaudium-et-spes_en.html), no. 76, the following conclusions can be arrived at:

- the Church reaffirms her traditional dualism in so far as she considers herself and the State to be independent and autonomous societies;

- this autonomy is based on the different natures of the two societies, since the Church is a society of the supernatural order and has as its aim the salvation of souls, whereas the political community is of the natural order and has as its aim the temporal common good;

- although they are of different natures, they are not isolated from each other such as to justify ignoring each other, since they share a common origin -- God, the author of the natural and supernatural orders -- and serve the same human persons.

> In an [*Address to the President of the Italian Republic*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2006/november/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20061120_italian-president.html), 20 November 2006, Pope Benedict stated: "Yes, Church and State, although quite distinct, are both called, in accordance with their respective roles and their own scope and means, to serve the human being, who is both the object of the Church's saving mission and a participator in it, as well as a citizen of the State. It is in man that these two societies meet and collaborate, the better to promote the integral good."

- the ecclesiastical hierarchy, in carrying out its specific mission, exercises true power over believers. As regards earthly affairs, its mission is to set out principles and provide moral judgements as part of its role of teaching the way of salvation, which includes the need to follow the precepts of the natural law.

> See the [*Address*](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/speeches/2010/september/documents/hf_ben-xvi_spe_20100917_societa-civile.html) of Benedict XVI at Westminster Hall, 17 September 2010, in which the Pope pointed out that religion "is not a problem for legislators to solve, but a vital contributor to the national conversation. In this light, I cannot but voice my concern at the increasing marginalisation of religion, particularly of Christianity, that is taking place in some quarters, even in nations which place a great emphasis on tolerance. There are those who would advocate that the voice of religion be silenced, or at least relegated to the purely private sphere. There are those who argue that the public celebration of festivals such as Christmas should be discouraged, in the questionable belief that it might somehow offend those of other religions or none. And there are those who argue -- paradoxically with the intention of eliminating discrimination -- that Christians in public roles should be required at times to act against their conscience. These are worrying signs of a failure to appreciate not only the rights of believers to freedom of conscience and freedom of religion, but also the legitimate role of religion in the public square. I would invite all of you, therefore, within your respective spheres of influence, to seek ways of promoting and encouraging dialogue between faith and reason at every level of national life"; going on say; "Your readiness to do so is already implied in the unprecedented invitation extended to me today."

- both the State and the Church seek to serve the human person: hence there is an area of juridical relations which affects both societies, and which according to the practice of the Church and of several nations can be formalised by means of Concordats.

**c) Religious freedom**

The Second Vatican Council dedicated an entire document, the Declaration [*Dignitatis Humanae*](https://www.vatican.va/archive/hist_councils/ii_vatican_council/documents/vat-ii_decl_19651207_dignitatis-humanae_en.html), to the question of religious freedom. In no. 2 it states: "This Vatican Council declares that the human person has a right to religious freedom. This freedom means that all men are to be immune from coercion on the part of individuals or of social groups and of any human power, in such wise that no one is to be forced to act in a manner contrary to his own beliefs, whether privately or publicly, whether alone or in association with others, within due limits. The Council further declares that the right to religious freedom has its foundation in the very dignity of the human person as this dignity is known through the revealed word of God and by reason itself. This right of the human person to religious freedom is to be recognised in the constitutional law whereby society is governed and thus it is to become a civil right."

> See also no. 6 of the same document.

Without abandoning the traditional teaching on Christian dualism, the Council is allowing for the fact that this should not be understood solely as a question of the relationship between the temporal and spiritual "powers", but must also be looked at from the perspective of the human person, open at the same time to the supernatural order and the natural order."

> In a *[General Audience](https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/audiences/2008/documents/hf_ben-xvi_aud_20080917.html#:~:text=The%20Visit%20began%20in%20Paris,played%20a%20fundamental%20civilizing%20role.)* on 17 September 2008, shortly after his visit to France, Pope Benedict commented: "The Visit began in Paris, where I met in spirit the entire French people, thereby paying homage to a beloved nation in which, since the second century, the Church has played a fundamental civilising role. It is interesting that precisely in this context the need developed for a healthy distinction between the political and religious spheres in accordance with Jesus' famous words: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (*Mk* 12:17). However, if the image of Caesar was stamped on Roman coins which for this reason were to be rendered to him, the human heart bears the imprint of the Creator, the one Lord of our life. Genuine secularism does not mean, therefore, leaving the spiritual dimension out of consideration but rather recognising that it is precisely this that radically guarantees our freedom and the autonomy of earthly realities, thanks to the dictates of creative Wisdom which the human conscience is capable of accepting and actuating."

? QUESTIONS

1\. What are the fundamental principles at the heart of the Vatican II's teaching on the relationship between the Church and political communities?

2\. On what considerations should true religious freedom be based?

    **Can. 127 §1** When the law prescribes that, in order to perform a juridical act, a Superior requires the consent or the advice of some college or group of persons, the college or group must be convened in accordance with can. 166, unless, if there is question of seeking advice only, particular or proper law provides otherwise. For the validity of the act, it is required that the consent be obtained of an absolute majority of those present, or that the advice of all be sought.

    **§2** When the law prescribes that, in order to perform a juridical act, a Superior requires the consent or advice of certain persons as individuals:

    **1°** if consent is required, the Superior's act is invalid if the Superior does not seek the consent of those persons, or acts against the vote of all or of any of them;

    **2°** if advice is required, the Superior's act is invalid if the Superior does not hear those persons. The Superior is not in any way bound to accept their vote, even if it is unanimous; nevertheless, without what is, in his or her judgement, an overriding reason, the Superior is not to act against their vote, especially if it is a unanimous one.

    **§3** All whose consent or advice is required are obliged to give their opinions sincerely. If the seriousness of the matter requires it, they are obliged carefully to maintain secrecy, and the Superior can insist on this obligation.

    **Can. 128** Whoever unlawfully causes harm to another by a juridical act, or indeed by any other act which is deceitful or culpable, is obliged to repair the damage done.

[^152]: **Can. 87** **§2** If recourse to the Holy See is difficult, and at the same time there is danger of grave harm in delay, any Ordinary can dispense from these laws, even if the dispensation is reserved to the Holy See, provided the dispensation is one which the Holy See customarily grants in the same circumstances, and without prejudice to can. 291 \[i.e. it does not extend to a dispensation from celibacy\].

[^153]: **Can. 1060** Marriage enjoys the favour of law. Consequently, in doubt the validity of a marriage must be upheld until the contrary is proven.

[^154]: **Can. 1084 §2** If the impediment of impotence is doubtful, whether the doubt be one of law or one of fact, the marriage is not to be prevented nor, while the doubt persists, is it to be declared null.

[^155]: **Can 15 §2** Ignorance or error is not presumed about a law, a penalty, a fact concerning oneself, or a notorious fact concerning another. It is presumed about a fact concerning another which is not notorious, until the contrary is proved.

[^156]: **Can. 144 §1** In common error, whether of fact or of law, and in positive and probable doubt, whether of law or of fact, the Church supplies executive power of governance for both the external and the internal forum.

    **§2** The same norm applies to the faculties mentioned in cann. 883, 966, and 1111 §1.

[^157]: **Can. 883** The following have, by law, the faculty to administer confirmation:

    **1°** within the confines of their jurisdiction, those who in law are equivalent to a diocesan Bishop;

    **2°** in respect of the person to be confirmed, the priest who by virtue of his office or by mandate of the diocesan Bishop baptises an adult or admits a baptised adult into full communion with the Catholic Church;

    **3°** in respect of those in danger of death, the parish priest or indeed any priest.

[^158]: **Can. 966 §1** For the valid absolution of sins, it is required that, in addition to the power of order, the minister has the faculty to exercise that power in respect of the faithful to whom he gives absolution.

    **§2** A priest can be given this faculty either by the law itself, or by a concession issued by the competent authority in accordance with can. 969.
